William E. Glenn (who read the paper) and Carvel Holton are with the Communications Technology Center, Florida Atlantic University, Boca Raton, Fla.
G. J. Dixon is with the Center for Research and Education in Optics and Lasers (CREOL), University of Central Florida, Orlando, Fla.
Philip J. Bos is with the Liquid Crystal Institute, Kent State University, Kent, Ohio.

William E. Glenn is Director of the NASA Space Communications Technology Center, as well as Distinguished Research Professor, Motorola Endowed Professor for Electrical and Computer Engineering, and Director of the Imaging Systems Laboratory, all at Florida Atlantic University (FAU) in Boca Raton. The ISL and SCTC specialize in advanced imaging and communications technology. — Dr. Glenn received a B.E.E. from the Georgia Institute of Technology, and M.S. and Ph.D. degrees in electrical engineering from the University of California at Berkeley. Previously, he served as Director of the NYIT Science and Technology Research Center and as vice-president and director of research at CBS Laboratories, where he worked very closely with Dr. Dennis Gabor, a Nobel Prize winner, on systems using holographic techniques. Prior to that time, Dr. Glenn was on the staff of the General Electric Research Laboratory, where he developed two totally new types of electro-optical imaging systems, the light-valve Talaria projector and thermoplastic recording. — Dr. Glenn is a Fellow of the SMPTE. He currently holds 110 U.S. patents and has written or co-authored over 65 technical papers in the areas of imaging and communications technology. In 1991 he was recognized with the Society's Agfa-Gevaert Gold Medal Award for his contributions in the research and development of imaging systems. Glenn has served on the Advanced Television Standards Committee (ATSC) since 1980, and on the FCC Advisory Committee to recommend terrestrial HDTV broadcast standards since 1987.

Carvel E. Holton is a research associate at the Fiber and Electro-Optics Research Center, Virginia Polytechnic and State University, Blacksburg, Va. He holds B.S.E.E. and M.S.E.E. degrees in electrical engineering and electro-physics from the University of Maryland. Holton was involved in the development of state-of-the-art electronics, electro-optics, and systems as a member of the staff of the Naval Surface Warfare Center. He served as senior engineer at the U.S. Naval Academy, United Technologies Research Center, United Technologies Optical Systems, and the Imaging Systems Laboratory at Florida Atlantic University before joining the Fiber and Electro-Optics Research Center at Virginia Tech. — His experience in electronics includes significant design and program work in digital circuits, analog circuits, RF circuits, and instrumentation systems. In electro-optics, he has participated in the development of numerous instrumentation systems based on visible and IR lasers, including CO2 and fiber-optic based lasers and systems. Holton has most recently participated in the development of diffractive liquid crystal projectors based on arc and laser sources at FAU. Holton is a member of SID and SPIE and has published in such diverse areas as hydrodynamics research, liquid crystal projection systems, and Lidar systems.

G. J. Dixon is on the faculty of the Center of Research and Education in Optics and Lasers (CREOL) at the University of Central Florida in Orlando where his group has developed a number of new diode-pumped solid-state lasers, including the pump-resonant sum frequency laser and the mid-IRA intra-cavity difference frequency laser. He holds a B.S. in physics from Eckerd College, a B.S. in electrical engineering from the University of Tennessee, an M.S. in applied physics from Stanford University, and a Ph.D. in electrical engineering from the University of South Florida. — While a student at Stanford, Dixon was involved in the early development of intracavity-doubled diode-pumped solid-state lasers. He then worked for Amoco Laser Co. on diode-pumped visible lasers. Since 1990 he has been on the faculty of CREOL. — Dr. Dixon currently serves on the Editorial Advisory Board of Laser Focus World and is a member of the Industrial Design Society of America. He holds 16 patents in the areas of diode-pumped solid-state lasers and resonant nonlinear frequency conversion.

Philip J. Bos is Associate Professor at Kent State University in Kent, Ohio. He received his Ph.D. in physics from Kent State in the area of orientational order of liquid crystals. Dr. Bos worked in the display research department of the corporate research laboratories of Tektronix Inc. from 1979 to 1993, following which he received a joint appointment as senior research fellow at the Liquid Crystal Institute and associate professor of chemical physics at Kent State University. His area of interest is applications of liquid crystals, and he has made contributions in the areas of fast switching devices, wide viewing angle devices, bistable smectic and nematic devices, and polymer stabilized devices.

Wiliam Y. Zou holds a B.S. degree in electrical engineering from Shanghai University, Shanghai, China, and an M.S. degree in electrical engineering from the State University of New York at Binghamton. From 1984 to 1986, Zou was employed by Shanghai Television Broadcasting Technology Research Institute as a design engineer. In 1988 he joined the Public Broadcasting Service (PBS) in Alexandria, Va., as a communication systems engineer. His current work includes HDTV, digital compression and transmission, subjective and objective video performance assessment, signal processing, and communications systems. He is actively involved in testing digital television systems for PBS and its member stations, as well as in HDTV standards development in the U.S. — Zou is a senior member of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) and a member of the SMPTE. He currently serves on the Board of Editors for the SMPTE Journal.

James A. Kutzner is currently vice-president of operations and engineering at Twin Cities Public Television in Saint Paul, Minn. In this capacity he is responsible for all technical operations including program production, post-production, broadcast and satellite communication, maintenance, and technical development. In addition, Kutzner chairs the PBS Engineering Committee and participates in other public television management and engineering activities. — Previously, Kutzner was associate director, engineering development, at PBS. He was instrumental in the development of the compressed video, audio, and data delivery system for PBS, which was inaugurated in February 1994. He was also instrumental in the early development of the Local Insertion System, a digitally based network control system for PBS and member stations. He served as Secretary on the FCC's ACATS Field Test Task Force, and on various ATV/DTV committees. Kutzner has also chaired SMPTE's Studio System Design Working Group (WG-SSD), which investigated design models for future digital television production plants and broadcast facilities. — Kutzner holds a B.E.E. degree from the University of Minnesota and is a member of IEEE and SMPTE.

David J. Bancroft is with Philips Digital Video Systems, U.K.

Dave Bancroft is business and technology development manager for the Film Imaging Group of Philips Digital Video Systems. Although his group is based in Weiterstadt, Germany, Bancroft operates out of the U.K. and contributes to long-term projects, such as DTV production, in the U.S. Bancroft began his career in broadcast engineering at the BBC in London, where he received his fundamental training and became an operations and maintenance engineer on outside broadcasts. He became particularly interested in videotape recording and related mechanical wonders and this led to an international odyssey, which kept him away from the U.K. for 20 years. During this time, he worked for RCA in Germany, Ampex Corp. in Greece, the Middle East, Africa, New York, and California. He joined Philips Digital Video Systems, or as it was formerly known, BTS, in 1992, with the assignment of HDTV marketing in Darmstadt. He moved his desk back to the U.K. in 1995 and took up his present position with Philips in 1997. Bancroft is a long-time member of SMPTE, where he represents Philips in several technology committees. He is an International Member of SMPTE's Executive Standards Committee. He is also a member of the Royal Television Society and the BKSTS in the U.K.

Steve Lyman and Craig Todd are with Dolby Laboratorie, San Francisco

Steve Lyman began his career designing custom audio equipment for a recording studio and for a console manufacturer. He joined the Canadian Broadcasting Corp. in 1980 and developed a system of standard audio and video measurement techniques. He was heavily involved with CBC's efforts to implement HDTV, digital audio broadcasting, and other new technologies. In 1996, he moved to the Research and Business Development department of Dolby Laboratories to help implement multichannel audio systems for digital television broadcasting. Lyman, a Fellow of the AES has been involved in the development of audio and video standards within that Society, the IEEE, and SMPTE throughout his career.

Craig Todd, currently senior member of the technical staff, has been with Dolby Laboratories for more than 20 years, He has been involved with the development of multichannel sound for over 20 years, beginning with his work on the Dolby Surround Sound matrix system. More recently he has worked on the development of technology for digital audio coding and broadcasting. For the last several years, Todd has concentrated on multichannel digital audio for television. The result of his efforts is the Dolby Digital (AC-3) coding technology, and its acceptance, by the U.S. HDTV Grand Alliance and the FCC Advisory Committee, for incorporation into the U.S. HDTV broadcast standard. Todd is active in many standards activities, including ATSC, DVB, IEC, AES, ITU, CEMA, and SMPTE. He is a Fellow of the AES, and is currently Chairman of ITU-R Working Party 10C.

Gregory Cermak specializes in applied psychophysics, using physical measures of perceptual stimuli to predict subjective responses by consumers. In addition to work on compressed video stimuli at the GTE Laboratories, he has conducted similar studies of speech quality there; and studies of traffic noise and acoustical measures, visual air quality and optical measures, and visual properties of painted surfaces and optical measures at the General Motors Research Laboratories. He has a Ph.D. in mathematical psychology from Stanford University.

Stephen Wolf received a B.S. in electrical engineering from Montana State University in 1979 and an M.S. in electrical and computer engineering from the University of California at Santa Barbara in 1983. From 1979 until 1988, he worked in design and development of radar signal processing techniques including inverse synthetic aperture radar (ISAR). Since 1988, he has been project leader for the Video Quality Standards Project at the Institute for Telecommunication Sciences, National Telecommunications and Information Administration, Boulder, Colo. Wolf is an active participant in the standardization activities of the ANSI-accredited T Committee's Working Group T1A1.5 (Multimedia Communications Coding and Performance) and has served as technical editor for two video performance standards, ANSI T1.801.01-1995 (Video Test Scenes) and ANSI T1.801.03-1996 (Objective Video Quality Parameters).

E. Patterson Tweedy graduated in 1940, with a degree in electrical engineering, from City and Guilds College, the engineering school of the Imperial College of Science and Technology in London. Most of his experience has been in the field of communication, including various forms of trunk telephone systems using both analog and digital transmission. In recent decades while employed by GTE Laboratories his attention has been devoted increasingly to video/audio systems, including satellite, cable, and broadcasting. For the last ten years he has been involved primarily in the use of digitally compressed video/audio applications, such as videoconferencing and entertainment to the home. Recent emphasis has been on evaluating applications using the H.261, H.323, and MPEG-1 and 2 standards.

Margaret H. Pinson is a programmer for the Institute for Telecommunication Sciences, part of the U.S. Department of Commerce, where she develops applications for use in video and voice quality measurement research. She has a masters degree in computer science from the University of Colorado at Boulder.

Arthur Webster received his M.S. in electrical engineering from the University of New Mexico in 1987. His work includes signal and image processing in such areas as radar, gyroscope testing, and laser speckle imaging. He has worked on video quality research since 1990 for the U.S. Department of Commerce, National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA), and Institute for Telecommunication Sciences (ITS) at their Boulder Laboratories. He is currently active in national and international standards activities pertaining to multimedia performance assessment

Currently, he is active in the operation of a center of excellence for Daikin DVD authoring software, with consultation and technical support in the areas of DVD pre-mastering. Dr. Yogeshwar received his Doctorate degree from Rutgers University in 1990. He later worked as a video engineer for Prism Interactive Corp., where he particated in MPEG standardization activities. Later, in 1992, he joined Toshiba America's Advanced Television Technology Center as a research scientist. He was involved in the development of advanced television, the simulation of video encoding and decoding, and in the design and implementation of an automated encoding system for DVD video. Dr. Yogeshwar is a member of SMPTE and IEEE. He is the holder of a U.S. patent, with five patents pending.

Mikhail Tsinberg received an MSEE in space and aviation technology from Rybinsk Institute of Aviation Technology, USSR. Since 1991, he has been senior research manager, Toshiba America Consumer Products, Advanced Television Technology Center, responsible for DVD authoring system software and architecture and embedded software. Tsinberg is a member of NATAS and chair of a subcommittee on motion estimation technology. In 1996, Tsinberg was chairman of the SMPTE Working Group responsible for recommending studio compression-based DVCR standard procedures and was chairman of SMPTE's conference session “DVD Authoring: A New Technology.” In 1995, he co-chaired the international conference of the ATV Working Group that developed the consumer DVCR MPEG-2 recording standard based on 6mm tape recording technology for DTV and DVB applications. In 1994, in cooperation with Warner Brothers, he developed architecture and system software for the world's first digital videodisk (DVD) MPEG-2-based authoring system. Tsinberg holds 32 U.S. and foreign patents. He is a SMPTE Fellow and a member of IEEE.

Donald A. Deel , vice-president of product development at Prisa Networks, has been involved in the design and development of highspeed network hardware and software interfaces for the past 15 years. For the three years prior to founding Prisa Networks, he served as system engineering manager at AMCC, where he supervised the definition and development of more than a dozen very large scale integrated (VLSI) circuits targeted at gigabit networking applications. Prior to his tenure at AMCC, Deel was senior engineering manager in charge of product development at In-Net Corp., San Diego, Calif., a startup supplier of fiber-distributed data interface backbone and channel extension systems. From 1984 to 1989, he headed the I/O subsystems group at Scientific Computer Systems, a startup mini computer supplier, where he managed the I/O hardware and software development of the world's first 1.4 Gbit/sec commercial computer network. From 1987 to 1989, as a key team member of the I/O subsystems group at Scientific Computer Systems, Green architected and implemented the software for the world's first 1.4 Gbit/sec commercial network. Green holds a B. A. in information science from the University of California, San Diego.

Keiichi Kubota joined Japan Broadcasting Corp. (NHK) in 1976. From 1979 to 1980 he worked at CBS Technology Center in Stamford, Conn., as a visiting engineer. In 1990 he moved to NTV's R&D Center, where his work focuses mainly on the development of the 525-line progressive scan production equipment. Hori is a member of the Institute of Television Engineers of Japan and chairs the engineering committee of the Digital Wide Image Forum. He has been recognized with the R&D 100 Award, the Development Award from the Japanese Society of Motion Picture and TV Engineers in 1995, the Nikkan-kogyo Newspaper Award for the top 10 annual products, the Development Award from the Institute of Television Engineers Japan, and the Hosobunka Foundation Award in 1994 for the development of the 525-line progressive scan TV camera. He also received the Hosobunka Foundation Award in 1993, and the Development Award from the Japanese Society of Motion Picture and TV Engineers in 1992 for the development of an ID signal insertion system into TV.

label: SMPTE Journal ( Volume: 109, Issue: 3, March 2000)

National Institute of Standards and Technology, Gaithersburg

Charles Fenimore graduated from Union College with a BS degree and from Berkeley with a Ph.D. in mathematics. He has worked on computational models for fluid and electrically driven flows at the Lawrence Berkeley Lab and at NIST. For several years, Fenimore has worked on measurements and models for quality assessment of moving digital imagery. This includes the development of measurements as well as the production of synthetic imagery and the acquisition of natural imagery as “probes” of compression systems.

Stephen Wolf received a BSEE from Montana State University in 1979 and an MS in electrical and computer engineering from the University of California at Santa Barbara in 1983. Since 1988, he has been project leader for the Video Quality Standards Project at the Institute for Telecommunication Sciences, an agency of the National Telecommunications and Information Administration in Boulder, CO. During this time, he developed innovative methods for performing in-service digital video quality measurements for which he was awarded two U.S. patents. Wolf, an active participant and contributor to the standardization activities of both ANSI and the ITU, has served as technical editor for two video performance standards, ANSI T1.801.01-1995 (Video Test Scenes) and ANSI T1.801.03–1996 (Objective Video Performance Parameters).

John M. Libert received a BS degree in experimental psychology and an MS in quantitative geology from the University of Maryland in 1970 and 1981, respectively. Joining Vitro Corp. in 1986 as principal investigator of its Signal and Image Analysis Laboratory, he led research to develop computational vision methods for image motion perception and stereopsis. He consulted with Sandia National Laboratories in developing a moving target detector for an infrared broad area surveillance system. In 1997, Libert joined the Electronics and Electrical Engineering Laboratory of the National Institute of Standards and Technology where he currently conducts research in video quality measurements a part of NIST's Video Technology Project.
affiliations: National Institute of Standards and Technology, Gaithersburg
Institute for Telecommunications Sciences

Philip Crosby received a B.S. in applied science from Portland University in 1965. He joined Tektronix, Inc., in 1957 as an intern. Crosby was the principal designer or project leader on many product efforts including oscilloscopes, video waveform monitors, vectorscopes, A/D converters, automatic video digital measurements systems, etc. Crosby led the design of the HDTV format converter at the Advanced Television Center, then later at Charles Rhodes. The format converter was crucial to the evaluation of the HD proponent systems in the early 90s. He has also contributed to several MPEG-2 and OC-48C products. Since retiring from Tektronix, Crosby has joined Network Elements Inc., as chief engineer, where he is currently engaged in the design of high-speed telecommunications equipment. He holds 28 patents.

Scott Lowrey received his BSEE and MSEE from the University of Southern California in 1981 and 1988, respectively. From 1982 to 1989, he worked at TRW Electronics and Defense, designing communications units for high-performance digital satellite systems, including analog-to-digital converters, multiplexers, and error-correction encoders. He then spent several years in the Motorola Government Electronics Group, designing high-speed encryption and decryption units, incorporating SONET and ATM data formats. At the Tektronix Video and Networking Division, he designed high-speed telecommunications systems that are used in the high bit rate transport of uncompressed HDTV digital signals. Lowrey is currently director of product engineering for Network Elements.

Arjun Ramamurthy received his B.E. in electronics and instrumentation from Annamalai University, India, in 1987, and an M.S. degree in electrical and computer engineering from Clarkson University, Potsdam, N.Y., in 1989. From 1989–93 he was with EOIS Corp., developing Machine-Vision for Paint Inspection and 3-D Gauging Systems. At PhotoResearch, Inc., from 1993–1996, his interests were in display imaging, color instrumentation, reproduction, and color imaging. Ramamurthy is currently the manager of software engineering at Warner Bros. Feature Animation, with development interests in color management systems, imaging and color algorithms, and workflow. He is a co-author of IT7.328-1995, the ANSI standard on Image Evaluation for Projection Systems and has published several papers on Machine Vision and Image Processing.

Lemuel L. Davis received a M.S. degree in electrical engineering from the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign in 1978. He joined Hughes Aircraft Co. in 1978, where he developed microprocessor-based control systems for realtime applications and automated testing systems. In 1981, he joined the Walt Disney Co. developing systems used for animation production. In 1985, Davis proposed the Computerized Animation Production System (CAPS) and was the technical lead for that project through 1990. From 1990 through 1993, he worked at the Naval Command and Control Center in San Diego developing scientific visualization systems. From 1993 through 1995, he was director of technology for Amblimation in London, England. Davis is currently the chief scientist at Warner Bros. Feature Animation with interests in color management systems, computer-assisted animation, imaging algorithms, and production management systems. He was a recipient of a technical Academy Award given for CAPS in 1992.

Franz Herbert has developed state-of-the-art software solutions for computer imaging for the past 15 years. He holds a Diplom Ingenieur degree in computer science from the Technical University of Vienna and a Master's Degree in computer and systems engineering from Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute in Troy, N.Y. His achievements include scanning, color correction, and photo retouching applications for various platforms. In August 1994, Herbert founded Color Solutions. The company's main objective is to bring color management tools to the end user. In September 1994, Color Solutions introduced ColorBlind, the first software application that allowed end users to profile all their input and output devices. In December 1997, Color Solutions was sold to Imaging Technologies Corp., a company focusing on digital imaging products. Herbert now heads the research and development group in charge of color technology. He is a member of the Society of Optical Engineering and has published several papers on various aspects of color management.

Yuji Nojiri is senior research engineer at the NHK Science and Technical Research Laboratories, Advanced Audio and Video Coding Research Division, where he has been involved in the research and development of the laser beam film recorder, the laser telecine, the HDTV standards converter, and HDTV image processing. He received an M.E. degree in electronic engineering from Waseda University in 1979 and joined NHK that year.

Kazuhisa Iguchi has been with the Advanced Audio and Video Coding Research Division of NHK Science and Technical Research Laboratories since 1993. He is involved in research on standards conversion and motion vector detection. Iguchi holds an M.E. degree in electrical engineering from the Tokyo Institute of Technology. He is a member of the Institute of Image Information and Television Engineers of Japan.

Yukio Sugiura received a B.E. degree in electrical engineering from Tokyo Denki University in 1963 and a Ph.D. in engineering from the University of Tokyo in 1995. He joined the Science and Technical Research Laboratories of NHK in 1958. As a senior research engineer in the Three Dimensional Audio-Visual Systems Research Division, he was engaged in research on the application of laser technology to optical communication systems, film recording, and telecine. He is currently involved in research on ultrahigh-definition and widescreen systems. Sugiura is a member of the Institute of Image Information and Television Engineers of Japan, the Optical Society of Japan, and the Motion Picture and Television Engineering Society of Japan.

Hiroshi Hirabayashi is deputy director of the Planning and Analysis Division, Broadcasting Satellite Department of the Telecommunications Advancement Organization (TAO) of Japan, in control of broadcasting satellites. He received his B.E. degree in electronic engineering from Osaka University in 1980 and joined the NHK that same year. From 1983 to 1995, while working at the NHK Science and Technical Research Laboratories, he took part in the research and development of the laser beam film recorder, the laser telecine, and the HDTV standards converter. Since 1995, Hirabayashi has been on loan to the TAO.

Edward Reuss has been the director of systems engineering at Tiernan Communications since 1996. His responsibilities include systems and architectural issues for MPEG-2 encoders, video processors, and telecommunications interfaces. He worked as a consultant for a variety of test and measurement, and television equipment manufacturers in the San Diego area before accepting his present position at Tiernan. Reuss earned his BSEE and MSEE degrees in 1976 and 1979, respectively, from Colorado State University. His principal field of interest was digital signal processing and estimation theory. Brian Quandt has been working in and around the world of MPEG for several years now. As president of HEURIS/Pulitzer, a joint venture between HEURIS Logic and Pulitzer Broadcasting, he has been responsible for designing and implementing the MPEG encoding system used for their video compression services. He is a contributing member of many of the ISO groups responsible for the MPEG specification, including ISO-IEC/JTC1/SC29/WG11 and WG1 as well as X3L3 2.1, 2.2, and 2.3. In particular, Quandt wrote significant portions of Part 5 of the MPEG-1 specification regarding the software implementation of system encoding. Quandt is a member of many other telecommunications, multimedia, and computer organizations including the ACM, IMA, and SMPTE. Often sought as an expert on the MPEG algorithm, he has written a chapter for a major college textbook on multimedia and presented this paper, on the parallelization of the MPEG algorithm, at the 136th SMPTE Technical Conference and World Media Expo in 1994. In addition, Mr. Quandt gave a brief paper on MPEG and served on a panel at COMDEX-Fall 1994.

Chaman Sabharwal received his B.A. (with honors) and M.S. degrees in mathematics from the Punjab University in Chandigarh, India. He earned his M.S. and Ph.D. in applied mathematics from the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign. Currently professor of computer science at the University of Missouri-Rolla, Sabharwal previously served as professor of mathematics and director of undergraduate computer science at St. Louis University. He has also been lead engineer and senior specialist at McDonnell Douglas Corp. Sabharwal has published in the areas of software engineering, feature recognition, robotics, and geometric modeling in various journals, including the SIAM Journal on applied mathematics, computer-aided geometric design, and pattern recognition. Among his research interests are the areas of computer graphics, computer vision, geometric modeling, machine learning, parallel processing, pattern recognition, and robotics. He is a member of ACM and IEEE.

Gavin Young is a technical area leader and project manager in the Networks and Systems Department at BT Laboratories, Ipswich, U.K. In 1986 he worked on the design of ISDN basic access transceivers and was subsequently involved in research and development for high-rate digital subscriber loop (HDSL) transceivers. In 1992 he was involved in leading feasibility work on the use of asymmetric digital subscriber loop (ADSL) technology for interactive television service. He is currently involved in progressing work on ADSL and its higher speed variants within ANSI and is a director of the ADSL Forum. He received a B. Sc. degree in electrical and electronic engineering from the University College of Swansea, Wales, in 1985, and an M. Sc. degree in communications engineering from the Imperial College of Science and Technology, London University, in 1986. He is a member of the IEEE and an associate member of the IEE of the U.K.

Don Clarke is a project manager in the Networks and Systems Department at BT Laboratories, Ipswich, U. K. He has been involved in fiber research since 1986 and was chief designer of the passive optical network (PON) transmission system for the BT optical access trials at Bishops Stortford, England, in 1990. Currently, he leads development activities for high-speed copper transmission and contributes to the ongoing technical analysis of scenarios for broadband access. He received a B. Sc. degree in computer systems from the University of Essex, England, in 1981, and holds several patents relating to PON technology. He is a member of the IEE of the U. K. and the IEEE.

Frederick J. Kolb, Jr. , retired from the Eastman Kodak Co. in 1986, having worked with them for 46 years in various areas of motion-picture film, television recording, and image processing. He is now a consultant in the fields of motion-pictures, electronic imaging, and magnetic recording. In addition to his consulting work, Kolb is an active participant in SMPTE's standards work. A former chairman of the Standards Committee, he is currently a member of Engineering Committees A12, P3, and H19. He was an ISO/TC36 specialist from 1970 to 1994, and he served on the National Association of Photographic Manufacturers' Committee IT9 from 1988 to 1994. Kolb earned his B. S., M. S., and Sc. D. degrees from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. He joined the Society in 1947 and has been a Life Fellow since 1988. He was the winner of the Journal Award in 1949, the Samuel L. Warner Memorial Medal Award in 1988, and the Technicolor/Herbert T. Kalmus Gold Medal Award in 1995. The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences presented him with a Technical Achievement Award in 1991. He is also a fellow of Tau Beta Pi as well as a member of the American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS), ACS, the American Institute of Chemical Engineers (AIChE), BKSTS, the Society for Imaging Science and Technology (IS&T), Sigma Xi, and Alpha Chi Sigma.

John Footen has been in the media technology business for more than 25 years. His career has focused on leading-edge product development and integration. He has led numerous projects for broadcasters, studios and other media companies around the world. He is degreed in film and television production, as well as computer science from New York University. He was most recently a vice president at National TeleConsultants, and is now chief technology officer at Chime Media. Footen is a regular speaker at conferences such as SMPTE, NAB, IBC, and Digital Hollywood. He is member of the Board of Directors for the Advanced Media Workflow Association, chairs the Media Services Architecture Group, and co-chairs the joint FIMS initiative with the EBU. He is co-chair of 32NF in SMPTE. He is an inventor on several media-related patents and has led teams whose work has received technical Emmy awards. John is author of articles for publications such as the SMPTE journal and Broadcast Engineering. He is a columnist for TV Technology and the co-author of a book about the application of SOA, BPM and Web Services in media, “The Service-Oriented Media Enterprise” with Joey Faust.

Dieter Van Rijsselbergen is a researcher and Ph.D. candidate in computer science and engineering at the Multimedia Lab of Ghent University in Belgium. He received an M.S. degree in computer science from Ghent University in 2005. In the past five years, Van Rijsselbergen has been involved in a number of projects that seek to enable advanced methods of media production by means of extensive use of structured production metadata and file-based production platforms. His research interests and areas of publication include IT-based broadcasting and drama media production, standardization, video coding, and GPU-driven signal processing.

Maarten Verwaest learned Information Technology on the job at Framatome Connectors, where he helped introduce Pro-engineer as a tool for model-driven development while in charge of the mechanics department. Since 1999, Verwaest has been a technology expert at VRT and as such is responsible for the design and implementation of several large-scale projects, including an integrated “Digital Newsroom Production System,” media asset management, and web content management systems, and a large-scale content delivery network serving broadband applications. Between 2005 and 2009, he has been responsible for research and development related to “virtual modeling” and search technology for audiovisual media production. Recently, Verwaest founded Limecraft, a provider of media production services in the cloud and a valorization partner of the technologies discussed in this paper. He is also author of several distinguished publications and is a well-known invited speaker to conferences worldwide.

Erik Mannens received an M.Sc. degree in electro-mechanical engineering from KAHO Ghent in 1992 and an M.Sc. degree in computer science from K.U. Leuven University in 1995. Before joining IBBT-Multimedia Lab in 2005 as project manager, he was a software engineering consultant and Java architect for more than a decade. His major expertise is centered on broadcasting, IDTV and (semantic) web development. He is involved in several projects as senior researcher and is finishing up his PhD on Semantic News Production. He's co-chair of W3C's Media Fragments Working Group and is actively participating in other W3C's semantic web standardization activities. He's also an active member of the technical committees of ACM MultiMedia, SAMT, and MAReSO.

Rik Van de Walle received masters and Ph.D. degrees in engineering from Ghent University, Belgium, in July 1994 and February 1998, respectively. After a post-doctoral fellowship at the University of Arizona, he returned to Ghent, became a full-time lecturer in 2001, and founded the Multimedia Lab at the Faculty of Engineering. Multimedia Lab later became one of the founding teams of the Interdisciplinary Institute for Broadband Technology (IBBT). Van de Walle's research interests include multimedia content delivery (including presentation and archiving), coding of multimedia data, metadata technology, content adaptation, interactive (mobile) multimedia applications, and e-health. He is author of more than 80 articles in international peer-reviewed journals and 250 articles in proceedings of international conferences. He has received awards for his work (a/o the ISO Award for Outstanding Technical Contributions, nominated by MPEG). Van de Walle is a member of the Board of Directors at Ghent University, and the IBBT Governing Board.

Paul Walland joined the management team of IT Innovation in 2006, where he is principal investigator in a number of European and U.K. collaborative research projects. His experience ranges from pure and applied research to product development and innovation management in a wide range of U.K.-based commercial organizations. Before joining IT Innovation, Walland was Projects Group Manager responsible for collaborative project research at Snell & Wilcox Ltd., U.K., where he initiated and led a wide range of U.K. and European research projects in the field of digital video and multimedia, including the metadata and image-processing-based projects MetaVision, 3-D Intercam, and WorldScreen. Walland was a founding director of the Multimedia Virtual Centre of Excellence, steering board member, and vice-president of the European Digital Television Action Group (DigITAG), and active contributor to both DTG and DVB. He is currently a Steering Board Member of the European Networked Electronic Media Technology Platform and a member of the U.K. Digital Content Knowledge Network advisory group. He has chaired workshops, conferences, and working groups and published widely at international conferences and in technical journals. Walland has an Honors degree in pure and applied physics from Manchester University.

Steve Taylor has worked on many Grid and SOA projects, including the FP5 GRIA project (2001–4) which began the GRIA middleware, the current version is available at www.gria.org. More recently, he has been working on the NextGRID (2004–7) and BREIN (2006–10) projects, with a focus on architecture, business modeling, trust and security, service-based computing, and Grid economics. In the U.K. MUPPITS project, he is responsible for the architecture of a media-centric combined storage, processing and tracking system for film productions. Taylor has a PhD in artificial intelligence.

Peter Brightwell is a senior R&D engineer with the BBC and a Chartered Engineer. He has significant experience in the technologies relevant to the changing world of television production, including file-based acquisition, networked delivery and asset management. This has included both research activity, and leading technical workstreams of BBC projects deploying new systems in program areas. He has also worked on projects related to sports innovation, including development of an award-winning graphics system used on a number of programs around the world. Brightwell has participated in SMPTE standards activity and led the development of the Media Dispatch Protocol (SMPTE 2032) for orchestrating delivery of large media files between organizations. He represents the BBC in EBU groups, addressing file-based and networked production.

Peter Wilson After working for Portsmouth University, The Royal College of Art & Design and The National Film and Television School during the 1970s, Wilson moved to Sony and from mid 1985 to 1992 was responsible for Sony's HD strategy in Europe. This was a pioneering time and laid the foundation for HD digital production and digital cinema. Wilson facilitated the first HD multicamera music shoot, Genesis at Wembley in 1987 and the first uncompressed digital delivery to a cinema at IBC in 1988. In 1991, he joined Snell and Wilcox where he planned and managed more than 20 HDTV and large-screen display products. Wilson currently runs a consultancy, high-definition and digital cinema Ltd., is the director of the European Digital Cinema Forum Technical Support Group, and sits on various governmental and professional Committees, consulting on HDTV, digital cinema, and 3D.

Brendan Slamin is the director of the U.K. High-definition Forum, a cross-industry group that brings broadcasters, program makers, manufacturers, and retailers together as part of the larger U.K. Digital TV Group. He also leads the MUPPITS research project, which is developing a software management system for film and TV production and post-production. This is designed to provide seamless production control and management systems for use with file-based production operations. Slamin coordinated the BBCs early work in high-definition research and, as part of the research, was responsible for the making of many of the early HD program in the U.K. and across Europe. He was presented with the Judges' Award of the Royal Television Society for his part in this activity. He has been an assessor for projects in pan- European research program and also served as an appeal assessor of projects judged to have failed. Slamin is the author of one book and the editor of a second, both on the subject of high-definition. He is a Chartered Engineer, a Fellow of the Institution of Engineering and Technology, and a Fellow of the Royal Television Society.

Roland Brown held the post of director of engineer at the Moving Picture Company (MPC), Soho, London, from 1985 to 2007. MPC specializes in digital visual effects for feature films and television commercials. Currently Brown is CEO of &&& Technology Limited and is a non-executive director at Quantel Ltd. and Imagineer Systems Ltd. His career has spanned four decades of major technological development, from being responsible for setting up commercial TV in South Africa, to working on every aspect of outside broadcasting and post- production. He is also the current president of the British Kinematograph Sound and Television Society (BKSTS) and chairman of the DTG Production Systems group, which focuses on HD research. Brown is also a member of ELBA's London Legacy 2020 committee. He is the external assessor for the post-graduate, digital post-production course and member of the advisory board at the National Film and Television School and a Partner in AndCubed LLP (A Technology Orientated Partnership).

Joey Faust, a senior consultant with National TeleConsultants, Inc., advises clients on process and technology analysis, workflow optimization and modeling, and software systems design. He is the co-author of the book “The Service-Oriented Media Enterprise: SOA, BPM, and Web Services in Professional Media Systems,” published in 2008.

Michael Bergeron currently serves as the strategic technical liaison for Panasonic Broadcast; managing co-development with Panasonic and U.S.-based companies. He later became manager and eventually director of engineering. He has been involved in the development and introduction of production cameras from the Aaton XTRprod S16 film camera, to the VariCam AJ-HPX3700; and has authored and presented white papers and technical presentations including co-authoring the camera chapter for the NAB engineering manual. Bergeron holds a B.S. in Physics, an M.S. in electrical engineering and is a member of the Advanced Television Systems Committee (ATSC), Hollywood Post Alliance (HPA), the Institute for Electrical and Electronics Engineering (IEEE) and SMPTE.

Michael Foti is director of engineering at the WGBH Educational Foundation—one of the largest broadcasting and program production operations in the public broadcasting system. At WGBH he oversees facility technical planning, project management, and engineering support. Foti has held engineering management positions with several broadcast and production organizations. He has also held senior engineering design positions with two systems integration firms. Foti is a member of SMPTE.

Tom Scott is Editorial Director, Motion Pictures, for SMPTE. He has been involved with sound for motion pictures since 1978, employed at American Zoetrope, Dolby Laboratories, Saul Zaentz Film Center, and Skywalker Sound. He has been the recipient of two Oscars, Academy Awards for Best Sound on the films The Right Stuff and Amadeus. Scott is currently employed as Vice President, Technology at Onstream Media in San Francisco, CA.

Kenneth Hunold is a broadcast applications engineer for Dolby Laboratories, Inc., where he works with broadcast and cable network engineers and production personnel as they transition to high-definition television with 5.1-channel audio. He also works with Dolby's motion picture clients on audio mastering and presentation for film and digital cinema. Before joining Dolby in 1999, Hunold worked with the ABC Television Network in a variety of engineering positions for 25 years. Most of that time was spent “on the road” for ABC Sports, and in ABC's Engineering Laboratory. He has worked on many major television events and received an Emmy Award as a video engineer for his work on the 1988 Winter Olympic Games in Calgary. From 1992 to 1999 he was a writer for Broadcast Engineering Magazine and an NAB “Pick Hits” judge. Hunold is a member of SMPTE, AES, and SBE. He is a former SMPTE Governor for the New York Region and a former New York Section Chair.

Eelco Grimm has been technical editor and editor in chief of the leading Dutch professional audio magazine. He owns the recording and acoustical consulting company Fairytapes. He is co-owner of the high-end professional audio equipment manufacturer Grimm Audio. Grimm teaches and researches at Utrecht School of the Arts—Faculty Art, Media and Technology—School of Music Technology. He has developed measurement techniques and surround sound recording techniques and has produced acclaimed CDs, written a book on optimizing professional audio systems, and chairs the Dutch Broadcasting Loudness Committee. Grimm is member of the EBU P/LOUD committee.

Richard van Everdingen started his career as a computer engineer at Getronics. He then moved to cable operator Casema, where he specialized in head-end systems. Everdingen led the development of a patented measurement system for FM modulated broadcasting; a loudness based leveling system for dedicated rebroadcasting use and a leveling system for DVB distribution, directly operating in the MPEG domain. He currently works as a consultant for broadcast companies at NKM in the Netherlands. Everdingen is a member of the Dutch Broadcast Loudness Committee and leads the Distribution Subgroup within the EBU P/LOUD committee.

Michel Schöpping studied musicology with additional courses in choir-direction and public relations. He started his career as a film music composer but soon got involved in sound design and film mixing. Schöpping designed, edited, and mixed dozens of documentaries, art films, and features for television and cinema. He was producer for several CD recordings and directed two music documentaries. Currently, he works as a sound designer, dubbing mixer, composer, music supervisor, and consultant. Additionally, he teaches at the Netherlands Film and Television Academy.

Patrick Waddell is manager, standards and regulatory, at Harmonic Inc., in Sunnyvale, CA, where he is responsible for compliance with industry standards and government regulations. A veteran of the broadcasting and performing arts industries, Waddell has more than 30 years experience serving a variety of staff and freelance positions with a number of different facilities. A second-generation broadcaster, his primary area of expertise is digital video system implementation for broadcast television. Waddell is a SMPTE Fellow and serves as Harmonic's representative to a number of industry standards bodies, including the SMPTE, the Society of Cable and Television Engineers (SCTE), Digital Video Broadcasting (DVB), and the ATSC. He currently serves as the Chair of the ATSC's TSG/S6, the Specialist Group on Video/Audio Coding and was the founding Chair of SMPTE's Technology Committee 32NF on Network/Facilities Infrastructure.

Kent Terry is currently a senior staff engineer at Dolby Laboratories in the Sound Technology Research group. Terry joined Dolby in 1992 to work on HDTV audio applications. He was part of the team that developed Dolby Digital for the ATSC, for which Dolby received an Emmy award, and he helped build the first working prototypes of the ATSC system. He was also part of the team that developed Dolby E for distribution of multichannel audio in broadcast distribution networks, also an Emmy award-winning technology. More recently, he has worked on solutions for problems in broadcasting such as lip sync. He has been active on SMPTE and ATSC standards committees, and has chaired the SMPTE group that helped revise SDI and HD-SDI embedded audio standards. Terry has been a key contributor to several SMPTE standards, including standards for conveying coded audio and other data on AES3 interfaces.

Regunathan Radhakrishnan joined the sound technology research team at Dolby Laboratories in June 2006 and is currently working on audio and video fingerprinting. Before joining Dolby, he worked at Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories (MERL) as a visiting researcher. He was one of the leading contributors to MERL's Video Summarization algorithm, based on audio classification which is now a differentiating feature of Mitsubishi Electric's DVD recorder in Japan. His current research interests include statistical machine learning, audio classification, video summarization, multimedia content identification, and security. Radhakrishnan has published several conference papers, journal papers, book chapters and a book on multimedia content analysis and security.

Frank Melchior received a Dipl.-Ing. in media technology from Technical University Ilmenau. After finishing his thesis on “Wave Field Synthesis for Cinema Applications” in 2003, he worked as a researcher and project manager at the Fraunhofer Institute for Digital Media Technology. Melchior is currently finishing his Ph.D. project “Spatial Sound Design” at the University of Technology Delft, The Netherlands. Since 2009 Melchior has been director research and development at the IOSONO GmbH, Erfurt. He has published more than 20 papers in journal and conference proceedings. His research interests include spatial array signal processing, spatial audio reproduction, and user interface technology for audio systems. Melchior is member of the Audio Engineering Society (AES) and the Deutsche Gesellschaft für Akustik (DEGA).

Jerry Whitaker currently serves as vice president of standards development at ATSC and is closely involved in work relating to educational programs. He supports the work of the various ATSC technology and planning committees and assists in the development of ATSC standards and related documents. — Whitaker is a Fellow of SMPTE and the Society of Broadcast Engineers (SBE). He is the author and editor of more than 30 books on technical topics, including: The Standard Handbook of Video and Television Engineering, 4th ed.; NAB Engineering Handbook, 9th ed.; DTV Handbook, 3rd ed.; and the Electronics Handbook, 2nd ed. Before joining the ATSC, Whitaker headed the publishing company, Technical Press, based in Morgan Hill, CA. He has served as a board member and vice president of SBE.

Wayne Bretl is a principal engineer in the R & D Department at Zenith Electronics. He received a BSEE from Illinois Institute of Technology in 1966, and joined Zenith in 1975. He holds more than 15 patents in television technology and related areas. Bretl is a senior member of IEEE, and a member of SMPTE, the Audio Engineering Society (AES), and the Society for Information Display (SID) and represents Zenith in ATSC and a number of professional and industry associations. Bretl is a co-recipient of the 2006 IEEE Masaru Ibuka Consumer Electronics Award, for his contributions to the development of the vestigial sideband (VSB) digital transmission system for digital television broadcasting. He also received the SMPTE David Sarnoff Medal Award in 2006, for his contributions to television engineering.

Sterling E. Davis, a broadcasting veteran for more than 40 years, is vice president, technical operations for Cox Media Group. Davis joined Cox Broadcasting's KTVU in Oakland in 1992, as director of operations, managing all aspects of engineering production, including electronic newsgathering editing, and traffic. He was promoted in 1998 to vice president of engineering for Cox Broadcasting in Atlanta and assumed responsibility for 15 television and 86 radio stations. — Davis was honored with the Broadcasting and Cable, “Technology Leadership Award” in 2006, Radio Ink's, “One of the Most Admired Engineers in Radio” in 2008, and the National Association of Broadcasters (NAB) “Engineering Achievement Award” in 2009. — Davis chaired the Advanced Television Systems Committee (ATSC) Planning Committee for three years. He is a member of the board of directors and participates on several technical committees. Davis has been a member of SMPTE since 1974. He is also a member of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE), the Audio Engineering Society (AES), Society of Broadcast Engineers (SBE) and Radio-Television News Directors Association (RTNDA).

Richard Chernock is currently chief technology officer at Triveni Digital, where he is developing strategic directions for monitoring, content distribution, and metadata management for emerging digital television systems and infrastructures. Previously, he was a research staff member at IBM Research, investigating digital broadcast technologies. Chernock is active in many of the ATSC and Society of Cable Television Engineers (SCTE) standards committees, particularly in the areas of monitoring, metadata, and data broadcast. He is vice-chair of the Technology Group on Distribution (TSG) and chairs the Non-Real-Time Services and mobile/handheld management layer activities within ATSC. Chernock is a major participant in the SCTE HMS video monitoring activity. He is also the Distinguished Lecturer Chair for IEEE BTS. In another life, he used transmission electron microscopy to study materials characteristics for advanced ceramics packaging and semiconductor technology at IBM. Chernock received a ScD from MIT in the field of nuclear materials engineering.

Peter Putman is president of ROAM Consulting, LLC, in Doylestown, PA, where he provides consulting, training, and product testing/development services to manufacturers of electronic displays, interfaces, and digital TV and video equipment. He also edits and publishes HDTVexpert.com, a website focused on digital TV, new media distribution and playback, and emerging display technologies. — Putman has written extensively on HDTV and display technology and has presented at numerous industry trade shows and technical conferences, including the Consumer Electronics Show, the National Association of Broadcasters trade show, the Hollywood Post Alliance Technology Retreat, and the InfoComm International trade show. — Putman is a member of the Academy Faculty for the International Communications Industries Association (ICIA) and was named their Educator of the Year in 2008. He is also a member of SMPTE and the Society for Information Display (SID). — Putman holds certifications from the ICIA (Certified Technology Specialist) and the Imaging Science Foundation (ISF), and has held Amateur Radio Extra Class license KT2B since 1982. He received a B.A. degree in Communications from Seton Hall University and an M.S. degree in Television and Film from Syracuse University.

Paul W. Jones is a senior principal scientist at Eastman Kodak Co. He received BS and MS degrees in imaging science from Rochester Institute of Technology and an MS degree in electrical engineering from Rensselaer Poytechnic Institute. He has over 24 years of experience in developing digital image processing solutions for still-frame and video applications. His primary activities have focused on designing and implementing algorithms for image compression and watermarking, and he holds 28 U.S. patents in those fields. Jones is coauthor of the textbook “Digital Image Compression Techniques,” as well as several book chapters on compression. He was a recipient of the 2005 C.E.K. Mees Award (Kodak's highest research honor) for his work on digital image watermarking.

Todd Roth received a BSE degree from Arizona State University in 1990. He has been leading the technical development of broadcast video servers since the introduction of the VR30 line in 1993, the industries first PC-based, videodisk recorder, through the current Nexio, the industries first software-codec-based HD/SD video server. — Innovations by Roth and his team led to the introduction of the industries first shared storage, multi-channel videodisk recorder in 1994. Roth led the team that pioneered the development of Fiber Channel-based shared storage and software RAID, introduced by the VR300 line in 1996. — In 2000, Roth was granted a patent for the invention of the “Shared Video Data Storage System,” which led to Leitch's 2001 Emmy for “Pioneering Developments in Shared Video-Data Storage Technology.” In July of 2002 Roth was granted a patent for the invention of the “Method and apparatus for synchronized multiple format storage”

Eisuke Nakasu received BE and ME degrees in electric engineering from Keio University, Japan, in 1980 and 1982, respectively. He joined Japan Broadcasting Corp. (NHK) in 1982. He is currently the senior associate director of the Human and information Science Division at NHK Science and Technical Research Laboratories, where he is in charge of research and development of digital broadcasting systems, video coding, and picture-quality evaluation. Nakasu was awarded the SMPTE Journal Certificate of Merit in 1996. He is a member of IEICE, ITE, IPS of Japan, and IEEE.

Yukihiro Nishida is a senior research engineer in the Human and Information Science Division at NHK Science and Technical Research Laboratories. Since graduating from Keio University, Japan, with a master's degree in electrical engineering, he has worked for NHK and has been involved in research and development of video coding, quality measurement, digital broadcasting, HDTV, and more. He has participated in many standardization activities in the area of broadcasting technologies and has served eight years as vice-chairman of Working Party 6A of ITU-R, dealing with digital television standards.

Mikio Maeda received BE, ME, and PhD degrees in electrical engineering from Hokkaido University in 1979, 1981, and 1993, respectively. He joined NHK in 1981. In 1984, he moved to the Science and Technical Research Laboratories, where he has been engaged in research on optical fiber transmission systems for high-definition television. His current interest is optical transmission systems for Super Hi-Vision, using the Dense Wavelength Division Multiplexing technique.

Masaru Kanazawa received BS, MS, and PhD degrees in electronics from Hokkaido University in 1977, 1979, and 2004. Since 1979, he has worked at NHK, where he is currently a senior research engineer in the Science and Technical Research Laboratories, engaged in the development of extremely high-resolution imagery systems. Kanazawa was awarded the best paper award of ITE Niwa-Takayanagi in 2004 and the Maezima prize in 2005. He is a member of the Institute of Electronics, Information, and Communication Engineers of Japan (EIC), the Institute of Image Information, the Television Engineers of Japan (ITE), and SID.

Sumio Yano received BA and PhD degrees in engineering from the University of Electro-Communications, Tokyo, Japan, in 1977 and 1993 respectively. He joined NHK in 1977 and worked at the NHK NARA Broadcasting Station until 1981. He was then transferred to the Science and Technical Research Laboratories in 1981. Yano worked at the ATR Human Information Processing Research Laboratories from 1992–1995, and at ATR Human Information Science Laboratories from 2002–2004. He was reinstated in his former position in 2004. Yano works in the Cognitive Science Group at the Technical Research Laboratories at NHK, where he studies the human vision system and its application of TV image systems.

Masayuki Sugawara received BS and MS degrees in electric communication engineering, and a PhD degree in electronic engineering from Tohoku University, Sendai, Japan. He joined NHK in 1983. Since 1987, he has been researching solid-state image sensors and HDTV cameras at the NHK Science and Technical Research Laboratories. He was an associate professor at the University of Electro-Communications in Tokyo from 2000–2004. Currently, Sugawara is a senior research engineer at NHK STRL, where he is engaged in the research of ultra-high-definition TV systems. He is a member of SMPTE, IEEE, IEICE, and ITE.

Kohji Mitani received BS and MS degrees in electronic engineering in 1985 and 1987, respectively, and a PhD degree in 1999, from Kyoto University. In 1987, he joined the NHK Science and Technical Research Laboratories. Since then, he has been working on solid-state image sensor cameras. His research interests include the very high data rate image pickup method, particularly a very high resolution and very high frame rate image acquisition system. Mitani is a member of the Institute of Image Information and Television Engineers of Japan, and SMPTE.

Kimio Hamasaki received an MS degree in acoustic design from the Kyushu Institute of Design in 1982. In 1982, he began a successful recording career at NHK, where he made numerous music recordings for broadcasting, CDs, and video releases. For his work, he received several prestigious awards, including the Prix Italia Perugia Award and the CATs Audio Award. In addition to audio engineering, he was engaged in the development of multichannel audio recording techniques, as well as digital mixing systems. Since 2000, he has been a senior research engineer at the NHK Science and Technical Research Laboratories where he works on advanced multichannel audio systems for reproducing immersive presence, and high-resolution audio. He is a Fellow member of the Audio Engineering Society, and a member of the Acoustical Society of Japan and the Institute of Image Information and Television Engineers.

Yuji Nojiri received MS and PhD degrees in electrical engineering from Waseda University, Japan, in 1979 and 2004, respectively. He joined NHK in 1979. Since 1981, he has been engaged in the research and development of HDTV, especially the HDTV laser beam film recorder and standards converter, and stereoscopic HDTV, at NHK Science and Technical Research Laboratories. His recent interests are in extremely high-resolution imagery, an Ultra-HDTV.

Thomas W. Hope, a SMPTE Life Fellow, was drafted by the U.S. Army on May 4, 1942, three weeks before graduating from college. He received a BA degree in absentia. After Army basic training and motion picture school, he was assigned to the First Special Service Force where he rose from private to T-4 sergeant. Nine months later, after graduating from Signal Corps Officer Candidate School as a 2nd lieutenant, he taught, and then became head of, the Army Motion Picture School in Astoria, NY, before going to Europe with a photo replacement unit on the Queen Elizabeth, arriving in Scotland on June 29, 1944. — His first assignment, in August 1944, was as photo officer of the VIII Corps, 3rd Army. In October, he was made photo officer of the new XIX Corps, 9th Army with the rank of 1st lieutenant. In April 1945, he was made photo officer of the 9th Army with the rank of captain. He was released from active duty in October 1945. — Before the war, after graduating from high school, Hope produced a film of the Boy Scout Fifth International World Jamboree in the Netherlands in 1937, the first of 67 films. He was one of the first cameramen to shoot football movies for coaches in 1939 to 1941.

Nagato Narita received BE, ME, and PhD degrees in electrical engineering from Waseda University, Tokyo. He joined Japan Broadcasting Corp. (NHK) in 1985. David Mouen Makoua received a degree in electrical engineering from INPG/ENSERG France in 1984. — He spent ten years in Thomson-CSF as senior engineer and was involved in military networking issues, mainly ATM equipment architecture. — Mouen joined Thomson Broadcast Systems in 1999 and is presently product manager for the network adaptor family, which addresses the delivery of high-quality audio/video over broadband telecom networks. He serves also as internal consultant for networking architecture issues.

Laurent Thehault received an engineering degree from Supelec (Ecole Supérieure d'Electricité, France) in 1989. He joined the Thomson group in 1990, where he currently manages the development of network adaptor and service multiplexer. — While at Thomson, Laurent has worked on the design of high-rate serial interfaces and switches for audio and video, and ATM-based multiplexing and transport systems. Currently he is involved in quality-of-service issues for the transport of high-quality video over emerging high-bandwidth IP networks.

Ian Oliver joined IBI in 1991 and has 20 year's experience in the television industries. Since joining IBI Group, Oliver has led the establishment and growth of the firm's communication systems practice, which specializes in the engineering and implementation of television production and distribution systems (including CATV and wireless technologies), voice and data systems, and general telecommunications systems. — Oliver and his colleagues work with major systems operators and television broadcasters in North America and overseas. He is a director of IBI Group and an active member of SMPTE and the SCTE.

Brian Holmes has been active in the electronics and communications industries since 1983. In ensuing years he has been directly involved in projects that incorporate high-performance/high-reliability electrical power systems, wireless communication systems, and state-of-the-art cable telecommunications systems. — Holmes has also held staff management positions in telecommunications operating companies. He has been responsible for the design, implementation, and maintainance of core-business, critical management of wired and wireless radio frequency communications systems, including advanced technology CATV master headends and primary hubs. Michael Bruns is a principal engineer with the Grass Valley Group, working on development for the company's Profile XP media server. He was responsible for the first MPEG decoder based on standard silicon at Tektronix in 1995 and has followed developments across three product lines up to the present. Before joining the media server development group, he led the architecture and hardware design of a high-definition serial video to OC-48 SONET/ATM interface. — Bruns is the author of several technical papers and one patent. A member of SMPTE, he participates in the study group on digital cinema.

James Whittlesey is senior hardware engineer at the Beaverton Design Center for the Grass Valley Group. A member of GVG since the company acquired Tektronix Inc.' s Video and Networking Division (VND), he was instrumental in designing the standard definition, 2-channel MPEG encoder board for the company's Profile XP media platform. As part of VND, he worked on the original Profile videodisk server prototype, designing the MPEG codec, SCSI disk interface, and realtime processor. — Whittlesey is a member of SMPTE and participates in the three study groups on digital cinema: audio, projection, and theater systems.

Chris Clarke graduated from Imperial College, London, and joined the BBC Research Department in 1970. For 30 years he has worked in many aspects of digital television including video coding, composite PAL, and NTSC decoding and television standards conversion. He led the team that developed the prototype hardware used for the first broadcast of signals conforming to the then newly agreed DVB-T standard in April 1996. He developed the single-card DVB-T modulator used in the wireless digital television camera.

Mike MacCormack has been producing and directing documentaries for BBC TV for over 20 years. He believes that he was the first BBC producer to use videotape on a full length single camera documentary (1985) and the first to use digital nonlinear editing (1991). He was attached to BBC R&D for six months in 1999/2000 to provide production advice to the team designing the wireless digital television camera.

Justin Mitchell joined BBC R&D in 1993 after graduating from Cambridge University and is currently a senior engineer. He has worked on a range of projects including those related to COFDM transmission and reception and MPEG-2 coding. Mitchell sat on the standardization committee that drafted the DVB-T specification and is the project leader for an ASIC development.

Peter Moss joined BBC Designs Department in 1980 after gaining a degree in physics from the University of Oxford. Initially involved in the design of transmitters and receivers for broadcast and ancillary services. he is now a senior R&D engineer at BBC Research and Development. In recent years he has worked in the areas of amplifier linearization for DAB and DVB applications, responsible for the Cartesian Loop PA design currently used in DAB broadcast transmitters. He is part of a team developing a wireless digital television camera based on the DVB-T COFDM standard where he has contributed in the areas of system simulation and RF design.

John Zubrzycki joined BBC Research in 1982 after gaining a Ph.D. at Kings College, London. He worked on the development of a high-capacity fiber-optic network for digital studios using dense-WDM as part of a European collaboration. In 1992, he worked in another European project, MBS, followed by its successor, SAMBA, developing broadband mobile networks and demonstrated the technical feasibility of using such networks for sending contribution signals for television program production. Currently, he is the project manager of the Digital Radio Camera Project, on which this paper is based.
affiliations: British Broadcasting Corp. Research and Development Dept., U.K.

Gary Demos attended the California Institute of Technology. In 1975, he joined Information International, Inc., where he supervised the development of the first digital film printer (for which he received an Academy Scientific and Engineering Award for scanning technology in 1995 and an Academy Technical Achievement Award for digital compositing technology in 1996 together with his colleagues). He also helped pioneer the field of computer graphics. — In 1981, Demos co-founded Digital Productions to produce photo-realistic images for film, television, and advertising.
