Mike Armstrong works on the interaction between people, stories, media and technology, spanning topics from access services, speech audibility, and video quality to human perception. Armstrong is the originator of Object-Based Media (OBM), a concept that had its origins while bringing computer-based playout to the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC), Salford, U.K., during the 1990s at Radio Bristol. Armstrong has recently been examining the way media experiences can respond to the user in a natural manner. This work combines the issues of storytelling and narrative structures, natural forms of agency for the user, the problems of personalization and the roles that the user can play in an experience. Armstrong’s latest work is attempting to automate the production of OBM experiences for interactive news from tagged clips and associated metadata.

Sally Bowman is a British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC), Nottingham, U.K., television journalist, longform filmmaker, and team leader who recently completed a Master’s in Research (Digital Media) at the University of the West of England, Bristol, U.K. Her research took a socio-technical approach to examine how the affordances of new software developed by BBC Research and Development may change the way producers and journalists tell factual stories for digital audiences.

Matthew Brooks works in British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) Research and Development’s Future Experience Technologies Group, Salford, U.K., leading their Object-Based Media Tools and Trials work. Brooks and his team build tools for creating responsive, interactive and adaptive stories, as well as researching the value these experiences have for the audience. Before joining the BBC, Brooks worked for Sony Computer Entertainment, and numerous other videogame companies. From videogames to broadcasting, he specializes in the creative application of technology to storytelling, helping development and production teams realize their interactive designs with new tools and techniques. Brooks has written publications for the Audio Engineering Society, IBC and ACM TVX (Interactive Experiences for Television and Online Video), presented at IBC, exhibited ongoing work at IBC and Sheffield Doc/Fest, co-created digital art installations at Tate Modern and Manchester Museum Of Science and Industry (MOSI), and launched the world’s first variable length radio program.

Andy Brown is a research scientist and software engineer at British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) Research and Development (R&D), Salford, U.K. He has a background in computer science, having gained a PhD degree and worked as post-doctoral research associate at the University of Manchester, Manchester, U.K. in the fields of human–computer interaction and accessibility. His work is currently focuses on object-based media where he is helping to develop the tools for creating and playing content. He has a particular interest in exploring how audience analytics can be used to provide insights into how the experiences bring value to users.

Juliette Carter is a research engineer with British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) Research and Development (R&D), Salford, U.K. She is currently investigating technologies that would enable the BBC to deliver Object-Based Media (OBM) experiences at scale and to any device. Her previous work focused on developing tools to author OBM content, using insights from producers to inform on the design and implementation. Carter has also had exposure to a number of other projects, including video compression, machine learning and audio, and software development for visual journalism.

Andy Jones, physics and astronomy graduate having published work on extragalactic star formation in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society (MNRAS), transitioned into British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) Research and Development (R&D), Salford, U.K., via ecommerce where he was formerly a software engineer and later a data scientist. Jones has extensive experience with software engineering front and back end technologies as well as research skills from academics. He has spent his time at BBC R&D working on the Object-Based Media (OBM) platform researching and engineering tools enabling our community of practice to create interactive “object-based experiences.”

Max Leonard is a research engineering technical lead currently working to ensure the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC), Salford, U.K., can continue to deliver its services to the British public and globally in an increasingly hostile and surveilled digital world. In his time at BBC Research and Development (R&D), he has also focused his time on Object-Based Media (OBM) and live Internet Protocol (IP) production systems.

Thomas Preece is a research engineer working at British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) Research and Development, Salford, U.K. For the past three years, he has been developing StoryKit, a set of tools for authoring and playing Object-Based Media (OBM) experiences. Before his work on StoryKit, Preece has been involved in a range of different areas including speech music discrimination, content enrichment using deep learning and website archiving, and playback. Preece is a full stack developer and develops mainly in Javascript, NodeJS, React, and Python but has the most experience in backend services, Amazon Web Services (AWS), and managing the StoryKit platform. Recently, as part of his Security Champion role, Preece has been applying his web application security knowledge to improve both StoryKit and the department’s web application security through workshops and code audits.

Mike Strein is the director of engineering and technology at ABC News, New York, NY, which is part of Walt Disney Television. For the past 30 years, he has been at the forefront of just about every technical advancement that the ABC TV network has made, from the transition from analog to digital, through the HDTV transition to the migration to video-over-IP and the expansion of streaming platforms. He has more than 40 Disney Innovation awards that have resulted in 22 U.S. patents, with several others still in process. He is active in the standards communities, has been an active SMPTE NY board member since 1997 and is a SMPTE Fellow. Prior to ABC, he spent seven years at Standard Microsystems Corporation, Hauppauge, NY, as part of a semiconductor design team. He has a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering technology from SUNY Polytechnic University, Utica/Rome, NY.

Karl Paulsen is currently the chief technology officer at Diversified, a global technology innovation firm head-quartered in Kenilworth, NJ. In his role, he provides technology thought-leadership and subject matter expertise to clients’ projects and to engineers, managers, sales, and marketing personnel. In mid-2017, he developed the multivendor “IP Roadshow,” a fully functioning mobile SMPTE ST 2110 technology laboratory that demonstrates and trains the industry in the practices, theory, and implementation of the SMPTE ST 2110/ST 2059/ST 2022 suite of standards. He has been contributing to TV Technology magazine on topics of storage, workflow, IP-infrastructure for more than 25 years and also pens the feature column for the Cloudspotter’s Journal. He held various senior level engineering positions, including VP-Engineering, director of engineering, and chief technology officer at broadcast and mobile television firms, post- and computer graphics interface (CGI)-production, and leading systems integration companies internationally. Among numerous other self-taught technologies, he studied electrical engineering at Oregon State University, Corvallis, OR, mathematics and economics at Portland State University, Portland, OR, and project management at Washington State University, Pullman, WA. He is a SMPTE Fellow, former co-chair of the SMPTE Standards TC 34CS technical committee, a certified professional broadcast engineer (SBE), and a member of the International Trade Association for the Broadcast & Media Industry (IABM), Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers-Broadcast Technology Society (IEEE-BTS), Video Services Forum, the Audio Engineering Society (AES), and the Alliance of IP Media Solutions (AIMS).

Brian Vessa is a dedicated audio professional with over 35 years of experience in the industry. After attending the University of California Los Angeles (UCLA) Engineering School, he became a recording engineer, producing albums, and recording orchestras. Vessa transitioned into film post as a music editor and sound editor, became a re-recording mixer at Cannon Films and Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer (MGM), then handled audio restoration at NT Audio. He was hired by Sony Pictures in 1998, and today is their Executive Director of Digital Audio Mastering and representative to Digital Cinema Initiatives (DCI). Vessa is a member of the AMPAS Sound Branch, SMPTE, and the Audio Engineering Society (AES). He is the founding chair of the SMPTE TC-25CSS Technology Committee on Cinema Sound Systems and serves on many SMPTE and AES committees. Vessa was a member of the original committee that conceived and created the Interoperable Mastering Format (IMF), helping write a fully detailed standard for IMF prior to it being brought to SMPTE. He has been instrumental in standardizing the IAB immersive audio distribution bitstream for Cinema and IMF as well as a host of related standards. Vessa is a past and current chair of the DCI Technical Committee, and has written many audio specifications, including a white paper on near-field mixing for home theater that has been widely adopted.

Ryokichi Komagata joined Japan Broadcasting Corporation (NHK) in 2009. After engaging in newsgathering and program production for four years, he has been focused on the development of production systems with the Engineering Adminis- tration Department. He is mainly responsible for the production studio facility design, especially in the video and lighting system. He developed Japan’s first 4K TV studio, which can simultaneously produce 4K and 2K programs. Currently, his team is developing the sixth 4K TV studio.

Kota Itakura joined NHK in 2006 and has been engaged in program production for dramas, music entertainment, and sports. In 2018, he began working with the Engineering Administration Department. keywordsSearch: SMPTE Motion Imaging Journal ( Volume: 129, Issue: 8, September 2020)

Siegfried Foessel received Diploma and PhD degrees in electrical engineering from Friedrich Alexander University, Erlangen, Germany. He is head of the Moving Picture Technologies department, at Fraunhofer IIS, Erlangen, Germany, and the head of the Technology Study Program at the University of Television and Film (HFF), Munich, Germany. His research areas include cameras, digital cinema, image compression, and post-production tools. He is a member and the chair of various national and international standardization bodies. He is a Fellow of the SMPTE and a Senior Member of the IEEE, with more than 70 publications. He is currently serving as the president of FKTG e.V., the German equivalent to SMPTE.

Jyrki Alakuijala is an active member of the open source software community and a data compression researcher. He is a technical lead/manager at Google, and his recent published work has been with Zopfli, Butteraugli, Guetzli, Gipfeli, WebP lossless, Brotli and Joint Photographic Experts Group (JPEG) XL compression formats and algorithms, and two hashing algorithms, CityHash and HighwayHash. Before joining Google, he was involved in the development of software for neurosurgery and radiation therapy treatment planning.

Touradj Ebrahimi is a professor at École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), Lausanne, Switzerland, and heads its multimedia signal-processing group. He is the co-founder of the startup company RayShaper based in Crans-Montana, Switzerland, which is active in computational vision for machine- and human-centric applications. He has been the convener (chairman) of the JPEG Standardization Committee since 2014. His research interests include image and video compression, quality of experience in multimedia, and media security. He is a Fellow of the SPIE and the IEEE and has been a recipient of numerous awards and distinctions, including the IEEE Multimedia Star Innovator Award for his contributions to quality of experience assessment solutions with applications to multimedia standardization.

Pierre-Anthony Lemieux co-chairs the High-Throughput JPEG 2000 (HTJ2K) activity in the International Organization for Standardization/International Electrotechnical Commission (ISO/IEC) JTC 1/SC 29/WG 1 committee. He is a partner at Sandflow Consulting, San Mateo, CA, where he works with Hollywood and Silicon Valley based clients on worldwide standards and research and development of software. He has been involved in the entertainment technology ecosystem, from content authoring to consumer devices, and is an active contributor to several standards activities and open source projects. He has a PhD degree in physics from the University of California at Los Angeles (UCLA), Los Angeles, CA, and a BSc degree from McGill University, Montreal, QC, Canada, and is the SMPTE fellow and standards director.

Fernando Pereira received BS, MSc, and PhD degrees in electrical and computer engineering from the Instituto Superior Técnico (IST), Universidade de Lisboa, Lisbon, Portugal, in 1985, 1988, and 1991, respectively. He is currently with the Electrical and Computer Engineering Department, IST, and Instituto de Telecomunicações. He has authored or coauthored more than 300 papers. His areas of research interest include visual information analysis, processing, coding and description, and interactive multimedia services. He has been participating in the work of ISO/IEC Moving Picture Experts Group (MPEG) and ISO/IEC JPEG for many years, notably as the head of the Portuguese delegation, and the chair of the MPEG and JPEG requirements subgroups.

Antonio M. G. Pinheiro is an assistant professor at Universidade da Beira Interior (UBI), Covilha, Portugal, and a researcher at Instituto de Telecomunicações (IT), Aveiro, Portugal. He received the BSc (Licenciatura) from Instituto Superior Técnico (IST), Lisbon, Portugal, in 1988 and the PhD in electronic systems engineering from the University of Essex, Colchester, U.K., in 2002. Currently, his research interests focus on image processing, namely on multimedia quality evaluation, emerging 3D imaging technologies, and medical image analysis. He is a Portuguese delegate to ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC29, currently involved with JPEG standardization committee, the JPEG Communication Subgroup chair and participating in the JPEG Pleno standard development. He is a Senior Member of the IEEE.

Peter Schelkens holds a professorship with the Department of Electronics and Informatics, Vrije Universiteit Brussel, Brussels, Belgium, and is the university group leader at IMEC, Brussels, Belgium. In 2013, he received an EU ERC Consolidator Grant focusing on digital holography. His research interests include multidimensional signal processing encompassing the representation, communication, security, rendering, and quality assessment of these signals, while especially focusing on multidisciplinary research. He chairs the coding, test, and quality subgroup of the ISO/IEC JTC1/SC29/WG1 (JPEG) standardization committee and is an associate editor of Signal Processing: Image Communication and the Journal of Physics: Photonics.

Jon Sneyers received a PhD degree in computer science at the KU Leuven, Leuven, Belgium. He created the free lossless image format (FLIF). Since 2016, he has been a senior image researcher at Cloudinary, an SaaS technology company, Santa Clara, CA, that is a market leader in image and video management on the web.

Jan Wassenberg is a senior software engineer at Google Research. He is the co-chair and an editor of ISO/IEC 18181, the JPEG XL standardization project. With 18 years of experience in SIMD, his work revolves around high-performance, hardware-friendly software. From 2012 to 2015, he worked on the DaVinci Resolve color correction and video editing system. In 2011, he completed a PhD degree in efficient image analysis at the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT), Karlsruhe, Germany, and Fraunhofer, Munich, Germany.

title: American Society of Cinematographers Motion Imaging Technology Council Progress Report 2020
label: SMPTE Motion Imaging Journal ( Volume: 129, Issue: 8, September 2020)

SMPTE Motion Imaging Journal ( Volume: 129, Issue: 8, September 2020)

Curtis Clark, Asc, studied theater at the Art Institute of Chicago’s Goodman School of Drama and cinematography at the London Film School. After graduation, he began his career by shooting and directing documentary films in the U.K. before transitioning to shooting feature films and TV commercials in the U.K. and the U.S. Following on the success of his short film, The Arrival, he completed his highly praised short film Eldorado. The most recent addition to Clark’s short film trilogy, Meridian (Netflix), is a creatively accomplished work that has gained the status of an essential demonstration for high dynamic range (HDR) imaging. In 2019, he was a producer for a critically acclaimed Turner Classic Movies (TCM) original documentary, Image Makers, about pioneering cinematographers in Hollywood who created compelling photographic looks that established the visual styles that informed narrative filmmaking. He is the chairman of the ASC Motion Imaging Technology Council (MITC). Since its inception in 2003, the council under Clark’s leadership has achieved a series of notable successes including its collaborative work with Digital Cinema Initiatives, LLC (DCI) to produce standardized evaluation material for assessing the performance of digital projectors and other elements of DCI standards-based digital cinema systems, as well as the 2009 Camera Assessment Series (CAS) and 2012 Image Control Assessment Series (ICAS). The ASC Motion Imaging Technology Council, at Clark’s instigation, embarked on the development of a groundbreaking project to create cross-platform data exchange for primary red, green, and blue (RGB) digital color correction known as the ASC CDL. The ASC CDL was recognized by the Academy of Television Arts and Sciences with a prestigious 2012 Primetime Emmy Engineering Award. He also received an AMPAS Technical Achievement Award recognizing his work developing the ASC CDL. He was a recipient of the prestigious ASC Presidents Award, as well as the Motion Picture Academy’s 2019 John A. Bonner Award in recognition of extraordinary service to the motion picture industry. In addition to being a member of the ASC and its Board of Governors, he is a member of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences and has worked on the development and implementation of ACES. He is also a member of the Directors Guild of America.

David Reisner received a 2014 Academy Technical Achievement Award, a 2014 Hollywood Post Alliance Judges Award for Creativity and Innovation, and was recognized by the Academy of Television Arts and Sciences with a prestigious Prime Time EMMY Engineering Award as a co-designer of the ASC CDL—now used in the workflow of nearly every motion picture, scripted TV, and visual effects turnover. He was the lead designer and co-producer of the ASC-DCI StEM Standard Evaluation Material used to determine the quality required to convert the world’s movie system from film to digital, and vice-chaired the SMPTE Working Groups responsible for digital cinema imaging—showing on nearly all cinema screens worldwide—and security standards—protecting $35 billion of IP each year. He also had leading roles in activities including design and production of the American Society of Cinematographers-Producers Guild of America (ASC-PGA) CAS, the ICAS, and elements of the Academy Color Encoding System. He has been a founder, a partner, and a chief technology officer in computer and in entertainment companies. He helped originate digital audio and his “firsts” include the programmable portable computer, the handheld digital video jukebox, the portable source-level debugger, 57,000-bit very long integer arithmetic, and Very Long Instruction Word (VLIW) computer architecture—one of the enablers of modern multiprocessor computing. He provided editorial assistance on the first textbook on neural network artificial intelligence and machine learning, originated pervasive computing—a parent of the Internet of Things (IoT), proposed emergent networking for smart dust, and helped develop the first popular byte-code virtual machine. He has shot celebrity and fashion for books and magazines including Vogue Italia, produced concerts internationally, and trained killer whales. He is well published in books and technical articles, has spoken widely including NAB, SMPTE, International Federation of Cinematographers (IMAGO), and a 29,000-viewer webcast, and on manned space exploration to a standing-room-only crowd at the 2014 International Space Development Conference. He is a member of SMPTE, the founding Secretary of the ASC Motion Imaging Technology Council, an ASC Associate, a Member of the Visual Effects Society, and a coauthor of the “VES Handbook of Visual Effects.” His committees have recommended some of the highest profile Academy Scientific and Technical Awards.

Bill Bennett, Asc is a cinematographer, primarily shooting television commercials for major clients including Ford, Lexus, Coca Cola, Apple Computer, and Budweiser. He worked as first or second unit camera operator for feature films including Superman III, The Black Stallion Returns, To Live and Die in LA, Silverado, The Right Stuff (aerials), Bugsy (miniatures), and Waiting to Exhale (title sequence), and as first or second unit DoP on TV series such as 24 The Fosters and Heart Breaker. He co-invented the Terra-Flite vehicle-mounted camera stabilization system. He co-designed the Preston Cinema Systems Micro-Force Zoom Control, now seen on every set in the world. He has long advised ARRI on the design of cameras from the 435 film to the Alexa Mini digital. He has shot multiple demonstration films for ARRI and Zeiss. He currently an ASC vice president and a member of the Board of Governors.

David Stump, Asc, is a working DP, visual effects DP, visual effects supervisor, and stereographer, earning an Emmy Award, an Academy Award for Scientific and Technical Achievement, and an International Cinematographers Guild Award. He is currently the chairman of the Camera Subcommittee of the ASC Technology Committee and a member of the AMPAS Science and Technology Council, where he chairs the Next-Generation Cinema Technology Work Group and participates in the AMPAS ACES project. Under his guidance, the combined efforts of the PGA and the ASC produced both the ASC-PGA CAS and the ASC-PGA ICAS, which are side-by-side comparisons of virtually all of the high-end digital cinema cameras against film. He has lectured and taught classes in cinematography and visual effects and has spoken at many conferences and trade shows, including the National Association of Broadcasters and the International Broadcast Convention.

Greg Ciaccio creative technologist, has served in executive operations management positions for Creative Service divisions at Sim, Ascent, Technicolor, and Deluxe, and has led product development teams creating leading-edge products including Technicolor’s DP Lights and Deluxe’s Mobilabs near-set dailies solutions. In 2014, he, with other core members of the ASC Technology Committee’s DI Subcommittee, won an HPA Judges Award for the creation of the ASC CDL, now a commonly used format for the exchange of basic primary color grading information. He serves as the chair of the ASC Motion Imaging Technology Council’s Workflow Committee, which includes the ACES and Advanced Data Management Subcommittees. He is a SMPTE Hollywood Section Manager, a member of HPA, and an Associate Member of the ASC.

Jesse Korosi is the director of Workflow at Sim, the 2016 HPA Emerging Leader Award winner, Studio Daily Top 50 Award winner, the former chair of the HPA’s Young Entertainment Professionals (YEP) committee, current chair of the ASC MITC Workflow Advanced Data Management subcommittee, and HPA’s “Through The Frame” podcast host. He currently oversees a global workflow and development team and provides technical-level direction and management. In the last 18 months, he and his team have overseen the dailies/post-production workflow on over 100 projects spanning the globe, collectively managing over 10 Petabytes of media. Aside from working on notable television shows and feature films, he counts creating Sim’s new client-facing metadata aggregation/automated transcoding service, Metabanq, as his greatest achievement.

David Morin is the head of the Epic Games Los Angeles Lab and the executive director of the Academy Software Foundation. At Epic Games, he works to develop the use of the Unreal Engine in the Film and Television industries. At the Academy Software Foundation, he works for the premier members to develop the use of open source software in the motion picture industry. Previously, he was the president of David Morin, LLC, a diversified consultancy specializing in immersive production with clients such as the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, ARRI Inc., Autodesk, Epic Games, Shotgun Software, and others. He is also the chairman of the Joint Technology Committee on Virtual Production and a past co-chair of the Joint Technology Subcommittee on Previsualization. He earned a BScA degree in computer science from Laval University, Quebec City, Canada, and has participated in the development of motion capture and 3D softwaresince Jurassic Park at companies such as Softimage, Microsoft, Avid Technology, Autodesk, and now Epic Games.

Michael Goi, Asc, Isc, is a three-time past president of the American Society of Cinematographers and is the editor of the tenth edition of the American Cinematographer Manual. He is the co-chair of the ASC MITC Joint Technology Committee on Virtual Production. He is a member of the National Executive Board of the International Cinematographers Guild, a member of the Academy of Television Arts and Sciences, and the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. He directed the feature film Mary starring Gary Oldman, to be released this fall.

Mike Sanders is the senior visual director for Activision overseeing innovation in art, animation, and production across Activision’s game franchises, most notably Call of Duty. He is focusing on bringing film VFX quality to game development and interactive entertainment. He was previously the director of virtual production for Industrial Light and Magic, collaborating with Disney’s Lucasfilm, Pixar, Marvel, and Imagineering, and built the creative technology of ILMxLAB. He has created cutting-edge imagery for more than 90 major motion pictures and AAA games and worked with top directors and major studios on projects including Titanic, Star Wars, Avatar, and Pirates of the Caribbean.

Joachim Zell is a consultant on production and post-production workflows, ACES, and Imaging Science. For 12 years he served as VP of Technology at EFILM/Deluxe, where he designed and monitored production workflows from on-set production to movie release. Previously, he was VP of Advanced Technology at Technicolor Thomson in Burbank and before that Marketing Manager Americas at Grass Valley Thomson. During his time in London, Zell worked as Product Manager digital film systems for Pandora Int. He supports SMPTE as Hollywood Section Manager, was on the ASC Technology Committee team that designed the ASC CDL, and holds the position of ACES Project Vice-Chair at the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. In February 2020 Joachim became a board member of the HPA. Joachim holds a master’s degree in Film and Television Engineering and has co-authored four image processing patents.

Tim Kang is a Los Angeles-based cinematographer, working in the film and TV industries primarily as the director of photography on narrative, commercial, music video, and documentary projects. In addition to multiple features, pilots, and shorts, his list of commercial clients includes Cover Girl, Delta, LA Kings, Disney Interactive, Dreamworks TV, NBC Universal, and YouTube. He has taught cinematography classes and seminars at AFI, Chapman University, Orange, CA, and Woodbury University, Burbank, CA. He received a Master of Fine Arts (MFA) degree in cinematography from the renowned American Film Institute Conservatory and proudly received mentorship from Stephen Lighthill, ASC; Robert Primes, ASC; David Stump, ASC; Greg McMurry, ASC; and Ron Garcia, ASC.

Emily Stadulis was a lighting designer and a technical educator for both live events and on camera for 15 years across the U.S. Following her design career, she transitioned to systems designs and sales, specializing in upgrading spaces to light-emitting diode (LED). Currently, she is the regional manager for Rosco Laboratories, covering the western region of the U.S. and Canada.

Adrienne Klotz Floyd is a film, TV, and media production professional with more than 20 years of experience. She is an IATSE Local 600 International Cinematographers Guild member, digital imaging technician, specialty photographer, and co-producer and host of FilmCraft.Biz.

Jay Holben is an independent producer and the director in Los Angeles, CA. A former cinematographer, he is the author of two commercially published books on cinematography, a previous technical editor for DV Magazine, a current editor and contributor for over two decades for American Cinematographer Magazine, faculty instructor for Global Cinematography Institute, and international lecturer. He is an Associate Member of the ASC and the chair of the ASC Motion Imaging Technology Council’s Lens Committee.

Pete Ludé is a prominent engineering consultant in advanced imaging and sound. He serves as the chief technology officer of Mission Rock Digital, a San Francisco-based engineering firm specializing in next-generation media including cinema display technology, immersive sound, and interchange pipelines for plenoptic (light field) imaging. He is the past-president of SMPTE, and a SMPTE Fellow. He currently serves as the co-chair of the ASC Plenoptic and Computational Imaging Committee, the chairman of IDEA—the Immersive Digital Experiences Alliance, the chair of the SMPTE Working Group on Immersive Audio for Cinema, and is a frequent speaker on the future of cinema, volumetric imaging systems, and advanced display technology.

Lou Levinson is a long-time Associate Member of the ASC and the Vice-Chair of the MITC Digital Intermediate Committee. A member of the ASC Technology Committee since its inception, he has been a frontline colorist from the “on the fly” analog era to today’s advanced ACES and beyond digital pipelines, having worked with/for everyone from Woody Allen to Rob Zombie. He is currently works at Apple, San Francisco Bay Area, CA.

Joshua Pines is the chief troublemaker and luddite at Technicolor Digital Intermediates, which provides the motion picture industry with digital color correction processes for theatrically released films. He is currently in charge of imaging and color science projects. He joined Technicolor after more than ten years at Industrial Light and Magic, where he supervised their film scanning/recording department from its inception, and worked extensively with both traditional and digital cinema technologies. He has received two Technical Achievement Awards from the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences and the Herbert Kalmus Award from SMPTE, and had his gender identity confirmed when SMPTE named him a Fellow.

Eric Rodli has been involved in the management and development of entertainment technology since the late 1980s when he became the president of Iwerks Entertainment. He is a pioneer in large-format films, motion simulation theaters, and other immersive technologies. He subsequently has had senior roles in a variety of entertainment and media organizations, including being a partner in the entertainment consulting practice of PwC as well as president of Kodak’s Motion Picture Division. He is currently an independent consultant and investor. He is an Associate Member of the ASC.

Michael Zink is the vice-president of technology at Warner Bros. (WB), Burbank, CA, where he is responsible for exploring emerging technologies to enhance WB’s capabilities for production, post-production, and distribution. He also participates in a number of standards associations—the Consumer Technology Association (CTA), Digital Cinema Initiatives (DCI), and SMPTE, among others—and also serves as the chairman for the Ultra High Definition Alliance (UHDA). Prior to joining WB, in 2014, he worked at Technicolor, London, U.K. and Los Angeles, CA, for more than ten years, most recently as the vice-president of technology strategy.

James Fancher developed next-generation technology in digital asset management for Deluxe Digital Media, Burbank, CA. Previously, he was the chief science officer at the Thomson Corporate Research facility in Burbank, where he worked on cluster computing architectures for image processing, 3D color correction systems, and digital asset management technology. As the chief technology officer for Technicolor Creative Services, the post-production arm of Technicolor, he was involved in the development of color management systems, image processing, and media asset management. Prior to his engagement at Technicolor, he was the chief science officer for Pacific Ocean Post, where he started POP Sound, POP Film, which won two Academy Awards for visual effects.

Gary Mandle is a senior research scientist at Baylor University FDM, Waco, TX. He has been working on new display development for more than 35 years as both a design engineer and a product strategist. He has been published in several journals and has been a contributing author on several technology textbooks with regard to cathode ray tube (CRT), plasma, liquid crystal display (LCD), and organic light-emitting diode (OLED) as well as serving as the vice-chair for the ASC MITC Professional Monitor Committee. Memberships include Commission Internationale de l’Eclairage (CIE), IEEE, Society for Information Displays (SID), The Optical Society (OSA), an Associate Member of the American Society of Cinematographers, and he is a SMPTE Fellow. He also serves on the SMPTE Board of Governors.
W. Thomas Wall is a retired computer systems designer and professional photographer. He is chief technology officer of LightView.

Gary Demos , received a BS degree in 1971 and a DAA degree from Caltech in 2018. He has been a pioneer in the development of computer-generated images and digital image processing for use in motion pictures. He was a founder of Digital Productions (1982–1986), and was awarded an Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences (AMPAS) Scientific and Engineering Award in 1984 along with John Whitney Jr. “For the Practical Simulation of Motion Picture Photograph By Means of Computer-Generated Images.” He also founded DemoGraFX (1988–2003), and Image Essence LLC, Perris, CA (2005 to present). He is a recipient of the AMPAS 2005 Gordon Sawyer Oscar for lifetime technical achievement. He is actively involved in the ASC Technology Committee and has worked on the AMPAS ACES project. He has presented numerous papers at SMPTE, given a SMPTE webinar, is a SMPTE Fellow, and received the 2012 SMPTE Digital Processing Medal. He is the inventor of approximately 100 patents.

title: Report from the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences’ Science and Technology Council
label: SMPTE Motion Imaging Journal ( Volume: 129, Issue: 8, September 2020)

SMPTE Motion Imaging Journal ( Volume: 129, Issue: 8, September 2020)

Craig Barron Co-chair, Academy Science and Technology Council. As a longtime innovator in the cinematic technique of matte painting, Craig Barron has contributed to the visual effects of more than 100 films. He began his career at ILM, working on such classic films as The Empire Strikes Back, Raiders of the Lost Ark and E.T. The Extra-Terrestrial. For nearly a quarter of a century he ran his own visual effects studio, Matte World Digital, which contributed to such productions as Titanic, Zodiac, Alice in Wonderland and Hugo. Barron received a Visual Effects Oscar® nomination for Batman Returns and won an Oscar for his work on The Curious Case of Benjamin Button. He is an Academy governor representing the Visual Effects Branch, and is now the creative director of Magnopus, producing augmented and virtual reality media in downtown Los Angeles.

Annie Chang Co-chair, Academy Science and Technology Council. As the vice president of creative technologies at Universal Pict-ures, Annie Chang is responsible for developing strategies and designing innovative next-generation workflows across film and emerging immersive media experiences. She was previously the vice president of technology for Marvel Studios and took on a variety of roles at the Walt Disney Studios during her more than one-decade tenure. Chang is a co-chair of the Academy’s Science and Technology Council and currently chairs the Council’s ACES project. A SMPTE fellow, she has also co-chaired the organization’s Essence (10E) Technology Committee and chaired its Interoperable Master Format (IMF) working group. Chang has been honored with the SMPTE Workflow Systems Medal Award and the Advanced Imaging Society’s Distinguished Leadership Award. She made StudioDaily’s inaugural list of “Exceptional Women in Production and Post” in 2018 and was named one of “Hollywood’s Top Innovators” by The Hollywood Reporter earlier this year.

Theodore E. Gluck Chair, Technology History Subcommittee. Theodore E. Gluck is a 29-year veteran of the Walt Disney Studios and is currently the director of library restoration and preservation at the company. He received his master’s degree in film studies from Boston University and was the teaching assistant for noted film scholar and author Roger Manvel. Since 2004 Gluck has been guiding the Walt Disney Studios’ restoration program, starting with the release of Bambi on DVD. He has worked on the restoration and preservation of more than 30 animated feature films, over 100 animated shorts, and several live-action features, and coordinated the digitization and preservation of a significant portion of the studio’s nitrate negatives of animated classics. A long-standing member of SMPTE, British Kinematograph, Sound and Television Society (BKSTS) and the Association of Moving Image Archivists (AMIA), Gluck has also lectured and written extensively on the history of cinema technologies, including widescreen processes, the development of Technicolor, and multi-channel stereo sound formats.

Leslie Iwerks Chair, Public Programs and Education Subcommittee. Leslie Iwerks is an Oscar® - and Emmy® -nominated director and producer. For over a decade, she has produced, directed, and edited award-winning feature and short documentaries, television specials, and digital content. Her body of work encompasses documentary films, including the recent critically acclaimed series for Disney+, The Imagineering Story, as well as Ella Brennan: Commanding the Table, The Pixar Story, Citizen Hearst, ILM: Creating the Impossible, Dirty Oil, The Hand Behind the Mouse, to her environmental documentaries that have all been nominated or shortlisted for Academy Awards; Recycled Life, Pipe Dreams, and Downstream, as well as her award-winning short documentary Selling Lies, chronicling the inside world of Macedonian fake news. Leslie is an active member of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences Documentary Branch, the Producers Guild of America, the Television Academy, the International Documentary Association, and serves on the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences’ Science and Technology Council as well as the USC School of Cinema Television Alumni Council.

Jeff Taylor Chair, Technology and Research Initiatives Subcommittee. Jeff Taylor began his entertainment career over thirty-eight years ago designing custom music recording consoles. In 1984, he moved into post-production at The Droid Works, a division of LucasFilm Ltd. There, Taylor wrote software for and trained editors on the EditDroid picture editing system, and served as an assistant picture editor on several television series and movies of the week. Taylor later consulted on the digital technology transformation of the animation department at Walt Disney Pictures Animation Group. He later worked at Sony Pictures as Managing Director of Research and Development. Taylor started at Universal Studios in 1995, where he currently serves as the vice president of Corporate Cinema Services. Taylor is a member of AES, SMPTE, the Academy of Television Arts and Sciences, and the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences where he serves on the Theater Standards Committee, the Scientific and Technical Awards Committee, and the Science and Technology Council.

Andy Maltz Senior Vice President, Science and Technology Council. Andy Maltz is the founding Head of Staff of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences’ Science Technology Council. He developed and implemented the Council’s operational plan, oversees the Council’s day-to-day operations, leads several Council projects and represents the Academy on motion picture science and technology matters at industry, government and academic forums in the U.S. and abroad. Prior to joining the Academy, Andy worked in the commercial world for over 20 years developing and deploying digital cinema servers and mastering systems, professional media authoring systems, nonlinear editing systems as well as working in film, television and commercial production. Andy is the chairman of ISO TC 36 Cinematography and is a fellow of the Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers (SMPTE), where he serves on the SMPTE Motion Imaging Journal Board of Editors. Andy is also a member of the Academy Software Foundation governing boardThe Council acknowledges the continued dedication and contributions to its work from its staff: Joe di Gennaro, Kathleen Dimpfl, Scott Dyer, Alex Forsythe, George Joblove, Ricardo Rodriguez, Dan Sherlock, Rita Sottile, Cesario Tio, Steve Tobenkin, Norma Vega, and Angiemarie Villafañe, and interns Stephanie Carlson, Bianca Cifuentes, Sarah Heysel and Simon Yahn.

Brad Gilmer is the president of Gilmer & Associates, Inc. He is a founding member of the Joint Task Force on Networked Media (JT-NM), the executive director of the Video Services Forum (VSF), and the executive director of the Advanced Media Workflow Association (AMWA). He is a SMPTE Fellow and the first recipient of the SMPTE Workflow Systems Medal. Earlier, he has worked with Turner Broadcasting System, Atlanta, GA, where he and his staff were responsible for engineering and operations for the entertainment division worldwide. He is an author and editor, contributing two times to the NAB Engineering Handbook, and serving as the editor-in-chief of the File Engineering Handbook. He has written many articles on computers and networking for industry publications.

Thomas Edwards is the vice president of Engineering & Development at Walt Disney Television, where he works on advanced technology development, such as ultrahigh-definition (UHD), over-the-top (OTT), and live IP production systems. Previously, he managed the engineering planning of the PBS video interconnection and streaming media for the ISP DIGEX. He holds an MS degree in electrical engineering from the University of Maryland, College Park, MD, and he is a board member of the AMWA, chairs the QoE/Measurement Working Group of the Streaming Video Alliance, chairs SMPTE 32NF-60 WG on Video over IP, is a SMPTE Fellow, and was awarded the SMPTE Workflow Systems Medal.

Felix Poulin is with the national public broadcaster CBC/Radio-Canada, where he is the director of the Media over IP Architecture and Lab. This Lab is currently evaluating IP-based equipment for the new headquarters to be on air in 2020. Before this mandate, he was a lead expert on live IP at the European Broadcasting Union (EBU), involved with the JT-NM, organizing training and events, coordinating expert groups and the multi-award winning VRT Sandbox LiveIP project. He received a Diploma degree in electrical engineering at Montreal’s Polytechnique, Montreal, QC, Canada, with his final thesis completed at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), Cambridge, MA. He is an active contributor to the SMPTE, EBU, and AMWA.

Neil Dunstan is the director, member, and marketing of the AMWA, managing recruitment and retention of members—and communicating the business value of AMWA projects to a broad audience. Daniel Silhavy is a scientist and project manager at the Business Unit Future Applications and Media (FAME) of the Fraunhofer Institute for Open Communication Systems (FOKUS) (Fraunhofer FOKUS, FAME), Berlin, Germany. He is also the lead developer of the dash.js project and the development coordinator for the 5G-Media Action Group (5G-MAG) Reference Tools. His main area of expertise includes adaptive bitrate (ABR) streaming focusing on MPEG-DASH, digital rights management (DRM), 5G media streaming, and video-encoding. He actively contributes to standardization work done in DASH-IF, 5G-MAG, and Consumer Technology Association-Web Application Video System (CTA-WAVE). Silhavy has published various technical papers covering topics around ABR media delivery and streaming analytics.

Christopher Krauss received a PhD degree (Dr.-Ing.) from the Technical University of Berlin (TU Berlin) with his dissertation “Time-Dependent Recommender Systems for the Prediction of Appropriate Learning Objects.” He works as media & data science lead at Fraunhofer FOKUS, FAME. He specializes in the research and development of topics dealing with machine learning, data science, technology enhanced learning, and connected TVs, and has been involved in multiple public funded projects (e.g., mEDUator, TripleAdapt, EXPAND+ER WB3, Smart Learning I & II, Digi-Hand, FI-Content I & II, User Centric Networking, and Global ITV) and managed many projects for different national and international industry customers.

Anita Chen has over ten years of technical management in the U.S., Germany, and China, with a focus on the research and development, automotive, health, and media industries. Chen received a BS degree from Business Information Technology, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA, in 2010, and an MS degree from Information Technology Management, TU Berlin, in 2020.

Anh-Tu Nguyen is a researcher and software developer at Fraunhofer FOKUS, FAME. He received bachelor’s and master’s degrees in industrial engineering from TU Berlin. Currently, he is involved in the deep encode project that optimizes video streaming processes using machine learning techniques. He is interested in the applications of machine learning in the computer vision field.

Christoph Müller studied computer science at TU Berlin. He received a degree from FOKUS, with the completion of his thesis “Machine Learning-Supported Adaptive Streaming Analytics” in 2018. He is currently employed as a project manager at FAME, where he is the lead technical project manager for “Deep Encode,” an AI-based solution for per-title and per-scene video encoding. His area of expertise lies in the research and development of modern web applications and machine learning in the context of video encoding, adaptive media streaming and streaming analytics, and has published numerous technical papers on these topics.

Stefan Arbanowski is director of Fraunhofer FOKUS, FAME. Arbanowski received PhD and MSc degrees in computer science from TU Berlin. Currently, he is managing Fraunhofer FOKUS’ NewTV activities, bundling expertise in the areas of interactive applications, web technologies, streaming and connected TV-channeling those toward networked media environments featuring live, on demand, context-aware, and personalized interactive content.

Stephan Steglich is director of the business unit at Fraunhofer, FOKUS, FAME. Steglich received MSc and PhD degrees in computer science from TU Berlin in 1998 and 2003, respectively. He is managing international and national level research activities and has been an organizer and a member of program committees of several international conferences. He is actively involved in standardization activities in these research areas and gives lectures at TU Berlin.

Louay Bassbouss is a scientist and senior project manager research and development at Fraunhofer, FOKUS, FAME. He works on future web applications, multiscreen technologies and standards, and 360° video technologies. Bassbouss actively participates in various standardization groups in the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C), Hybrid broadcast broadband TV (HbbTV), and CTA. He is the co-chair of the W3C Second Screen Working and Community Groups and actively contributes to various testing activities in HbbTV and CTA-WAVE.

Hojatollah Yeganeh received a PhD from the University of Waterloo, Waterloo, ON, Canada, in 2014. He is the principal video architect with SSIMWAVE Inc., Waterloo, where he leads the Research and Development (R&D) Team. He has designed and implemented many algorithms in the field of image and video quality assessment and has published number of journals and conference papers and holds several U.S. patents. He is a Senior Member of IEEE and is one of the recipients of the 2020 Technology and Engineering Emmy Award, which is given by the National Academy of Television Arts and Sciences (NATAS) for outstanding achievement in the development of perceptual metrics for video encoding optimization.

Kai Zeng received a PhD in electrical and computer engineering from the University of Waterloo, Waterloo, ON, Canada, in 2013. He is the Co-Founder and a Lead Researcher at SSIMWAVE Inc., Waterloo, with research interests including computational image and video processing, computer vision, multimedia communications, with emphasis on image and video quality assessment. He was one of the recipients of the 2020 Technology and Engineering Emmy Award which is given by the National Academy of Television Arts and Sciences (NATAS) for outstanding achievement in the development of perceptual metrics for video encoding optimization.

Zhou Wang received a PhD from the University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX, USA. He is a professor at the University of Waterloo, Waterloo, ON, Canada, holds the position of Canada Research Chair in Multimedia QoE, and directs the Image and Video Computing Laboratory focused on image/video quality assessment and optimization, machine learning, computational vision, and multimedia coding research. He is a co-founder and chief science officer of SSIMWAVE Inc., Waterloo, directing video quality-of-experience measurement and optimization solutions for industry. He received an Engineering Emmy Award for contributions to video quality assessment theories and technologies. He is a Fellow of the IEEE, the Royal Society of Canada, Ottawa, ON, Canada, and the Canadian Academy of Engineering, Ottawa. He has more than 200 publications with over 70,000 citations. His awards include IEEE Signal Processing Society Best Paper, IEEE Signal Processing Magazine Best Paper, IEEE-SPS Sustained Impact Paper, University of Waterloo Faculty of Engineering Research Excellence Award, and Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council Steacie Memorial Fellowship Award.

In 2018, he joined Ateme, Rennes, where he contributed to the world-first implementation of realtime VVC transcoder for video-on-demand and live streaming applications. He is currently with IRT b<> com, Rennes, holding the position of standardization engineer. His research interests include areas of signal processing, encoder optimization, machine learning, and quality assessment.

Thibaud Biatek received a PhD degree in signal and image processing from the Institut National des Sciences Appliquées, Rennes, France, in 2016. Since 2020, he has been director of technology and standards at Ateme, working on partnership projects and multimedia standards, contributing to MPEG, DVB, and 3GPP groups. His research interests include compression, processing, and delivery of audiovisual signals over broadcast and broadband networks.

Marina Bosi, a pioneer in the development of digital audio coding, is a founding director of the Moving Picture, Audio and Data Coding by Artificial Intelligence (MPAI) Organization, Geneva, Switzerland, and the chair of MPAI-Context-Based Audio Enhancement (MPAI-CAE). Gérard Chollet studied linguistics, electrical engineering, and computer science at the University of California at Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, CA, where he was granted a PhD in computer science and linguistics. Franesco Banterle is a researcher with the Visual Computing Laboratory at Consiglio Nazionale delle Richerch- (CNR)-Institute of Information Science and Technologies (ISTI), Pisa, Italy. Alessandro Artusi received a PhD in computer science from the Vienna University of Technology, Vienna, Austria, in 2004. He is the team leader of the DeepCamera Group at CYENS Nicosia, Cyprus. Francesco Gissi received an MSc in computer engineering. He is currently pursuing a PhD in information technology for engineering with the University of Sannio, Benevento, Italy. Attilio Fiandrotti received a PhD in computer science from the Politecnico di Torino, Turin, Italy, in 2010. Giovanni Ballocca received a master’s in physics from the Università di Torino, Turin, Italy. Marco Mazzaglia is a video game evangelist for Synesthesia, Italy. Since 2008, he has worked on more than 30 original titles and conversions on last-generation game consoles and for the B2B world. He is an adjunct professor of game design and gamification for the Polytechnic of Turin, Turin, Italy, at the master’s degree courses for cinema and media engineering and computer engineering.

Scott Moskowitz graduated cum laude from the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. He holds more than 110 patents in digital watermarks, product license keys, address space layout randomization (ASLR), and so on. He is a senior member of Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE), Assoication for Computing Machinery (ACM), and Society of Photographic Instrumentation Engineers (SPIE). Curtis Clark, ASC studied theater directing at the Art Institute of Chicago’s Goodman School of Drama and cinematography at the London Film School. After graduation, he began his career by shooting and directing documentary films in Britain before transitioning to shooting feature films and TV commercials in Britain and the U.S. Curtis received the 2012 American Society of Cinematographers (ASC) President’s Award, as well as the prestigious 2019 Motion Picture Academy’s John A. Bonner Award in recognition of his extraordinary service to the motion picture industry. As a member of the Academy of Motion Pictures Arts and Sciences (AMPAS), Clark worked on the development and implementation of ACES, the Academy’s Color Encoding System. Curtis has also overseen numerous achievements as Chairman of the ASC Motion Imaging Technology Council, which he has helmed since its inception in 2003. Under Clarke’s leadership, the Council collaborated with Digital Cinema Initiatives, LLC (DCI) to produce standard evaluation material for assessing the performance of projectors and other elements of DCI standards-based digital cinema systems, as well as the 2009 Camera Assessment Series and 2012 Image Control Assessment Series. Curtis also supported the Council’s groundbreaking project to create cross-platform data exchange for primary RGB digital color correction, known as the ASC CDL (Color Decision List). The ASC CDL was recognized by the Academy of Television Arts and Sciences with a 2012 Primetime Emmy Award, and Curtis received a 2014 AMPAS Technical Achievement Award for his work on the ASC CDL. Most recently, Clark served as executive producer on the “Standard Evaluation Material V2” (StEM2), the follow-up to the ASC’s original StEM project. StEM2 has been created to address the challenges of utilizing an increasingly complex digital motion imaging workflow to create and maintain the integrity of the filmmaker’s creative intent. In recognition of his motion imaging technology leadership over the past 20 years, the ASC has created this year a new ASC Award, the “Curtis Clark Technical Achievement Award,” which will be awarded annually to a selected recipient acknowledging outstanding technical achievement.

David Reisner received a 2014 Academy Technical Achievement Award, a 2014 Hollywood Post Alliance Judges Award for Creativity and Innovation, and in 2012 was recognized by the Academy of Television Arts and Sciences with a prestigious Prime Time EMMY Engineering Award as co-creator, co-designer, and project lead of the ASC CDL – used in the workflow of nearly every motion picture, scripted TV, and visual effects turnover worldwide. Reisner conceived, proposed, was lead-designer, and co-producer of the ASC-DCI StEM Standard Evaluation Material which set the quality required to convert the world’s movie system from film to digital, and Vice-Chaired the SMPTE Working Groups responsible for digital cinema imaging - showing on nearly all cinema screens worldwide - and security standards - protecting $35B of IP each year. He also had leading roles in conception, design, and production of the ASC-PGA CAS Camera Assessment Series, the ICAS Image Control Assessment Series, and elements of the Academy Color Encoding System. Reisner has been a Founder, a Partner, and a CTO in computer and in entertainment companies. He helped originate digital audio and his “firsts” include the handheld programmable computer, the handheld digital media player, the portable source-level debugger, 57,000-bit Very Very Long Integer arithmetic, and VLIW computer architecture - one of the original enablers of multi-processor computing. He provided editorial assistance on the first textbook on neural network Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning, originated Pervasive Computing - a parent of Internet of Things/IoT, proposed emergent networking for smart dust, and helped develop the first popular byte-code virtual machine (before Java’s JVM). He has shot celebrity and fashion for books and magazines including Vogue Italia, produced concerts internationally, and trained killer whales. Reisner is well-published in books and technical articles, has spoken widely including NAB, SMPTE, IMAGO, and a 29,000-viewer webcast, and on manned space exploration to a standing-room-only crowd at the 2014 International Space Development Conference. He is a SMPTE Fellow; Vice-Chair and Founding-Secretary of the ASC Motion Imaging Technology Council; an ASC Associate; a Member of the Visual Effects Society; a co-author of the “VES Handbook of Visual Effects”; and his committees have recommended some of the highest profile Academy Scientific and Technical Awards.

Gary Demos has been a pioneer in the development of computergenerated images and digital image processing for use in motion pictures. He co-founded Digital Productions (1982–1986), and was awarded an Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences (AMPAS) Scientific and Engineering Award in 1984 along with John Whitney Jr. “For the Practical Simulation of Motion Picture Photograph By Means of Computer-Generated Images.” Demos also founded DemoGraFX (1988–2003), and Image Essence LLC, Perris, CA (2005 to present). Annie Chang is the co-chair of the Academy Science and Technology Council. Prior to joining Universal Pictures, Chang was the VP, Technology for Marvel Studios and held various roles at the Walt Disney Studios. During her career, she has chaired many industry-leading committees and has been honored with numerous industry awards including being named on The Hollywood Reporter’s list of top “Hollywood Innovators” in 2020. Theodore E. Gluck is the chair of the Technology History Subcommittee. Theodore E. Gluck is currently the Director of Library Restoration and Preservation at Visual Data Media Services after 30 years with the Walt Disney Studios. He received his master’s degree in film studies from Boston University. During his tenure at Disney, Gluck worked with film operations, distribution, foreign language dubbing, and library restoration. Gluck worked on the restoration and preservation of more than 30 animated feature films, over 100 animated shorts, and several live-action features, and coordinated the digitization and preservation of a significant portion of the Disney’s nitrate negatives of animated classics. A long-standing member of SMPTE, BKSTS and AMIA, Gluck has also lectured and written extensively on the history of cinema technologies, including widescreen processes, the development of Technicolor, and multi-channel stereo sound formats.

Leslie Iwerks is the chair of the Public Programs and Education Subcommittee. Leslie Iwerks is an Oscar- and Emmy®-nominated director and producer. For two decades, Leslie has created enterprise documentaries (Superpowered: The DC Story, The Imagineering Story, Ella Brennan: Commanding the Table), along with environmental and social issue documentaries (Selling Lies, Recycled Life). Leslie has filmed on all seven continents, and her work can be seen across multiple streaming platforms. Leslie is a member of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences Documentary Branch, the Directors Guild of America, the Producers Guild of America, the Television Academy, and serves the USC School of Cinema Television Alumni Council. Mauricio Aracena serves as the president of the Virtual Reality Industry Forum (VRIF), Fremont, CA, and is the media standardization manager at Ericsson, Stockholm, Sweden. With more than 20 years of experience working with multimedia technologies for the mobile phone industry, he has actively contributed to defining the next generation of multimedia standards for 3GPP, ATSC, and DVB. He is currently is leading the standardization strategy for XR within Ericsson.

Mick O’Doherty works as a technical solutions manager with Irdeto, Sligo, Ireland, focusing on partners in the video content security domain. He is originally from Dublin, Ireland, and has worked in a number of countries over the last 20 years, mainly the U.K., Turkey, and Canada. His background is in telecoms audio and video software and systems development, but he has worked on the operator side of the table also as well as with a number of web and mobile start-ups, mainly in the West of Ireland. He has previously worked in standards in the Java JAIN area and supported standards efforts in the SIP domain. He is currently active in the VRIF, focusing on immersive media security.

Oliver Schreer is the head of the Immersive Media and Communication Research Group, Vision and Imaging Technologies Department, Fraunhofer HHI, Berlin, Germany, and an associate professor at Technical University, Berlin. His main research fields are 3D video processing and immersive and interactive media services and applications exploiting augmented and virtual reality (VR) technologies. He has published more than 140 articles and acted as the main editor of several books. In May 2019, he and his colleagues I. Feldmann and P. Kauff were awarded the Joseph-von-Fraunhofer Prize titled “Realistic People in Virtual Worlds—A Movie as a True Experience.”

Sebastian Schwarz is a research leader in the Video Coding Research Team, Nokia Technologies, Munich, Germany. His main research topics are compression and delivery of volumetric video content. He has authored more than 40 conference papers and journal articles on immersive media and video coding topics. He was an editor of the ISO/IEC committee draft for video-based point cloud compression (ISO/IEC 23090-5) and a cochair of the MPEG Ad Hoc Group on System Technologies for V-PCC.

Thierry Fautier most recently was the vice president of video strategy at Harmonic, San Jose, CA, where he defined and drove the execution of innovation and standards for the company’s video business. He was also responsible for building strategic partnerships through active participation in industry groups such as the Streaming Video Alliance (SVA), Fremont, CA, (co-chair of the virtual reality (VR) group), the Ultra HD Forum, Fremont (co-founder and past president), the VR Industry Forum (VRIF), Fremont (co-founder and past board member), the IABM, Tewkesbury, U.K., and the 8K Association, Beaverton, OR. Additionally, he was part of the team honored with the 2020 Technology and Engineering Emmy® Award for its pioneering work in artificial intelligence (AI) optimization for realtime video compression.

Patrick Gendron is the director, Innovation at Harmonic for Digital Television Applications, San Jose, CA. He recently moved from managing the Harmonic Research and Development Innovation team to the Marketing Innovation and Evangelism team and is Harmonic’s representative at Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP (DASH) IF, DVB TM, and Streaming Video Alliance. He joined Harmonic with the acquisition of Thomson Video Networks. Previously, he held the senior program and engineering management positions in the digital television headend domain, with international research and development management activities at Grass Valley and Nextream.

Xavier Ducloux is the senior innovation manager at Harmonic, San Jose, CA, and oversees monitoring technological breakthroughs and developing innovation in the video delivery domain, including technology and ecosystem partnerships. With 28 years’ experience in the digital TV industry, he has led a vast range of video compression projects with the Thomson Group and Harmonic, representing both companies in MPEG. He frequently speaks at industry-leading conferences across the world, is the author of many international publications and holds multiple patents in video compression and delivery.

Vincent Lepec is a research and development engineer in the Innovation Team at Viaccess-Orca (VO), managing anticipation, prototypes, and studies. He is a recognized digital and media expert in innovation initiatives, from research on collaborative projects to standardization actions in advanced video domains, including immersive video experiences. He holds a double research master’s degree in innovative and immersive technologies from the Arts & Metiers ParisTech Engineering Institution, Paris, France, (in collaboration with Laval Virtual, LAMPA Lab, and CLARTE Association), some of the pioneering institutions developing virtual reality (VR) technologies in France.

Pascal Perrot is the head of video coding and distribution solutions at Orange Innovation. Previously, he was the senior innovation director at Viaccess-Orca (VO). He joined VO from Orange, where he had worked for seven years at Orange Labs in the field of broadcast TV systems and metadata. He worked for VO as a standardization expert and remains active for VO and Orange in many different ongoing standardization efforts, including DVB, VRIF, SVA, HbbTV, and more. He is a member of the Solutions for Content Services Orange Expert community, and takes the lead for VO in many innovative and collaborative projects for the company in the fields of VR, data analytics, and antipiracy. He holds a masters in computer science from Rennes University.

Frederic Plissonneaugraduated from INSA, Rennes, France, in 1988 and has worked in the video compression domain as an engineer/team leader and project leader in the field of ASIC technologies. He is currently focused on HDR within R&I Video Lab, Rennes.

Bill Redmann is the director of Standards for Immersive Media Technologies at Interdigital, Wilmington, DE. He contributes to Next-Gen Media standards in several standards organizations. Robin Le Naour is a senior engineer at Interdigital, Wilmington, DE. He has a background in real time software development, system architecture and image/video processing. He currently works on HDR at the R&I Video Lab, Rennes, France.

Patrick Morvan is a senior research and development engineer at Interdigital, Wilmington, DE. He joined Thomson Research Labs, Rennes, France, in 1990. He has been involved in several innovative projects aimed at developing new video formats. Over the past 15 years, he has developed an expertise in color science for cinema and broadcast applications. His current research is focused on color management and perception for high dynamic range workflows.

Laurent Cauvin is a senior engineer at Interdigital, Wilmington, DE. He has been working on image and video processing since 1985. He is now involved in HDR imaging, mainly in the inverse tone mapping domain (algorithms, system architecture, and hardware and software porting).

Nick Mitchell is an accomplished entertainment technology professional with two decades of experience. As CTO and senior technology consultant at WildAcre Company, his technology and creative services firm, he plays a pivotal role in developing and delivering innovative technologies, strategies, and services for a diverse range of organizations.

Alan Stein leads InterDigital’s Visual Standards team of technical experts participating in video standards and industry forums. He is a board member and marketing chair of MC-IF and long-time chair of ATSC’s TG3/S41 group, the video group for ATSC 3.0. He received ATSC’s Bernard Lechner Award in 2021. In this role, he develops and improves core Dolby imaging technology as well as performs research to model human perception for the design of image-processing algorithms. He received a BS degree in motion picture science from the Rochester Institute of Technology (RIT), Rochester, NY, in 2019. While at RIT, he performed a senior research project to assess the creative preference of highly saturated colors in content mastered for wide color gamut display.

Jaclyn Pytlarz is a senior staff researcher at Dolby Laboratories, Sunnyvale, CA, where she leads Dolby’s Vision Science Research Organization. Her research includes studying human perception surrounding color mapping, accessibility, and display management algorithms for high dynamic range and wide color gamut imagery. She holds a BS degree in motion picture science from the Rochester Institute of Technology, Rochester, NY, and an MS degree in computational and mathematical engineering from Stanford University, Stanford, CA. Prior to joining Dolby, she worked as an intern for both the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, Los Angeles, CA, and iCONN Video Production, Mount Vernon, OH. Robert Wanat is a staff researcher, Media Technologies at LG Electronics Zenith R&D. His work includes research collaboration with industry and academia partners as well as standards organizations participation. He is an active participant of multiple industry and standards organizations. Prior to joining LGE Zenith R&D, he was a color scientist at Dolby Laboratories, conducting research that would eventually become Dolby Vision IQ. His professional interests include human visual perception modeling, high dynamic range imaging, objective image quality metrics, and matching image perception across varying viewing conditions. He holds a PhD degree in computer science from Bangor University, Bangor, U.K.

Alexander Carpenter contributed research for this project with Media Technologies Engineer for the Strategic Technology Projects Team at LG’s Silicon Valley Lab. They earned a BSc degree in motion picture science from the Rochester Institute of Technology, Rochester, NY, where they conducted research in ambient adaptation for consumer displays. They currently act as a color management software engineer in the Bay Area. They are passionate about enabling the artist to achieve their vision and preserving creative intent when their art is shared with the world.

Michael D. Smith has worked as a digital imaging and intellectual property consultant for 20 years. He has worked on projects for many organizations including Warner Bros., Sony Pictures Entertainment. He was the coeditor of the High-Throughput JPEG 2000 image compression standard that was published in 2019. In 2018, he received a screen credit for his color science work on Mary Poppins Returns. From 2013–2015, he was the co-chair of Blu-ray Disc Association’s UHD-TF Video subgroup which defined the video-related requirements for the Ultra-HD Blu-ray disk format. In 2012, his work on Warner Bros. Digital End to End (DETE) system led to winning a Technical Emmy. In addition to novel technology achievements, he has done extensive work in intellectual property. His work on more than 40 IP matters related to infringement and validity of patents has resulted in settlements and judgments of approximately $1.7 billion. He was the editor of the book titled 3D Cinema and Television Technology: The First100 Years published by SMPTE in 2011 and achieved SMPTE Fellow in 2019. He received BS and MS degrees in electrical engineering from UCLA, Los Angeles, CA, in 2001 and 2004, respectively.

Sally Hattori is the director, product development at StudioLAB, The Walt Disney Studios, where she works on advanced technology projects for post-production and distribution technologies such as workflow development for next generation media (4K/UHD, HDR, and immersive audio), machine learning for content production and management, and new entertainment experiences. Prior to joining 20th Century Fox in 2014, now part of The Walt Disney Studios, she served as a senior engineer of technology strategy and standards at Sony Corporation, where she was responsible for various strategic planning and standardizations on video codecs, media applications, and media services. She has contributed to developing various technologies and standards working with various manufactures, content providers, and technology companies. She has received multiple awards for innovative patents and international standards development. She holds a master’s degree in information and communication engineering from Waseda University, Tokyo, Japan.

Yasser Syed is a distinguished architect at Comcast, whose work focuses on developing and implementing next-generation video technologies and workflows. He received a PhD in electrical engineering from the University of Texas at Arlington. He has contributed a substantial amount of content and effort to many video standards-related areas. Currently, he chairs the Society of Cable Telecommunications Engineers (SCTE) Working Group 7 (WG7) on DASH/adaptive streaming and also leads its Advanced Coding Technologies group, which created the high-dynamic-range (HDR) application and next-generation codec constraint specifications for the cable industry. He is also a 2021 recipient of the SCTE award for excellence in standards.

Alex Giladi is a Comcast fellow and an Emmy-winning technologist. He has been working on issues related to video content encoding and distribution since 2000. His current areas of interest are video encoding and adaptive streaming. He currently leads an advanced technologies group within Comcast. Prior to Comcast, he worked on various aspects video transport and video coding in InterDigital, Huawei, Vubiquity, Digital Fountain, and Harmonic. He has been a prolific contributor to the MPEG-DASH standard and served as an editor of several standards and amendments related to DASH, content security, and MPEG-2 Systems. He is the vice president of the DASH Industry Forum since 2019. He is the founder and co-organizer of the popular Mile-High Video annual conference series held in Denver, CO, since 2017. He holds an MSEE degree from Stanford University, Stanford, CA, and a BSc degree from Technion, Haifa, Israel. He is a senior member of the IEEE and holds more than 50 U.S. patents.

Erik Reinhard is a distinguished scientist at InterDigital Cesson-Sévigné, France, since June 2019. Before that, he held the same position at Technicolor R&I Cesson-Sevigné, starting in July 2013 and before that he held various academic positions at universities and research institutes in Europe and North America. He was the founder and editor-in-chief of ACM Transactions on Applied Perception and authored books on high dynamic range (HDR) imaging, color imaging, computer graphics, and natural image statistics. He has published more than 100 papers and was a member of more than 50 program committees. He was a program co-chair of six conferences and workshops, including the Eurographics Symposium on Rendering 2011. He delivered keynotes at Eurographics 2010, the Computational Color Imaging Workshop 2011, the IS&T European Conference on Color in Graphics, Imaging, and Vision 2012, the IS&T Color Imaging Conference 2022, and the ACM/SIGGRAPH Conference on Visual Media Processing 2022. He is the co-chair of the Rapporteur Group on Energy Aware Broadcasting at ITU-R and co-lead of the Study Mission on Energy Aware Service Delivery and Consumption at DVB. Finally, he won a test of time award for his color transfer paper in IEEE Computer Graphics and Applications

Claire-Hélène Demarty is a senior scientist at InterDigital Cesson-Sévigné, France. She graduated from Telecom ParisTech, Paris, France, in 1994 and received a PhD degree in computer science and mathematical morphology, from Mines ParisTech, Paris, in 2000. She joined InterDigital Research & Innovation Center in 2019 as a senior scientist. Before InterDigital, she worked at Technicolor Cesson-Sevigné (2004–2018), LTUTechnologies, Paris (2002–2004), and INRIA Rennes—IRISA, Rennes, France (2003–2004), as a researcher in image analysis and computer vision technologies. Her research focuses on multimedia indexing technologies and perceptual understanding of content, through the use of machine learning, and more recently energy-aware media. She is the author or coauthor of more than 30 papers and holds several patents.

Laurent Blondé is a seasoned principal scientist at InterDigital Cesson-Sévigné, France. He graduated from Institut d’Optique Graduate School Palaiseau, France, in 1985 and received a PhD degree in signal and image processing from Rennes University, Rennes, France. His career has focused in part on various applications of image analysis, synthesis, depth, and color vision, mainly for TV and cinema applications. He has also focused on optics, light propagation understanding, light-matter interaction at wavelength scale, and metasurfaces. In his toolbox, he has image processing, mathematics, teamwork experience, and, mostly, creative thinking. He likes working in an international environment and enjoys interacting with diverse people from various cultures and fields of expertise. He is the author and co-author of papers and patents.
