He is currently conducting studies and experiments on converged networks and systems. He has participated in many European projects and is the author of several technical papers.

Assunta De Vita received an MS degree in telecommunications engineering and a PhD degree in information technology for engineering from the University of Sannio, Benevento, Italy, in 2006 and 2010, respectively. Since 2012, she has been a research engineer with the RAI—Radiotelevisione Italiana Research Center, Turin, Italy. Her current scientific interests include all the aspects related to mobile and fixed networks, that is, the study of different network solutions for large-scale TV content delivery toward personal consumer devices. In this context, she is currently involved in the activities promoted by European Broadcasting Union (EBU) and 5G-Media Action Group (5G-MAG) aimed to investigate the potentialities offered by 5G technology for media companies and follow the evolution of the standardization process within the 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP).

Alessandro Lucco Castello received a bachelor’s degree in computer engineering from the Polytechnic of Turin, Turin, Italy, in 2017. His current scientific interests include all the aspects related to mobile and fixed networks with a particular focus on field measurement and testing in the perspective of a possible 4G/5G mobile TV converged scenario.

Vittoria Mignone graduated from Politecnico di Torino, Turin, Italy, in 1990. Since 1992, she has been with the Center for Research of RAI Radiotelevisione Italiana, Turin, involved in studies related to the definition of Digital Video Broadcasting (DVB) standards for digital television by satellite, cable, and terrestrial channels. Her activities are in the field of physical layer system definition, particularly concerning advanced digital modulation and channel coding techniques for satellite and terrestrial transmissions, participating in several European research and development projects and standardization bodies. She chairs the DVB TM-S group, which develops technical specifications related to satellite transmissions, and is a member of the Steering Group of the 5G-MAG consortium, which promotes the use of 5G in the media world. She is an author of patents and technical articles in leading international journals and conferences.

Giovanni Vitale received an MS degree in telecommunications engineering from Politecnico di Torino, Turin, Italy, in 2007. He has been employed at Radiotelevisione italiana (RAI) Research Center (RAI-CRITS), Turin, since 2008. He has been involved in the standardization process of several Digital Video Broadcasting (DVB) standards (DVB-SH, DVB-T2, DVB-C2, DVB-S2/S2X, and DVB-NGH), then he moved to RAI-CRITS Laboratory Tests and Field Trials Department, where he is mainly involved in studies related to 5G-broadcast and DAB+. He is also an author of several technical papers and a patent inventor.

Les Kozlowski is currently a chief Technologist at Rockwell Scientific. He heads a team that is being spun off as a separate company for the specific purpose of supplying CMOS imaging systems-on-a-chip for high- and ultra-high definition cameras. Les received the B. S. and M. S. degrees in Electrical Engineering from the University of Illinois at Chicago in 1975 and 1977, respectively. He joined Rockwell Scientific in 1987, previously led the Mixed-Signal VLSI department, and was honored as a Rockwell Engineer of the Year for 1995. At Rockwell, Mr. Kozlowski has served as Principal Investigator on many development programs that advanced significantly the state-of-the-art of electro-optic sensors with respect to reducing noise while increasing array size. An example known to the general public is the infrared sensor in the Hubble Space Telescope, which has helped revolutionize astronomy and our understanding of the universe. Previously, as a Principal Scientist at Hughes Aircraft in Canoga Park, CA, he had similar responsibilities. In addition to helping to develop the world's largest high-performance imaging sensors, he has developed other imagers having unique performance attributes including extremely low read noise and power dissipation at high data rates. His areas of expertise include compact, low-noise analog circuits, high-density silicon CMOS and CCD multiplexers, and electro-optic sensors. He has helped design about 100 imaging sensors, has well over one hundred publication, eleven patents, and is a member of the IEEE Electron Devices Society, SMPTE and SPIE.

Larry Thorpe is a renowned industry expert in the field of video acquisition, and is generally considered to be one of leaders of the HDTV movement. His impressive list of accomplishments include pioneering HDTV market development in the United States, and holding ten patents in the field of broadcast development. Mr. Thorpe was promoted to his current position as Vice President of Acquisition Systems for the Broadcast and Professional Company, Sony Electronics Inc., in 1995. He has business responsibility for all of the broadcast studio and portable cameras (including HDTV) for the Sony Division. Prior to his current position, Mr. Thorpe was Vice President of Production Technology for Sony Advanced Systems. He was responsible for HDTV market development and represented Sony on ATSC technology groups, as well as various SMPTE working groups dealing with High Definition Electronic Production. Additionally, Mr. Thorpe is a Fellow of SMPTE. He sat on the advisory committees and working groups for ATSC, FCC and SMPTE in HDTV standards development. In this role, he has published many papers on camera technology and the topic of HDTV imaging. In 1982, Mr. Thorpe joined Sony Electronics as Director of Studio Product Management, which included Sony's entire line of broadcast video cameras and field equipment Additionally, he served as principal technical consultant on HDTV which was in its infancy at the time. Mr. Thorpe worked for RCA's Broadcast Division from 1966 to 1982, where he developed a range of color television cameras and telecine products. In 1981, Mr. Thorpe won the David Sarnoff Award for his innovations in automatic studio color cameras. From 1961 to 1966, Mr. Thorpe worked in the Designs Dept. of the BBC in London, England, where he participated in the development of a range of color television studio products. Mr. Thorpe is an IEE Graduate (1961) of the College of Technology in Dublin, Ireland and received his Chartered Engineer (C. Eng) and MIEE distinction in 1961 from the Institute of Electrical Engineers in London, England. Mr. Thorpe currently lives in Monte Sereno, California, with his wife.

Tom Coughlin, President, Coughlin Associates is a widely respected storage analyst and consultant. He has over 28 years in the data storage industry with multiple engineering and management positions at high profile companies. — Tom has many publications and six patents to his credit. Tom is also the author of Digital Storage in Consumer Electronics: The Essential Guide, which was published by Newnes Press in March 2008. Coughlin Associates provides market and technology analysis (including reports on several digital storage technologies and applications and a newsletter) as well as Data Storage Technical Consulting services. Coughlin Associates publishes an annual Digital Storage for Media and Entertainment Report. — Dr. Coughlin is active with SMPTE, IDEMA, SNIA, the IEEE and other professional organizations. Tom is the founder and organizer of the Annual Storage Visions Conference (www.storagevisions.com), a partner to the annual Consumer Electronics Show as well as the Creative Storage Conference held before the NAB show (www.creativestorage.org). Tom is also the chairman of the annual Flash Memory Summit. He is also a Leader in the Gerson Lehrman Group Councils of Advisors and a member of the Consultants Network of Silicon Valley (CNSV). For more information on Tom or his publications go to www.tomcoughlin.com.

Steve Bilow received his BFA from California Institute of the Arts in 1982 with studies in music technology and video. He pursued graduate studies in computer science at Portland State University with research interests in computer graphics, object-oriented methodology, and software metrics. Bilow has held positions on the executive committees for the ACM OOPSLA conferences, the Los Angeles chapter of the Audio Engineering Society, and the Computer-Human Interaction Forum of Oregon. He was book review editor for the Journal of Object-oriented Programming and is the author of more than 60 publications. He is currently marketing manager for the ContentShare Platform and other Media Software Products at the Grass Valley Group Inc., Beaverton, Oregon. Mr. Bilow is a member of SMPTE and the Association of Computing Machinery.

Scott Libert received his BFA from the University of Hawaii in 1987 with studies in electronic music and computer programming. Libert has worked 12 years in the telecommunications, multimedia and video industries designing and implementing distributed systems applications with a focus on object-oriented design. He has authored several articles on distributed software architecture and has a U.S. patent pending for the ContentShare Platform. He is currently Chief Architect for the ContentShare Platform at the Grass Valley Group Inc., Beaverton, Oregon.

Anil M. Murching received the B. Tech. degree in electronics and communication engineering from the Indian Institute of Technology, Madras, India, in 1991, and the MS degrees in electrical engineering and mathematics, and the PhD degree in electrical engineering from Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute (RPI), Troy, New York, in 1992, 1995 and 1997, respectively. He is currently with the Grass Valley Group Inc., Beaverton, Oregon. His research interests include content-based image and video indexing, parsing, searching, and browsing, video compression, and video segmentation. He is the author of seven journal and conference papers, and has twelve U.S. patents pending in image and video segmentation. Dr. Murching is a member of the IEEE and Sigma Xi.

Dave Slack has an extensive background in television technology having served as chief engineer at the New England Sports Network and in a variety of applications engineering, marketing and engineering management positions. Mr. Slack is currently Program Manager for the ContentShare Platform at the Grass Valley Group Inc., Beaverton, Oregon.

Joseph A. Flaherty received a degree in physics from the University of Rockhurst, Kansas City, Missouri, in 1952 and began his television career at WDAF-TV in that city. From 1953–1954 he served with the U.S. Army Signal Corps and in 1955 joined NBC-TV in New York City as a television engineer. In 1957, he joined CBS as a television design engineer. In 1959, he became the network's director of technical facilities planning, and in 1967 was promoted to general manager, and subsequently appointed vice president and general manager, engineering and development. He is responsible for all television and radio engineering and development activities for the CBS Broadcast Group, including planning and coordinating the development of new equipment and installation of technical facilities. He is a Fellow of the SMPTE and has been the SMPTE Vice President for Television Affairs and the SMPTE Executive Vice President. Mr. Flaherty is a Fellow of the Institution of Electrical Engineers (IEE), United Kingdom, a Fellow of the Royal Television Society (RTS), United Kingdom, a member of the Society Fernseh-und Kinotechnischen Gasellschaft (FKTG), F. R. Germany, a member of the Societe des Electriciens, des Radiolectriciens (SEE), France, and an honorary member of the Institute of Television Engineers of Japan. Mr. Flaherty is chairman of the Planning Subcommittee of the FCC's Advisory Committee on Advanced Television Service, a member of the Executive Committee of the Montreux International Television Symposium, a member of the Executive Committee of the Advanced Television Systems Committee (ATSC), and a member of the USIA Advisory Committee on Television Telecommunications. Mr. Flaherty was a recipient of an Emmy Award citation for the CBS Minicam color camera in 1969 and was the 1974 recipient of the David Sarnoff Gold Medal for progress in television engineering. Mr. Flaherty received for CBS the 1975 technical Emmy Award for electronic news gathering, and in 1979 received the Montreux Achievement Gold Medal for the development of the concept and the operational implementation of electronic news gathering. In 1983, Mr. Flaherty was the recipient of the National Association of Broadcasters Engineering Award. In 1984 he received the SMPTE Progress Medal Award. In February 1985 Mr. Flaherty was nominated to the rank of Chevalier de l'Ordre National de la Legion d'Honneur by President Mitterand of the Republic of France. In September 1986 Mr. Flaherty received for CBS the Emmy Award for the electronic editing system for programs produced on film.
affiliations: CBS Engineering and Development Dept. New York, New York

Andy Lippman is associate director of MIT's Media Laboratory. He is currently director of the electronic publishing group within the lab and is principal investigator of a new reseach program addressing the “future of the movies.” This program focuses on the intelligent interaction between computing and sequential visual images. A highlight of it is “paperback movies,” work to compress a movie into a digital representation suitable for distribution on a compact disc. In the past, he directed the architecture machine group and led the development of such interactive systems as the Movie-Map, a videodisc-based map of Aspen, Colorado, and the Movie Manual, an electronic book. In addition, he directed research programs on teleconferencing, news information systems, display technology, and high-definition television.

Dr. Arun N. Netravali is director of the Computing Systems Research Laboratory at AT&T Bell Laboratories, with reponsibility for research in artificial intelligence, VLSI design aids and architectures, communication networks, distributed computing, programming languages, software engineering, and interactive systems. He joined Bell Laboratories in 1972 as a member of the technical staff, became head of the Visual Communications Research Department in 1978, and assumed his current position in 1983. He was at NASA from 1970 to 1972, where he worked on problems related to filtering, guidance, and control for the space shuttle. He has been an adjunct professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology since 1984, and has taught graduate courses at City College, Columbia University, and Rutgers University. Dr. Natravali received the B. Tech (Honors) degree from the Indian Institute of Technology, Bombay, India, in 1967 and M.S. and Ph.D. degrees from Rice University, Houston, Texas, in 1969 and 1970, respectively, all in electrical engineering. He received the Donald G. Fink Award for the best review paper published in the Proceedings of the IEEE in 1980, the journal award for the best paper from the Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers in 1982, and the L. G. Abraham Award for the best paper by the IEEE Communications Society in 1985. He is an avid tennis player and has won several local championships.

Edward H. Adelson received a B.A. in physics and philosophy from Yale in 1974 and a PH.D. in experimental psychology from the University of Michigan in 1979. From 1981 to 1986 he was on the research staff of RCA Sarnoff Labs in Princeton, N.J., where he worked on visual psychophysics, machine vision, and digital image processing. He was awarded the Adolph Lomb Medal by the Optical Society of America in 1984. In 1987 he joined the MIT Media Laboratory as an associate professor; he also holds a joint appointment with the MIT Department of Brain and Cognitive Science. He has published over twenty papers and holds four U.S. patents.

W. Russell Neuman is an associate professor in the Media Laboratory and Department of Policital Science at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. His publications include: The Future of the Mass Audience, Harvard University Press, forthcoming; The Paradox of Mass Politics: Knowledge and Opinion in the American Electorate, Harvard University Press, 1986; The Social Impact of Television, Aspen Institute, 1981; “Television and American Culture,” Public Opinion Quarterly, 1982; “Patterns of Political Cognition,” in Kraus and Perloff (eds.) Mass Media and Political Thought, Sage, 1985; and “The Flow of Information into the Home” in Ball-Rokeach and Cantor (eds.) Media, Audience and Social Structure, Sage, 1986. His Ph.D. in sociology is from the University of California at Berkeley. Before joining the faculty at MIT he taught at Yale University. His current research includes projects on telecommunications policy, interactive media, and public learning from broadcast and print news media.

Dr. Schreiber worked at Sylvania from 1947 to 1949 and at Technicolor Corp. in Hollywood, Calif from 1953 to 1959. Since then he has been a faculty member at MIT, where he is now professor of electrical engineering and director of the advanced television research program. This work has included theory and extensive practical applications. He is a Fellow of the IEEE, an Honors Award recipient of the Technical Association of Graphics Arts, and has twice received the best paper award of the SMPTE Journal.

Matthew Addis leads a diverse portfolio of collaborative applied research projects at the University of Southampton IT Innovation, including media archiving and digital preservation, risk management in online communities, and smart laboratory systems to name a few. Addis currently works on cost models, uncertainty and service-oriented approaches to distributed systems. He has spent more than ten years working closely with broadcasters, post houses, and film archives to develop strategies, models, tools and systems for audiovisual restoration, preservation, and archiving. Through projects including AVATAR-m in the U.K. and PrestoPRIME in Europe, Addis has investigated the “cost of risk of loss” for long-term data retention and access when using ICT systems and has developed related strategies for data integrity management, file format migration, and archiving as a service.

Richard Wright's background in computer science and signal processing led to his current position as Technology Manager of BBC Archives, which he has held since 1994. For the past four years he has been involved in PrestoSpace, an EU-funded project aiming to provide technical solutions for digital preservation of audiovisual collections. Through PrestoSpace, Wright has championed the needs of underfunded audiovisual archives, developing the preservation factory concept to enable commercial providers to work with these archives on mutually beneficial terms. Wright continually pushes for greater accessibility to digital resources and as such is particularly interested in developments in creative commons licensing and open source technologies.

Rajitha Weerakkody is a research technologist at the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) (R&D), focusing on the digital preservation of audiovisual archives. Weerakkody obtained his PhD in multimedia and digital signal processing (distributed video coding) from the University of Surrey, U.K. He has experience and interests in video coding and compression, error control coding, digital signal processing, digital storage systems for data archiving, digital preservation technologies, telecommunications, and wireless communications.

Sean McKee is the director of restoration and new technology for Point.360 Digital Film Labs, in Burbank, CA. In the past year, McKee and team have developed a number of proprietary technologies for both the classic movie/archival market, as well as for current productions. The most recent being Visionary Archive, a patent-pending process that allows a full color motion picture to be archived onto a signal reel of 35mm black-and-white film stock, eliminating traditional YCM archival issues. Other developments include Advanced Restoration Tools (ART) grain and noise reduction, best-in-class RAW camera image processing, automated color matching, a perceptually uniform color space, and other bleeding-edge algorithms/software which McKee says are based on “alien” technology. For 12 years prior, McKee was CEO of Screen Time Images, a Chicago based company specializing in film restoration, rights acquisition, and distribution. McKee was the world's first user of the popular Revival film restoration system, and worked closely with da Vinci to develop the software. He has been featured in numerous interviews on national TV, radio, and industry magazines.

Victor Panov is a key member of the Point.360 Digital Film Labs development team headed by Sean McKee. He is a theoretical physicist, and high-level programmer. Before working at Point.360, Panov was part of team at the Motion Picture Marine that received a Sci-Tech Academy Award for camera stabilization hardware. He was a consultant to NASA JPL, creating communications hardware and software for picosatellites. Before that, Panov worked with Rockwell to design hardware and software devices for reliable wireless transmission. Before migrating to the U.S., Panov worked at the Kurchatov Institute of Atomic Energy of the Russian Academy of Science and the Institute of Molecular Genetics of the Russian Academy of Science, creating software for finite element model visualization and processing, hardware oriented programming for video adapters for finite element model, as well as data stereo visualization and 3D stereo graphics software and GUI design.

Karel Braeckman started working at VRT-medialab in 2008 after graduating as Master of Electrical Engineering. His interests are in the management of media material, with a focus on optimizing the search within large media collections.

Julie Dutrisac is head of the research and development division of the National Film Board of Canada which she joined in 1989. Among other responsibilities, she oversees technological partnerships, implementation of new technologies, maintaining audiovisual encoding standards, audiovisual process optimization, and evaluating the impact of emerging technologies. She participates in research projects in areas such as voice and visual recognition, image processing algorithms, media management, production metadata, and workflow optimization. — Dutrisac and her team are currently involved in areas such as an ambitious NFB digitization plan, numerous projects in the areas of file-based production, D/E-cinema project encompassing all aspects of digital film post-production, including capture, editing, distribution, and collection preservation. Dutrisac also participates in various Canadian committees and working groups in the field of new digital technologies. She holds a B.S. in engineering from École Polytechnique de Montréal.

Luisa Frate is the director general of the finance, operations and technology division of the National Film Board of Canada. She is the strategic lead of information technologies, information management, technical services, R&D, administration and finances. As the COO, Frate oversees the NFB's operations. Frate joined the NFB 12 years ago; she is a Chartered Accountant with more than 20 years experience in both the private and public sectors. Before becoming the NFB's COO, CFO, and CTO, Frate served as director of administration at the National Film Board. She also worked as assistant director general with the English Program where her experience contributed to her production knowledge. Frate leads the NFB technological vision, which includes the NFB's ambitious digitization plan, a major initiative of the NFB's important transition to digital production, post-production and accessibility. She holds a bachelor's degree in commerce, a Graduate diploma in accountancy, and a Chartered Accountant Degree from McGill University.

He is currently working on YouView. In his spare time, Pinks runs Sixth Stage productions. He recently became a Chartered Engineer and is a member of the IET.

Sean Casey is a technologist at BBC R&D. He gained an MSc in computer science at Lancaster University. Dale Stolitzka is chief systems architect at Analog Devices, based in San Jose, California. He defines system architecture and design for advanced television and mobile display integrated circuit products. He is an active proponent at several industry standard organizations spanning both professional advanced television systems and consumer electronics with special interest in advancing display capabilities in portable handsets. Stolitzka is co-editor of the in-process MPEG-2 Systems amendment concerned with the carriage of JPEG 2000 video over an MPEG-2 transport stream. Dale also chairs the MIPI® Alliance Display Working Group. — His experience includes computer systems and mixed-signal systems design at Analog Devices, National Semiconductor, Maxtor and Raytheon. Stolitzka holds a bachelor's degree in applied physics and a master's degree in materials science & engineering, both from Cornell University.

Walt Husak is the director of image technologies at Dolby Laboratories, Inc. He began his television career at the Advanced Television Test Center (ATTC) in 1990 carrying out video objective measurements and RF multipath testing of HDTV systems proposed for the ATSC standard. — Before joining Dolby, Husak worked on issues related to the deployment of HDTV systems in the U.S. and the rest of the world. He spent many years lecturing on topics such as video compression, RF transmission for DTV, and overcoming multipath signals in urban and rural environments. — Joining Dolby in 2000, Husak has spent the past several years studying and reporting on advanced compression systems for digital cinema, digital television, and Bluray. He has managed or executed visual quality tests for Digital Cinema Initiatives (DCI), the Advanced Television Systems Committee (ATSC), Dolby, and Moving Picture Experts Group (MPEG). — Husak is now a member of the CTO's office focusing his efforts on 3D for digital cinema and digital television. He provides industry lectures on digital cinema systems, image compression and 3D. Husak has authored numerous articles and papers for a number of major industry publications. — Husak is an active member of SMPTE, MPEG, JPEG, ITU-R, and SPIE. He currently chairs the SMPTE 3D Home Master Image ad hoc group (AHG), the SMPTE Frame Packing AH, the DVB 3D Technology Providers Group, and co-chairs the MPEG Frame Compatible AHG in MPEG.

Siegfried Foessel received a Diploma degree (MS) in electronic engineering from the University of Erlangen, Germany, in 1989. He started his professional career as a scientist at the Fraunhofer Institute IIS in Erlangen. He was team leader and project manager in the field process automation, image processing systems and digital camera design. In 2000 he received his Ph.D. degree on image distribution technologies for multiprocessor systems. In 2001, he became head of the group digital cinema within the Fraunhofer IIS. He was responsible for projects like ARRI D21, DCI certification plan, JPEG 2000 standardization for Digital Cinema or field recorder developments and coordinated several funded projects such as WorldScreen or CineVision2006. Michael Bruns is a senior video DSP application engineer at Coherent Logix. He has worked in the domain of video processing and video compression since 1995 and parallel computing since 2004. His role at Coherent Logix is as technical lead for video compression codec development. Before joining Coherent Logix, Bruns was a senior software engineer at Elemental Technologies where he was responsible for high-definition video encoder development using a general purpose graphics processing unit (GPU) programming model. Previously, Bruns was among the original engineers at Ambric, a fabless semiconductor manufacturer that developed a massively parallel processor array (MPPA) chip. Bruns earned a MSEE degree from the University of California, Berkeley and a BSEE from Northwestern University. He is a member of IEEE, has published eight papers and holds one patent.

Martin Hunt is currently an image processing program manager at Coherent Logix, where he provides both programmatic and technical leadership on all image processing projects at the company. He has more than 20 years of signal/image processing and pattern recognition experience. Before joining Coherent Logix, Hunt worked at Synopsys where he led an engineering team in applying statistical software and pattern recognition tools to analyze electrical and other semiconductor manufacturing data in order to accelerate yield ramp and improve overall product yield. He also worked at at nLine Corp. as the vice president of engineering where he was responsible for the development of an automated semiconductor inspection tool based on the disruptive technology of direct-to-digital holography. Hunt has published more 20 papers. He is a senior member of IEEE, a licensed Professional Engineer and holds three patents from his work at ORNL and nLine Corp. Hunt holds a Ph.D. in electrical engineering from the University of Tennessee, an M.S.E.E. from Vanderbilt University, and a B.S.E.E. from Tennessee Technological University.

Lin Tong has extensive experience in the design and analysis of video coding systems and image processing algorithms. Her responsibilities at Coherent Logix include algorithm development and implementation and systems design and verification. At Coherent Logix, she has worked on projects to implement a variety of algorithms using HyperX technology including GPS anti-jam, JPEG decoding, image stabilization, and super-resolution enhancement. Tong holds a Ph.D. in electrical engineering from the University of Texas at Arlington, an M.S.E.E. from Alfred University, and a B.S.E.E. from the University of Science and Technology of China.

Keith Bindloss is a system architect at Coherent Logix. His career has evolved from his early work on digital signal processing, especially in speech recognition and coded voice messaging (vocoding) systems. His experience in DSP algorithm development and hardware implementation led to extensive work on the improvement of DSP design and architecture. He addressed the requirements of realtime processing problems and implementations by extending his efforts to System-on-Chip (SoC) architecture and development tools. Bindloss provides valuable technical leadership and effective hands-on technical development, informed by long experience in processing, microarchitecture design, and system engineering. He is the co-inventor on 7 US patents related to processor architecture. Bindloss has more than 20 years experience in product development, technology development and technical leadership of DSP VLSI systems, architectures and HW/SW development tools.

Alexander Hornung is a research scientist at Disney Research Zurich, heading the group for imaging and video processing. He is also an adjunct lecturer at ETH Zurich and supervises undergraduate as well as M.S. and Ph.D. students. Aljoscha Smolic received a Dr.-Ing. degree from Aachen University of Technology (RWTH) in 2001. He joined Disney Research Zurich in 2009, where he leads the “Advanced Video Technology” group. Before that, he was a scientific project manager at Fraunhofer HHI in Berlin. He conducted research in video processing, video coding, computer vision and computer graphics and published more than 100 referred papers in these fields. Since 2003 Smolic had teaching appointments at TU Berlin, ETH Zurich, Universitat Politécnica de Catalunya, Universidad Politécnica de Madrid, and Universitat de les Illes Balears. He is area editor for Signal Processing: Image Communication and served as guest editor for the Proceedings of the IEEE, IEEE Transactions on CSVT, IEEE Signal Processing magazine and others. Markus Gross is a professor of computer science at ETH Zurich, head of the Computer Graphics Laboratory, and the director of Disney Research Zurich. For more than 20 years Gross has been pursuing basic and applied research in computer graphics, image generation and display, geometric modeling, and computer animation. His research interests include point-based graphics, physically-based modeling, immersive displays, and video processing. He has published more than 200 scientific papers and holds various patents on core graphics and visualization technologies. Gross was chair of the papers committee of ACM SIGGRAPH 2005 and is a fellow of the Eurographics Association. He serves on the boards of numerous international research institutions, societies, and governmental organizations. He is a co-founder of Cyfex AG, Novodex AG, LiberoVision AG, and Dybuster AG.

M. J. Addis leads a portfolio of applied research projects at the IT Innovation Centre on media archiving and digital preservation, risk management, and smart systems. Current work includes cost models, uncertainty management, and service-oriented approaches to distributed media systems. Addis has ten years of experience in working with broadcasters, post houses and film archives to develop strategies, tools, and systems for audiovisual restoration, preservation, and archiving. Through AVATAR-m in the UK and PrestoPRIME in Europe, Addis has investigated long-term data retention and access for AV when using ICT systems and has developed related strategies for risk management, migration, and archiving as a service. Recently, this has resulted in the IT Innovation Centre, forming the Arkivum Ltd., which provides data archiving as a service, with Addis as chief technology officer.

His current work involves using the agent- and event-based simulation models to model large-scale archive systems, media format migration workflows and internet communities in order to identify risks and costs inherent in these systems. His main interests are in the area of complex systems modeling and distributed AI.

Martin Hall-May holds a PhD. in computer science. He is currently a senior research engineer at the University of Southampton IT Innovation Centre, where he is involved in research and integration activities in the EC FP7 PrestoPRIME and SERSCIS projects. These and other projects in which he has been involved focus on the modeling of risk, especially as applied to the dependability of service oriented architectures. However, the application of these techniques is not limited to the preservation of AV content. Hall-May's research aims to show the application of similar techniques to the management of information flows in critical infrastructures, such as air traffic management, as well as in the long-term preservation of engineering data. Before joining IT Innovation, he researched large-scale system safety and the implications of deploying autonomous vehicles in safety-critical applications.

He began his professional career working on several R&D projects—in particular the 5th PCRD EU “G-FORS” project, which involved BBC, Philips, and Snell & Wilcox. In 2003, he founded OpenCube, a Toulouse–based company, which provides MXF solutions for the broadcast and D-Cinema industries. In 2010, OpenCube Technologies was acquired by EVS, a global leader in broadcast and media production systems. Fevrier is currently general manager of the OpenCube business unit in the EVS group, where he continues to carry out MXF tapeless workflow analyses, among other activities.

Valérie Popie is an engineer with a master's degree in software design and architecture from the University of Le Mans, France. She started her career at OpenCube in 2006 as a software engineer and is now product manager of the EVSOpenCube MXF software product line, where she works, among other things, on SMPTE standardization for comprehensive MXF implementation in EVS-OpenCube Products. Popie has developed an in-depth knowledge of the theoretical and practical aspects of MXF implementation as well as significant expertise in real-life MXF-based workflow interoperability and metadata management issues.

Ludovic Dupont holds a master's degree in computer science from Toulouse's Paul Sabatier University of Science with a specialty in digital image engineering. Dupont started his career at OpenCube in 2004 as one of the very first employees of the “start-up.” He is now project leader of EVS-OpenCube video server product range; his R&D activities are focused in large part on the challenges of preserving and transferring metadata from physical baseband video streams to MXF files for tapeless production workflows.

John Footen is an acknowledged industry expert in such areas as Business Process Management (BPM), Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA), and the Cloud, all of which have a major impact on today's broadcast television and professional media systems. As head of Cognizant's broadcast consulting practice, Footen is responsible for business and technology consulting throughout the broadcast industry. Footen is a sought-after speaker and expert writer on software architecture and workflow issues. He serves as co-chair of the Framework for Interoperable Media Services (FIMS) joint taskforce of the Advanced Media Workflow Association (AMWA) and European Broadcasting Union (EBU). Footen is a SMPTE member and chairs the 34CS Media Systems Control and Services technology committee. He has been responsible for managing many large and complex media solutions projects for many types of media enterprises. He has extensive international experience; having lived and worked in North America, Asia, and Europe, the Middle East and Africa (EMEA). Footen holds degrees in computer science and film and television from New York University. He is also the co-author of “The Service-Oriented Media Enterprise: SOA, BPM, and Web Services in Professional Media Systems,” published by Focal Press.

Mohan Ananthanarayanan has extensive experience in information technology, SOA, BPM and the Enterprise Application Integration (EAI) space. Ananthanarayanan's experience includes consulting, IT presales, solution architecture, systems analysis, technical design and development, spanning multiple Industry domains. His areas of specialization include IBM Websphere suite of products and he has been involved in architecture assessment and product evaluation exercises for multiple clients. At Cognizant, Ananthanarayanan is a principal architect focusing on IBM Websphere suite of products and is part of the Integration Consulting Group which oversees complex integration projects under EAI practice. In his current role Ananthanarayanan leads the IBM Business Process & Integration practice within Cognizant responsible for business development and consulting.

Al Kovalick is a principal member and founder of Media Systems Consulting. Previously, he was a Corporate Fellow at Avid and chief technology officer of Pinnacle Systems. Kovalick has an MSEE degree from the University of California at Berkeley, holds 18 US and foreign patents, and has authored more than 50 papers. Peter Defreyne is currently a media infrastructure expert at CandIT-media. He graduated as an electrotechnical engineer from the Leuven University, Belgium, where he specialized in multimedia processing. Defreyne started his career at VRT-medialab, the research department of the Flemish public broadcaster as a research engineer. He joined the group that optimizes the performance of IT solutions in media environments. His first expertise is focused on SAN networks, IP networks and workflow optimization on large-scale storage clusters. Defreyne's work on editing on generic storage was published at IBC and the SMPTE Technical Conferences in 2010. Since then he has been working on his first large project on innovative production workflows in the cloud. Defreyne can be contacted at peter.defreyne@candit-media.com.

Luk Overmeire obtained a MSc in electronics engineering from the University of Ghent, Belgium. Before joining VRT, he was a research engineer in Alcatel Bell, working on software-based services and ADSL digital filter design, respectively. In 2002, he joined VRT's research and innovation department where he first performed research in the signal processing area such as metadata-based video encoding and rate control. He presently leads the competence group focusing on media production and audiovisual content processing. Overmeire is a member of several European Broadcasting Union (EBU) working groups, the Advanced Media Workflow Association (AMWA) and SMPTE. Since 1996, Overmeire has been involved in patent applications and authored several papers presented at international conferences. He can be contacted at luk.overmeire@vrtmedialab.be.

Matthias De Geyter obtained a MSc in electronics engineering from the University of Ghent in 2001, after which he joined the image processing research group (IPI) of this university. In 2004, he started working in the VRT's R&D department, where he performed research on media adaptation and media exchange formats such as MXF and AAF and their use in system integration. Other topics of interest include file-based quality control and production systems in the cloud. In 2012, he joined the newly founded Media Innovation Center. Since 2001, De Geyter (co-)authored several papers presented at international conferences. His e-mail address is matthias.degeyter@ibbt.be.

Rik Van de Walle received masters and PhD degrees in engineering from Ghent University, Belgium in July 1994 and February 1998, respectively. His PhD focused on magnetic resonance imaging. After a post-doctoral fellowship at the University of Arizona, he returned to Ghent, became a full-time lecturer in 2001, and founded the Multimedia Lab at the Faculty of Engineering and Architecture. — Van de Walle is a senior full professor at Ghent, where he teaches several courses, dealing with the fundamentals of multimedia, and (advanced) multimedia applications. His research interests include multimedia content delivery, coding of multimedia data, metadata technology, content adaptation, interactive (mobile) multimedia applications, and e-health. Throughout his career, Van de Walle has closely collaborated with a large number of research groups and partners in engineering, biomedical technology, sciences, arts, (digital) rights management, media, and communication sciences. He has been a member/secretary/chairman of a large number of committees, not only within his own faculty but also outside of Ghent University. Van de Walle can be contacted at rik.vandewalle@ugent.be.

Wim Van Lancker holds a masters degree in computer science. He worked as a researcher at the Multimedia Lab at Ghent University until the end of 2011, investigating format-independent media resource adaptation and delivery techniques. His current interests include scalable video coding technologies, media content adaptation and delivery, video quality, video streaming, media content presentation, Semantic web technologies and multichannel publishing. — Van Lancker's track record shows his broad experience in research projects: he participated in projects about video quality assessment, error concealment, content adaptation and delivery, multichannel publication, in cooperation with several companies such as Alcatel-Lucent, VRT-medialab, Televic, Belgacom. His work has been published in scientific journals such as Multimedia Tools and Applications.

Brad Gilmer is president of Gilmer & Associates, Inc, a management and technology consulting firm, providing business and technical consulting services to the television industry. Gilmer is executive director of the Video Services Forum (VSF), and executive director of the Advanced Media Workflow Association (AMWA). Gilmer is a Fellow of SMPTE and has been an active participant within SMPTE since 1984. He was previously employed as director of engineering and operations at Turner Broadcasting System, Inc. in Atlanta. His staff managed technical and operational aspects of Turner Entertainment's television networks worldwide, including TBS, TNT, and Cartoon Network. Gilmer is author of the monthly Computer and Networks column in Broadcast Engineering magazine, editor-in-chief of the “File Interchange Handbook” (Focal Press), a contributor to the “NAB Engineering Handbook,” and is a frequent presenter at broadcast conventions including SMPTE, VidTrans, NAB and IBC.

Yoshiaki Shibata has started his career as a semiconductor researcher at Sony Corp. in 1991. He then moved into the IT/Multimedia field in 1996, studying video over internet and video compression technology. — In 1998, Shibata joined the MPEG-7 standardization activity; he took a leadership in the MPEG-7 schema design as a working group chair and a project editor for ISO/IEC 15938-5. — Since 2001, he has been working in the media and entertainment industry, where initially he made a significant contribution to update the UMID specification (SMPTE ST330/RP205) as well as invent the EssenceMark for professional AV products. In 2003, he took part in the XDCAM development project, where he played a crucial role in the metadata part of the product development and applied for more than 40 patents in metadata related technology. — In 2011, Shibata left Sony Corp., making a trail to provide Japan's first independent consulting service for the media and metadata technology in the media and entertainment industry. Then, following a one-year preparation period, he founded metaFrontier.jp, LLC in Jan. 2012.

Jim Wilkinson first worked in the area of broadcasting, joining the Independent Broadcasting Authority's (IBA) Engineering Headquarters in1974. During his time with the IBA, he worked on DICE, video compression using differential pulse-code modulation (DPCM) at 34 Mbits/sec and other video projects. — In 1979, Wilkinson joined the newly created Advanced Development Laboratories of Sony Broadcast as one of the founding members. His many activities and projects during his 28 years with Sony included digital video recording, image compression and processing, digital audio, metadata and file/stream formats. — Wilkinson has been awarded more than 80 patents; both U.K. and international. He has participated in many standards activities in the Audio Engineering Society, SMPTE, and the European Broadcasting Union, with particular emphasis on metadata, compression and file/stream formats. — In 1995, he was awarded the Alexander M. Poniatoff Gold Medal for Technical Excellence by SMPTE. He is a Chartered Engineer and a fellow of the Institution of Engineering and Technology and SMPTE. — In 2006, Wilkinson retired from Sony and now works as an engineering consultant in the areas of video and sound with an ongoing interest in compression and file/stream formats.

Michael Chenery is a color scientist and engineer specializing in the color issues and needs of the film and broadcast industries. Involved with the cineSpace color management system from its beginnings, Chenery has spent the past 12 years developing cineSpace and solving the color management problems faced by these industries. — Today, Chenery is the senior color scientist for THX Ltd., providing color science expertise for the Imaging Technology Dept., as well as technical support for THX's cineSpace customers. Chenery also provides training courses on topics such as color management, color workflows, and the color science involved in film and television production. He can be contacted at mchenery@thx.com.

Putman edits and publishes HDTVexpert.com, a web blog focused on digital TV, HDTV, and display technologies. He is also a columnist for Pro AV magazine, the leading trade publication for commercial AV systems integrators. — Putman holds a B.A. degree in communications from Seton Hall University, and a M.S. degree in television and film from Syracuse University. Jon McElvain is currently with the Image Tech Research division of Dolby Laboratories, based in Burbank, CA. He specializes in camera and display systems, image quality quantification, and image processing algorithm development. His previous positions were with Digital Imaging Systems GmbH, Micron Inc. (imaging division, now Aptina) and with Xerox Corp. He has more than 20 publications and holds 24 patents, with another 12 patents pending. He is a member of SMPTE, IS&T and IEEE, and is the past-chair of the IEEE Standing Committee on Industry Signal Processing Technology (IDSP). McElvain received a B.S. in physics from the University of California, San Diego; a M.A. in physics from the University of California, Berkeley; and a Ph.D. in physics from the University of California, Santa Barbara.

David Ruhoff is a senior staff engineer in the Image Technology Research department at Dolby Laboratories. He has more than 30 years of software development experience in diverse applications such as logic simulation and compilers. Since 1982, he has focused on computer graphics, film scanning and recording, video, and compression. In 1984, he received screen credit for his work on The Last Starfighter, one of the first full-length motion pictures to use extensive CGI. In 1996, he received an Academy Technical Achievement Award for pioneering efforts in the creation of the Digital Film Compositing System at Digital Productions.

Glenn Woodruff is a project engineer at Dolby Laboratories, concentrating on color engineering, video processing, and monitoring. Before joining Dolby, Woodruff was Employee #1 at Cine-tal Systems and has previously held positions with Truevision and Pinnacle Systems. He received a B.S.E.E. degree from Purdue University in 1997.

Walter Gish is principal member at Dolby's Image Technology Research and Development group, where he leads research and development efforts for next-generation imaging technology. He has more than 30 years of experience in signal and image processing, high-performance computing, and hardware development. Gish began his career working on classified (Top Secret) sonar, radar, and image analysis applications for the U.S. government. Since the early 1980s he has focused on computer graphics, video, and display technology. Prior to joining Dolby Laboratories he was Principal Engineer at Evans & Sutherland, executive scientist at Terabit, and chief technology officer at Interactive Machines, Inc. — Gish received screen credit for his work on The Last Starfighter, the first full-length motion picture to use extensive CGI. He received special recognition from ISO/IEC for his contributions to the development of the High Profiles for H.264/AVC, which were awarded an Emmy in 2008. His current interests include compression algorithms, high dynamic range and wide color gamut imaging technology, and forensic watermarking. Gish received a B.S. and M.S. in physics and applied mathematics from the California Institute of Technology in 1968 and 1970, respectively.

Dave Schnuelle represents Dolby Laboratories as senior director, image technology, and is responsible for guidance in Dolby's efforts in the television, cinema, and consumer imaging areas. He began his career as an engineer on television outside broadcasts while attending Purdue University. Schnuelle later held positions as chief engineer at various post-production facilities such as Editel and Modern VideoFilm in Los Angeles.

He has carried out original research in compression coding, transcoding and analysis, motion estimation, motion compensated de-interlacing, standards conversion and other temporal processing of image sequences. Martin Banks received a bachelor's degree at Occidental College in 1970, majoring in psychology and minoring in physics. After a year in Germany, he entered graduate school, receiving a master's in psychology at University of California, San Diego in 1973 and Ph.D. in developmental psychology from the University of Minnesota in 1976. He was assistant and associate professor of psychology at the University of Texas at Austin from 1976–1985. Banks moved to UC Berkeley School of Optometry in 1985 where he is professor of optometry and vision science. He was chair of Vision Science from 1995–2002. Banks has received several awards for basic and applied research on topics including human visual development, visual space perception, the development and evaluation of stereoscopic displays, and inter-sensory perception.

Jenny Read studied physics at Oxford University, graduating in 1994, and stayed on to do a doctorate in theoretical astrophysics. She began her neuroscience career in 1997 with a Wellcome Trust Training Fellowship in mathematical biology from Oxford's Laboratory of Physiology, receiving an M.Sc. in neuroscience in 1999. In 2001, she moved to the U.S. to work at the National Eye Institute at the National Institutes of Health in Maryland. Since 2005, Read has been at Newcastle University in the northeast of England on a Royal Society University Research Fellowship. Her research includes computational models of disparity encoding and psychophysical measurement of depth perception.

Robert Allison is associate professor of computer science and engineering at York University in Toronto (Canada). He received a BASc in computer engineering from the University of Waterloo in 1991. After graduation, he worked as an electrical engineer at Atlantis Aerospace in Brampton, Canada, where he designed electronics for flight training devices. Following this, he completed a MASc in electrical engineering (biomedical engineering) from the University of Toronto before obtaining a Ph.D. specializing in stereoscopic vision from York University in 1998. He was on the experimental team for the 1998 Neurolab space shuttle mission and did post-doctoral research at York University and the University of Oxford. Allison works on perception of space and self-motion in virtual environments, the measurement and analysis of eye-movements, and stereoscopic vision.

Simon Watt received a bachelor's degree in psychology from Cardiff University, Wales, in 1994, and a masters in psychology from Surrey University, England, in 1996. He completed a Ph.D. in human vision and visuo-motor control at Surrey in 2001. He was then a postdoctoral researcher at the School of Optometry, UC Berkeley, before moving to a faculty position at the School of Psychology, Bangor University, Wales, in 2004, where he is now a senior lecturer. He does basic and applied research on several topics related to 3D perception and binocular vision. In particular, he works on perceptual and ergonomic problems with current 3D display technologies. He also carries out research on depth perception, how 3D vision is used to control everyday movements such as reaching to grasp, and how the brain combines 3D information across sensory modalities such as vision and touch.

Daniele Siragusano has worked in the field of stereoscopic media for ten years. He started his career as a stereoscopic video projectionist, after receiving bachelor's and master's degrees. Siragusano currently works in the field of stereoscopic post-production and has been a post-production supervisor and stereographer since March 2010. He implemented the stereoscopic post-production workflow for feature films at CinePostProductions. — Siragusano has been involved in films such as Darkest Hour (Stereo3D full-length feature, director Chris Gorak, 2010) BMW X3 (Stereo3D commercial, Hochkant Film, 2010) Goesser 3D (Stereo3D commercial, Neue Sentimental Film, 2010) Animals United (Stereo3D Full-length feature, Constantin Film AG, 2010) If Buildings Could Talk (Stereo3D Short feature, Wim Wenders, Alain Derobe, 2010) Hybrid (Stereo3D Full-length Feature, 2010) and Topper (Stereo3D Short Feature, Stallion Production, 2010).

Jonathan Thorpe is a principal engineer at Sony BPRL in the U.K., with an MEng in information engineering from the University of Southampton. With more than 14 years experience in the broadcast and professional video domain, his main research interests include pattern recognition, image processing and stereo video processing. He has been working on stereo 3D related projects for the past four years and contributed to Sony's MPES-3D01 stereo processor that has been used in many recent live 3D productions such as the World Cup and Wimbledon.

Mark J. Russell is a principal engineer at Sony BPRL in the U.K., with a BEng in electronic and electrical engineering from Birmingham University. He joined Sony in 1996, and now has more than 24 years of experience in the broadcast and professional video sector. In the early part of his career, Russell focused on digital video effects and chroma keying, his work contributing to Sony's HDS7000 digital video switcher and XPRI nonlinear editor. Takayuki Yamashita is currently a senior research engineer in the Science and Technology Research Laboratories at NHK (Japan Broadcasting Corp.) he is working on the research of ultrahigh-definition TV systems. His research fields include the development of image sensors and the high-bandwidth digital signal processing. He joined NHK in 1995 and has been engaged in research of HDTV camera systems since 1999. Yamashita received B.E. and M.E. degrees in electronic engineering and information science from Kyoto Institute of Technology in 1993 and 1995, respectively. He is a member of SMPTE and the Institute of Image Information and Television Engineers of Japan (ITE).

Kenichiro Masaoka received a B.S. in electronics engineering and M.S. in energy engineering from the Tokyo Institute of Technology, Japan and joined NHK in 1996. Masoaka is a principal research engineer for the Advanced Television Systems Research Division, NHK Science and Technology Research Laboratories (STRL), Tokyo. He received a Ph.D. in engineering from the Tokyo Institute of Technology in 2009. He worked with Professors Mark Fairchild and Roy Berns for a six-month residency as a visiting scientist at the Munsell Color Science Laboratory (MCSL) at the Rochester Institute of Technology (RIT) in 2012. His research interests include color science, human vision, and digital imaging systems. He is a member of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) and ITE of Japan.

Kohei Omura received B.S. and M.S. degrees in engineering from Hokkaido University in 2002 and 2004, respectively. From 2007 to 2011, he worked toward developing ultra-high-definition television systems at NHK Science and Technical Research Laboratories. His research interests include future television systems that have both a high spatial resolution and excellent motion portrayal. He is currently employed in NHK's Broadcast Engineering department, where he is primarily involved in building computer systems for data broadcasting services.

Masaki Emoto received B.S. and M.S. degrees in electronic engineering and a Ph.D. degree in human and environmental studies from Kyoto University in 1986, 1988, and 2003, respectively. He has been working on future television systems and human science, especially human visual system, at NHK Science and Technology Research Laboratories. His research interests include future television systems incorporating desirable effects such as a heightened sensation of presence, and eliminating undesirable side effects to the viewer such as photosensitive response, visually induced motion sickness, and visual fatigue.

Yukihiro Nishida is senior research engineer, Advanced Television Systems, at NHK Science and Technology Research Laboratories in Tokyo. He has been involved in many areas of broadcasting technologies including HDTV, digital broadcasting, video coding, multiplexing, and quality evaluation. One such area is the study of new television systems like UHDTV. He is also active in the standardization of broadcast technologies in the International Telecommunications Union, Radiocommunications Sector (ITU-R), Association of Radio Industries and Businesses (ARIB) and the European Broadcasting Union (EBU). Nishida is Vice-Chair of ITU-R Study Group 6 on broadcasting services, and is also Chair of Working Party 6B covering source coding, interfaces, multimedia and interactivity. He was a visiting research engineer at RAI Research Center in Turin, Italy, in 1992. He graduated from Keio University, Japan, with an M.Sc. in electrical engineering. Nishidia is also a member of ITE of Japan.

Masayuki Sugawara received B.S. and M.S. degrees in electric communication engineering and a Ph.D. degree in electronic engineering from Tohoku University, Sendai, Japan. He joined NHK, Tokyo, Japan, in 1983 and since 1987, he has researched solid-state image sensor and HDTV camera in the Science and Technology Research Laboratories. He was an associate professor at the University of Electro-Communications in Tokyo from 2000 until 2004. He has been attending ITU-R SG6 meetings since 2004 and has been active in the working parties that deal with program production. Currently, Sugawara is an executive research engineer at NHK STRL and is engaged in the research of the ultra-high-definition TV system. He is a member of SMPTE, the Institue of Electrical and Electronics Engineering, the Society for Information Display, The Institue of Electronics, Information and Communication Engineers, and ITE of Japan.

Matthew Goldman is senior vice president, TV compression technology at Ericsson. He has been actively involved in the development of DTV systems since 1992. He was a prominent participant in MPEG, where he helped create the MPEG-2 Systems standard, and he also has been influential in the Advanced Television Systems Committee, SMPTE, Society of Cable Telecommunications Engineers, and the Consumer Electronics Association. Goldman has presented numerous papers at industry trade events and has been a contributing writer to various trade magazines. Goldman received BS (high honors) and MS degrees in electrical engineering from Worcester Polytechnic Institute. He holds six patents related to digital video transport. A SMPTE Fellow, Goldman is also a senior member of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers and an inductee of the Academy of Digital Television Pioneers. He currently serves on the SMPTE Board of Governors.

title: AVC-I: Yet Another Intra Codec for Broadcast Contribution?
label: SMPTE Journal ( Volume: 121, Issue: 5, July 2012)
keywordsSearch: AVC-I: Yet Another Intra Codec for Broadcast Contribution?

Pierre Larbier is chief technology officer ATEME and a renowned expert in the field of algorithmic design and MPEG / H.264 video compression. He has specifically dealt with video encoder architecture and designs for a wide range of platforms and applications: from low-power single DSP solutions to ultra-high-quality FPGA-based HD broadcast encoders. Larbier obtained an engineering degree from INSA, Rennes, France, with specialization in electronics. He is an active member of SMPTE and DVB.

title: MPEG DASH: The Enabler Standard for Video Delivery over the Internet
label: SMPTE Journal ( Volume: 121, Issue: 5, July 2012)
keywordsSearch: MPEG DASH: The Enabler Standard for Video Delivery over the Internet

Thomas Stockhammer received Dipl.-Ing. and Dr.-Ing. degrees from the Munich University of Technology, Germany. He is co-founder and CEO of Novel Mobile Radio (NoMoR) Research, a privately owned company providing consulting and software development services, products on emerging communication networks, as well as on TV-related matters. He has published more than 150 papers, is member of several technical program committees and holds about 70 patents. Stockhammer regularly contributes to different standardization activities, such as MPEG, ITU-T, IETF, 3GPP, and DVB and has led working and adhoc groups in 3GPP and DVB and also acts as rapporteur/editor of several standardization documents. In particular, he is rapporteur and editor of 3GPP and MPEG's DASH specifications and the technical lead for DASH Promoters Group. His research interests include video transmission, cross-layer and system design, forward-error correction, content delivery protocols, adaptive streaming protocols, rate-distortion optimization, information theory, and mobile communications.

Iraj Sodagar is currently a principal multimedia architect at Microsoft. He joined Microsoft in January 2008, where he has been working with various research and product groups in the standardization of multimedia technologies. He has been engaged in ITU-T, JPEG, MPEG, AMQP, W3C and DLNA standards. He is currently leading Microsoft's engagement in MPEG-DASH. Throughout the years, Sodagar has served on various standard committees including as technical chair of Wireless Multimedia Forum, chair of MPEG-4 visual texture coding adhoc group, and co-chair of JPEG-2000 scalability and progressive-to-lossless coding adhoc group. He is currently the co-chair of MPEG's Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP (DASH) subgroup. Sodagar received a Ph.D. degree in electrical engineering from Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, in 1994.

title: Next-Generation Broadcast Television: An Overview of Enabling Technology
label: SMPTE Journal ( Volume: 121, Issue: 5, July 2012)

Luke Fay is a senior staff SW systems engineer for Sony Semiconductor's Component Solutions Business Division. Currently, he is involved with ATSC and its efforts toward developing the next generation TV broadcast standards. He has more than 16 years of experience in digital communications systems engineering and receiver design and received an MS degree in electrical engineering from National Technological University. He was recently named vice-chair of the Advanced Television Systems Committee (ATSC) Technology Group 3 (TG3), which will develop standards for the next generation of digital television broadcasting.

James Kutzner is senior director of advanced technology at Public Broadcasting Service (PBS) where he manages engineering and technical projects within PBS. Kutzner is a member of the ATSC Board and chaired the ATSC Planning Team on the Next Generation of Broadcast Television. He currently chairs the successor group of the ATSC Technology Group 3 on ATSC 3.0. He is also vice chair of the Open Mobile Video Coalition's Technical Advisory Group. He holds a Master's degree in Engineering Management from George Washington University and a bachelor of electrical engineering degree from the University of Minnesota. Kutzner is a Fellow of SMPTE and a member of the IEEE.

Skip Pizzi is director of digital strategies at the National Association of Broadcasters, based in Washington, D.C. His career has spanned the broadcast and new media industries, as an engineer and technology manager at NPR and at Microsoft, with more than a decade of experience at each. He also spent seven years as technical editor at Broadcast Engineering magazine, and has been a frequent contributor to numerous technical journals in the broadcast and new-media fields. He is the author of two books, and a contributor to several others, including the NAB Engineering Handbook and other technical reference books. Pizzi is a graduate of Georgetown University, where he studied electrical engineering, International Economics, and Fine Arts. He was recently named vice-chair of the Advanced Television Systems Committee (ATSC) Technology Group 3 (TG3), which will develop standards for the next generation of digital television broadcasting.

Jerry Whitaker is vice president for standard development at the Advanced Television Systems Committee. He supports the work of the various ATSC technology groups and assists in the development of ATSC Standards and related documents. He currently serves as Secretary of the Technology and Standards Group and Technology Group 3 on ATSC 3.0, and is closely involved in work relating to educational programs. Mr. Whitaker is a Fellow the Society of Broadcast Engineers and a Fellow of the Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers. He has served as a Board member and Vice President of the Society of Broadcast Engineers. He is the author and editor of more than 30 books on various technical topics.

Yiyan Wu is a principal research scientist with the Communications Research Centre in Ottawa, Canada. His research interests include broadband multimedia communications, digital broadcasting, and communication systems engineering. Dr. Wu is an IEEE Fellow, an adjunct professor of Carleton University in Ottawa, Canada, a member of the IEEE Broadcast Technology Society Administrative Committee, and a member of the Advanced Television Systems Committee (ATSC) Board of Directors, representing IEEE. He is the Editor-in-Chief of the IEEE Transactions on Broadcasting.

William Zou is director of corporate strategy and development at DTS responsible for standards and business development. He has over 25 years of experience in digital video and audio systems engineering, DTV standards, and business development. His cross-industry experience includes working for The Walt Disney Studios, PBS, General Instrument/Motorola and Harmonic. Since late 1980's he has been an active participant and contributor in industry-wide DTV standards development including ATSC, BDA, SMPTE, IEEE, SCTE, ATIS, and MPEG. He was a vice-chair of ATSC Planning Team on Next Generation Broadcast Television. He is the author or co-author of more than 50 journal publications and conference papers in the areas of digital compression, DTV system engineering and content distribution. Zou is a Fellow of SMPTE and Senior Member of IEEE. He serves on the Board of Editor for the SMPTE Motion Imaging Journal.
