SMPTE Motion Imaging Journal ( Volume: 121, Issue: 6, 2012)

Hans Hoffmann was born in Munich, Germany. He holds a diploma in telecommunication engineering from the University of Applied Sciences in Munich. In 2007, he completed his Ph.D. studies at Brunel University West London, at the School of Engineering and Design. From 1993 to 2000, Hoffmann worked at the Insitut fuer Rundfunktechnik in research and development for new television production technologies. In 2000, he joined the European Broadcasting Union (EBU) as a senior engineer in the technical department. Hoffmann has chaired the EBU project groups P/BRRTV and P/PITV, which were both involved in standardization activities such SDTI and file formats. — Hoffmann is currently SMPTE Engineering Vice President. He chaired the SMPTE technology committee on Networks and File Management and has served as Engineering Director, Television. He has been involved in EBU activities on high-definition television production and emission and set up the HDTV testing laboratory at the EBU. Hoffmann is a fellow of SMPTE and a member of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE), FKT (Germany), and the Society for Information Display (SID).

Michael A. Dolan (31FS) is founder and president of Television Broadcast Technology, providing specialized professional encoders, test tools, and technical consulting in the field of digital television. He holds a BSEE degree from Virginia Tech and has worked for and founded various leading-edge computer graphics and realtime systems companies, including early foundational work in W3C technology and analog data broadcasting. Dolan has been involved in digital television engineering for the past eight years, including data broadcast system architecture and digital receiver design and compliance. He also currently chairs the ATSC Data Broadcasting Specialist Group (TSG/S13) and is active in the Consumer Electronics Association (CEA) and the Society of Cable Telecommunications Engineers (SCTE). A SMPTE Fellow, Dolan authors the SMPTE Journal Almanac column and holds several patents in computer web technology.

Bob Edge (33TS) is an independent consultant (Bob Edge TV Consulting). During his career, he has worked as an engineer, project leader, systems architect, and program manager on several products and research projects. Edge has served as an Engineering Director for SMPTE and he is a Life Fellow in the Society. He is active in Television standards work including his participation in SMPTE, some EBU projects, and other organizations. Edge has a BS in computer science from Oregon State University.

John Fletcher (33TS) is a lead technologist at BBC Research & Development, London, U.K. He studied natural and electrical sciences at Cambridge University before joining the BBC in 1986. He has worked in a variety of fields including acoustics, video coding and subtitling. His main interest in recent years has been the application of information technology to the TV production process, with projects such as the Ingex tapeless recording system. He is a Chartered Engineer and member of the Institution of Engineering and Technology.

John Footen (34CS) is an acknowledged industry expert in such areas as Business Process Management (BPM), Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA), and the Cloud, all of which have a major impact on today's broadcast television and professional media systems. As head of Cognizant's broadcast consulting practice, Footen is responsible for business and technology consulting throughout the broadcast industry. Footen is a sought-after speaker and expert writer on software architecture and workflow issues. He serves as co-chair of the Framework for Interoperable Media Services (FIMS) joint taskforce of the Advanced Media Workflow Association (AMWA) and European Broadcasting Union (EBU). Footen is a SMPTE member and chairs the 34CS Media Systems Control and Services technology committee. He has been responsible for managing many large and complex media solutions projects for many types of media enterprises. He has extensive international experience; having lived and worked in North America, Asia, and Europe, the Middle East and Africa (EMEA). Footen holds degrees in computer science and film and television from New York University. He is also the co-author of “The Service-Oriented Media Enterprise: SOA, BPM, and Web Services in Professional Media Systems,” published by Focal Press.

Paul Gardiner (10E) is standards manager at Sony Broadcast & Professional Research Labs, within Sony Europe Ltd., based in Basingstoke, U.K. He studied electronic engineering at the University of Southampton before joining the Independent Broadcasting Authority (IBA) in 1974. His career has included a variety of roles related to the introduction of the UHF color television networks in the U.K. He has been involved in television technical regulation, and in R&D project management with responsibility for several international collaborative research projects. He became head of technical standards and Information at the Independent Television Commission (ITC), the regulatory and licensing body for commercial television in the U.K. and subsequently at successor body Ofcom. Gardiner has been an active SMPTE member since joining Sony in 2007, and is co-chair of TC-10E. He is also a regular participant in the work of ITU R and is chair of the AMWA-EBU FIMS Technical Board. He is a Chartered Engineer and a member of the Institution of Engineering Technology (IET).

John Hudson (10E) is director of broadcast technology at Semtech Corp. in Burlington Canada. He began his career in the broadcast industry in 1984 when he joined the Design and Development group of Sony Broadcast and Professional Europe as a technician engineer. During his career, he has worked as a design engineer, project leader, system architect, program manager, product-definition engineer, and technology strategist. Hudson is active in television standards work. He is co-chair of TC10E and chairs the 32NF20 Electrical Interfaces Working Group in SMPTE. He also chairs the Technical Committee of the HDcctv Alliance, which is responsible for the development of standards for the HDcctv Industry.

John Hurst (21DC) is co-founder and chief technology officer at CineCert, LLC, an internationally recognized developer of digital cinema technology, where he is currently engaged in the development of the D-Cinema Comprehensive Test Plan for Digital Cinema Initiatives (DCI). Hurst has been an active participant in the SMPTE Digital Cinema technology committee and has served as editor of several of the standards published by that committee. He has more than 25 years of experience in sound recording and post-production, including the design and construction of well-known recording studios and post-production sound facilities in the Los Angeles area. He has technical responsibilities for many location recordings and live-to-air broadcasts. Hurst is a member of the Audio Engineering Society and is an active radio amateur and community volunteer.

Alan Lambshead (32NF) is vice president of engineering, at Evertz Microsystems Ltd., in Burlington, Ontario, Canada, where his responsibilities include the general oversight of R & D and product development, focusing on timecode and postproduction products. During his 33 years at Evertz, Lambshead has been an active member of SMPTE Technology committees and is the author of several SMPTE recommended practices. Currently, he is co-chair of the 32NF Network and Facilities Architecture committee and chair of the 3 Gbit/sec Multilink Ad Hoc Group. He is a member of the Toronto Section and has presented papers at local chapter and national conferences of SMPTE. Lambshead is a widely recognized expert in the field of HDTV timecode and sync issues, HDTV production, HDTV metadata, and film-to-video transfers. Lambshead graduated from McMaster University, Hamilton, Ontario with a B. Eng in electrical engineering in 1972 and became licensed as a Professional Engineer (P. Eng.) in Ontario in 1988. He became a SMPTE Fellow in 2009.

Pierre-Anthony Lemieux (31FS) is a partner at Sandflow Consulting, where he works with both Hollywood and Silicon Valley clients on proof-of-concept development, worldwide standards, and product architecture. His expertise covers the entertainment technology ecosystem, from content authoring to playback, including digital audio and video, file formats, Internet protocols and content protection. Lemieux's recent engagements include architecting and implementing an audio processing engine, representing clients at industry forums, and performing video IP due diligence. Lemieux has been participating in SMPTE since the early days of D-Cinema. In addition to chairing TC 31FS, he currently serves as document editor in TC 35PM and 21DC projects. Lemieux has a Ph.D. in physics from UCLA and a B.Sc. from McGill University.

Howard Lukk (35PM) is vice president of production technology at The Walt Disney Studios. There he is responsible for helping to incorporate new technologies into the workflow of the studio. Prior to that, he was director of technology for DCI where he was responsible for researching and documenting Digital Cinema Specifications. Before that he was chief engineer at IVC a post-production facility in Burbank. He has also worked as a freelance engineer in the past on HDTV productions such as Woodstock 25th Anniversary and Major League Baseball. Lukk is an active member of SMPTE since 1995 and is also an associate member of the ASC.

Thomas Bause Mason (35PM) is a digital video engineer in the Advanced Engineering department at NBCUniversal. As part of the NBCUniversal Technology Strategy team he helps to implement emerging technologies and standards for file-based workflows in production, post-production and distribution including traditional broadcast, cable and the web. His responsibilities also include 3D and Automated Content Recognition (ACR) technology as well as engineering support for NBCUniversal R&D efforts. He works with many different NBCUniversal operational teams to implement standards and technology on a corporate level. In the past he worked at Ascent Media where he ran the encoding as well as the DAM system ingest operations and helped business development to implementing new media workflows. Before that he worked in Germany as a programmer for process visualization software and as a developer of database solutions. Additionally he managed a Quality Control department for several private broadcast networks at a large broadcast service provider. Thomas has a bachelor degree in Media Technology and is a SMPTE member since 2007. He is an associate member of AMWA and recently joined W3C.

Nelson Meacham (21DC) retired after more than 30 years of employment with the Walt Disney Company. The majority of his career was spent designing audio and video systems for theme park attractions in the U.S., Japan, France, and Hong Kong. For five years starting in 1981, Meacham was the assistant sound director for Walt Disney Pictures and in 1994/1995 supervised the installation of a new film and digital screening room for Walt Disney Feature Animation. Meacham graduated from California State Polytechnic University, San Luis Obispo. He is a Life-Fellow of SMPTE, a member of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, and member of the Audio Engineering Society.

Ann Marie Rohaly (24TB) is director of accessibility policy and standards for Microsoft's Corporate Accessibility Group. Before joining Microsoft in 2003, she spent five years at Tektronix, Inc., in several senior positions, including strategic technology manager for the Video Product Line. Rohaly has been an active participant in the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), leading the standardization of Tektronix's Emmy award-winning PQA300 picture quality measurement technology, and in many other international standards-setting organizations and industry consortia. She played a lead role in the standardization of VC-1 as SMPTE 421M and more recently, in the standardization of SMPTE Timed Text (ST 2052). In 2010, she was appointed to the U.S. Federal Communications Commission's Video Programming Accessibility Advisory Committee, which issued a report on closed captioning for internet-delivered video. Rohaly is a SMPTE Fellow and has served as Western Region Governor since 2009.

Dave Schnuelle (20F) represents Dolby Laboratories as senior director, image technology, and provides guidance in Dolby's efforts in the television, cinema, and consumer imaging areas. He began his career as an engineer on television outside broadcasts while attending Purdue University. Schnuelle later held positions as chief engineer at various post-production facilities such as Editel and Modern VideoFilm in Los Angeles. Schnuelle worked with Lucasfilm's THX Division, beginning in 1991, where he was responsible for founding the THX Digital Mastering Program for quality-assurance of home video masters and duplicated software. As director of technology for THX, he directed research efforts into new technology for cinemas. During that period, he directly supervised the international digital cinema exhibition of the new Star Wars movies— Episode 1 (1999) and Episode 2(2002). Schnuelle holds four patents on imaging and audio technology and has been deeply involved with film and television standards activities for 30 years. He is a SMPTE Fellow and a member of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences.

Chris Simons (34CS) spent the early part of his career working for U.K. terrestrial and satellite broadcasters then joined Drake Automation Ltd. in 1996. As head of customer support, he established a global support infrastructure delivering major automation projects including BSkyB, DirecTV, Network Ten, SkyPerfecTV, Dish Network etc. Following the acquisition of Encoda Systems by Harris in 2005 Simons managed the Automation Services organization covering both ADC and D-Series globally. After a working at Miranda Technologies in 2006, Simons returned to Harris and heads the Automation and Asset Management Product Group, responsible for the ADC, D-Series and Invenio product suite.

John F. Snow (32NF) represents Xilinx, Inc., where he is a senior staff design engineer in the Digital Video Processing group focused on developing FPGA cores that implement SMPTE interface standards. Prior to joining Xilinx in 2001, he was director of engineering at Evans & Sutherland where he was involved in realtime computer graphics for flight simulation for 20 years. Snow is active in SMPTE standards work. He is co-chair of TC32NF and chairs the 33TS.20 Working Group on Synchronization. He is also a senior member of the IEEE.

Paul Treleaven (30MR) obtained a First Class Honours degree in electrical engineering from Imperial College, London in 1972. He started his career in broadcast engineering with BBC Designs Department. His work included design of the interpolation system for the BBC's ‘ACE’ four-field standards converter. In 1979, Treleaven co-founded Avitel, a company that designs and manufactures video, audio and timecode distribution and processing equipment. He continued with Avitel as technical director until 2001. Treleaven is a member of the International Association of Broadcasting Manufacturers' (IABMs) Technical Task Group, representing the IABM at SMPTE and AES standards meetings and ABU technology committee meetings. He is also a member of the U.K.'s National Standards Body for IEC TC100. Treleaven has served as SMPTE International Region Governor and is a SMPTE Fellow. He is currently co-chair of the SMPTE 30MR Technology Committee and has chaired other SMPTE standards groups.

Phil Tudor (30MR) is a principal engineer at BBC Research & Development, London, U.K. He read electrical and information sciences at Cambridge University. Tudor's technical background includes software engineering, video compression algorithm development, MPEG standardization, metadata interoperability and the development of AAF and MXF standard file formats for use in tapeless production. Tudor is responsible for R&D projects in the areas of production tools, formats, workflow, media management and wide area production. He chairs the SMPTE 30MR Technology Committee and is a board member of the Advanced Media Workflow Association. Tudor is a SMPTE fellow, a Chartered Engineer and a member of the Institution of Engineering Technology.

title: Report from the Science and Technology Council of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences
label: SMPTE Motion Imaging Journal ( Volume: 121, Issue: 6, 2012)
keywordsSearch: Report from the Science and Technology Council of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences
SMPTE Motion Imaging Journal ( Volume: 121, Issue: 6, 2012)

Bill Kroyer, Chair, Science and Technology Council, was trained in classic hand-drawn animation at the Walt Disney Studios, but he also was one of the first to explore digital approaches as a computer image choreographer on Tron 1982. In 1988 he received an Academy Award nomination for his short film Technological Threat, which pioneered the technique of combining hand-drawn and computer animation. Kroyer has since directed the feature Ferngully: The Last Rainforest 1992 and contributed to such films as The Flinstones in Viva Rock Vegas 2000, Cats & Dogs 2001, Scooby-Doo 2002 and Garfield 2004. Kroyer is currently the co-chair of the Academy's Science and Technology Council and the director of digital arts at the Dodge College of Film and Media Arts at Chapman University.

George Joblove, Co-Chair, Science and Technology Council, is a digital media technology executive and consultant who throughout his career has played key and pioneering roles in the development and application of digital technology to the entertainment industry. He served for three years as executive vice president of Advanced Technology at Sony Pictures Entertainment, where his focuses included facilitating the application of digital asset management, 4K, and 3D across production, post-production, and distribution. Previously he was at Sony Pictures' visual-effects and animation unit, Imageworks, for ten years, where he served as chief technology officer. Prior affiliations include Industrial Light & Magic (where he co-founded and led the team that pioneered the use of computers to create visual effects for feature films, including such milestones as The Abyss, Terminator 2, and Jurassic Park) and the visual-effects unit of Warner Bros. — Joblove is co-chairman of the Academy's Science and Technology Council. He received a Scientific and Engineering Academy Award in 1994. He is also a member of the Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers and the Visual Effects Society.

Peter Anderson, Chair, Technology History Subcommittee, was the director of photography and visual effects supervisor on U2 3D, the first live-action feature film recorded in digital 3D. After a career in advertising, he joined Douglas Trumbull's Future General visual effects company during the making of Close Encounters of The Third Kind 1977. Anderson went on to create Universal Studios' Hartland visual effects facility, which was used for Buck Rogers in the 25th Century 1979 as well as numerous other Universal productions. In 1981 he joined Disney Studios to film and supervise the visual effects for features such as Tron 1982 and Something Wicked This Way Comes 1983. It was for Disney's Epcot that Anderson developed the modern 3D systems and technologies for filming Magic Journeys 1982, Captain EO 1986 and Muppet* Vision 1991. Since leaving Disney, Anderson has continued to film and supervise many three-dimensional productions including the 3D IMAX releases of Cirque Du Soleil: Journey of Man 1999, Ultimate G's: Zac's Flying Dream 2000 and Wild Oceans 2008.

Jonathan Erland, Chair, Research Subcommittee, is a London Film School graduate and was a member of the visual effects team on Star Wars 1977 before he went on to become the director of research and development for Apogee Productions. The owner of numerous patents, Erland is also the recipient of four Academy Scientific or Technical Awards for photographic effects innovations that include advances in a traveling matte process for motion picture compositing. In 2008 he received an Award of Commendation from the Academy for his testing and coordination work on the “High-Speed Emulsion Stress Syndrome” in motion picture film stock. Erland is a SMPTE life fellow, a founding member of the Academy's Science and Technology Council and a co-founder (with his wife Kay Beving Erland) of the Composite Components Company.

Rob Hummel, Chair, Public Programs and Education Subcommittee, began his career at Technicolor Laboratories then joined Douglas Trumbull's visual effects company during the making of Blade Runner 1982, a Visual Effects Oscar nominee, and went on to do post-production work on the groundbreaking Tron 1982. A former president of DALSA Digital Cinema LA, Hummel has also served as senior vice president of production technology at Warner Bros., where he oversaw digital post-production and restoration work on such classics as Gone with the Wind 1939 and The Wizard of Oz 1939. He worked in post-production, animation and Imagineering at Walt Disney Studios, headed animation technology at DreamWorks, and helped launch digital cinema units at Technicolor and Sony. Hummel is a founding member of the Academy's Science and Technology Council and is currently president of digital archival company Group 47, Inc.

Andy Maltz, Director, Science and Technology Council. The Academy reconstituted its Science and Technology Council in 2003, and as its first director, Maltz is responsible for developing and implementing its operational plan, administering the Council's day-to-day operations and individual contributions to selected Council initiatives. Previous to the Academy, Maltz was CEO of Avica Technology Corporation, where he led the first worldwide commercial deployment of digital cinema servers, drove the development of key technologies for digital cinema, and was heavily involved with the digital releases of many major motion pictures in the U.S., Europe, and Asia. Previous to Avica, Maltz served as a consultant to companies such as Sharp Electronics and Microsoft, where he spearheaded the development of the Advanced Authoring Format. Prior to these assignments, he was executive vice president of operations and engineering for nonlinear editing pioneer Ediflex Digital Systems. — Maltz serves on the U.S. National Archives Public Advisory Committee for Electronic Records Archives, is an associate member of the American Society of Cinematographers, and is a fellow of SMPTE where he serves on several engineering committees and the SMPTE Journal Board of Editors. Maltz received a BSEE from the State University of New York at Buffalo.

title: Recent Developments in Acquisition and Workflow
label: SMPTE Motion Imaging Journal ( Volume: 121, Issue: 6, 2012)
keywordsSearch: Recent Developments in Acquisition and Workflow
SMPTE Motion Imaging Journal ( Volume: 121, Issue: 6, 2012)

Curtis Clark, ASC studied theater at the Art Institute of Chicago's Goodman School of Drama and cinematography at the London Film School. After graduation, he began his career by shooting numerous documentary films in Britain before transitioning to shooting feature films. — Clark's feature film credits include such critically acclaimed narrative films as The Draughtsman's Contract; Alamo Bay; Dominick and Eugene; Extremities and Triumph of the Spirit. He started shooting television commercials in the early 1990s, which put him on the forefront of the digital/film frontier. He continues to add to his hundreds of commercial credits working with cutting-edge directors and ad agencies. Clark recently completed his highly praised short film Eldorado which was shot with Sony's innovative new F65 4K digital motion picture camera. — Clark is a member of the American Society of Cinematographers and its Board of Governors, as well as chairman of the ASC Technology Committee, an important motion picture industry forum that both investigates and influences the development of emerging digital technologies that impact filmmaking practice. Since its inception in 2003, The ASC Technology Committee has achieved a series of notable successes including its collaborative work with Digital Cinema Initiatives (DCI) to produce standardized evaluation material for assessing the performance of digital projectors and other elements of digital cinema systems.

Dave Stump, ASC, began his career in film in the late 1970s, first as a TV producer for several cable shows and then at ABC where he helped put together a late night TV show called “Completely Off the Wall.” He worked on a number of pictures with Clive Donner then worked for Francis Coppola in his camera department at Zoetrope Studios, working on all Zoetrope pictures such as One from the Heart until the studio moved to San Francisco. He worked on “The Day After” TV miniseries that won a VFX Emmy Award. — In 1991 Stump started a rental company, Motion Control Rental Services, which grew into the model for Visual Effects rentals in Hollywood. He has worked as DP, VXF DP and VXF supervisor on numerous large motion pictures and television productions and earned another Emmy nomination and an Academy Award for Scientific and Technical Achievement. He is a member of the ASC and chairs the Camera subcommittee of the ASC Technology Committee, helping to shape the future of digital cinematography.

David Reisner's motion picture work emphasizes creative flexibility and best practices in image quality, color, workflow, Digital Intermediate (DI), and digital imaging in production and post-production. — Reisner has been Secretary of the ASC Technology Committee since its founding and is an industry leader in areas including DI, workflow, advanced imaging, and camera assessment. He was a principal in designing and creating the ASC Color Decision List (ASC CDL), ASC-PGA Camera Assessment Series, ASC-DCI StEM (Standard Evaluation Material) test movie, and the ISDCF 3D projection luminance demonstration. He helped educate cinematography societies worldwide about the digital cinema transition. — Reisner designed one of the first digital music synthesizers, the first VLIW computer, the first popular portable video player, an early Internet music and movie distribution service, and co-designed the first lightweight portable computer. He has trained killer whales and shot magazine covers and book jackets. Reisner is an Associate Member of the ASC.

title: Progress in Standardization of Digital TV
label: SMPTE Motion Imaging Journal ( Volume: 121, Issue: 6, 2012)

SMPTE Motion Imaging Journal ( Volume: 121, Issue: 6, 2012)

Philip Laven is chairman of the DVB Project, acting on behalf of the European Broadcasting Union (EBU) where he was director of the Technical Department from May 1997 until August 2007. Before joining the EBU, he worked for the British Broadcasting Corp. (BBC) where most of his work was associated with R&D, including being Chief Engineer R&D with responsibility for all of the BBC's R&D activities. As controller of engineering policy from 1993 to 1997, he played a leading role in the development of the BBC's policy on many technical developments, such as the introduction of digital audio broadcasting and digital television. Between 1994 and 2009, he was chairman of the ETSI/EBU/CENELEC Joint Technical Committee (which is responsible for setting European standards for broadcasting systems). In April 2012, he was appointed vice-chairman of the FOBTV initiative.

Mark Richer is the president of the Advanced Television Systems Committee, Inc. (ATSC). The ATSC is an international, nonprofit organization developing voluntary standards for digital television. Richer first joined the ATSC after 16 years with the Public Broadcasting Service (PBS) where, as vice president of engineering & computer services, he was responsible for development of new technologies for PBS and its member stations. — Richer was the 2010 recipient of the National Association of Broadcasters Engineering Achievement Award for Television and a recipient of Broadcast & Cable's Technology Leadership Award in 2007. He is a Fellow of SMPTE and serves on the FCC Technology Advisory Council. Richer is the chairman of the Future of Broadcast TV (FOBTV) initiative. He holds two patents and has a BS degree from the Rochester Institute of Technology.

As co-founder and CEO of SyncCast, he played a seminal role in launching Microsoft's Xbox Video Market Place. Technicolor subsequently acquired SyncCast in July of 2007. — Ware is currently an advisor to FotoKem and involved in a variety of non-profit activities. Lance regularly speaks at national and international events including NAB, CES, Digital Hollywood, CDSA, HEW Summit and PEVE. He holds a B.S. in Imaging Science from the Rochester Institute of Technology.

Tom Coughlin, president, Coughlin Associates, is a widely respected storage analyst and consultant. He has more than 30 years in the data storage industry with multiple engineering and management positions at high profile companies. Coughlin has many publications and six patents to his credit. He is also the author of “Digital Storage in Consumer Electronics: The Essential Guide,” which was published by Newnes Press. Coughlin Associates provides market and technology analysis (including reports on several digital storage technologies and applications and a newsletter) as well as Data Storage Technical Consulting services. Coughlin publishes the Digital Storage Technology Newsletter, the Media and Entertainment Storage Report, and the Capital Equipment and Technology for the Hard Disk Drive Industry Report. — Coughlin is active in SMPTE, the Storage Networking Industry Association (SNIA), International Disk Equipment and Materials Association (IDEMA), the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) Magnetics Society, IEEE CE Society, and other professional organizations. Coughlin is a senior member of the IEEE, Leader in the Gerson Lehrman Group Councils of Advisors and a member of the Consultants Network of Silicon Valley (CNSV). Scott Miller is a senior member of the technical staff at Dolby Laboratories where he serves in the Image Technology Research group. He specializes in image display technology and video signal processing, most recently working on Dolby's Professional Reference Monitor. Miller received a B.S. in electrical engineering from Cornell University and has spent nearly 30 years working in the video industry, including several years with Panasonic Research where he helped develop the Emmyaward winning Universal Video Format Converter.

Scott Daly received a B.S. EE degree in 1980 from North Carolina State University, and then worked with early high-resolution laser scanning systems at Photo Electronics Corp. in West Palm Beach, FL. Shifting from hardware to wetware, he obtained an M.S. in bioengineering from the University of Utah in 1984, completing a neurophysiology thesis on the temporal processing of cone photoreceptors. He then worked in the Imaging Science Division at Eastman Kodak in the fields of image compression, image fidelity models, and image watermarking. — Daly then worked at Sharp Laboratories of America in Washington state, where he led a group on display algorithms. Becoming a research fellow, he applied visual models towards digital video and displays, with publications on spatiotemporal and motion imagery, human interaction with wall-sized displays, and stereoscopic displays. These topics led him to join Dolby Laboratories in 2010 to focus on overall fundamental perceptual issues, and efforts to preserve artistic intent throughout the entire video path to reach the viewer. He is currently a member of Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE), Society of Photo-Optical Instrumentation Engineers (SPIE), and Society for Information Display (SID).

Craig Todd is Sr. vice president and chief technical officer at Dolby Laboratories. He has a Bachelors degree in physics from the California Institute of Technology, and has been with Dolby since 1977. Todd is one of the primary designers of Dolby Digital and Dolby E coding technologies, and he was heavily involved in the ACATS/ATSC effort to set the DTV standard for the U.S. Current interests include bringing 3D, wide color gamut, and high dynamic range imagery into the home via both legacy, and new electronic media, formats. — Todd has participated in a variety of standards-setting activities in the International Telecommunications Union-Radiocommunication Sector (ITU-R), Digital Video Broadcasting (DVB), Audio Engineering Society (AES), International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC), Consumer Electronics Association (CEA), Advanced Television Systems Committee (ATSC) and SMPTE. He currently serves on the Board of ATSC and is a vice-chair of ITU-R Working Party 6C. He is a recipient of the SMPTE Samuel L. Warner Medal for achievement in motion picture sound, and of an Emmy for loudness metering, and holds more than 20 patents.

Nanci Linke-Ellis, partner and general manager of Captionfish, the premiere web and mobile content site for captioned entertainment, has spent the past 18 years working on film and television access issues critical to individuals with hearing loss. Her film industry advocacy, which began in 1993, has resulted in the recent agreements by Regal, Cinemark, and AMC Theatres to provide accessible technology in all of its theaters across the U.S. by the end of 2013. — Linke-Ellis is a governor appointee on the California State Rehabilitation Council and recently joined the World Institute of Disabilities, a think tank based in Berkeley, CA. Captionfish was recently honored by the FCC for its innovative technology by Phlixie, its sister site, the search engine geared towards online, streaming, Netflix and iTunes content. Prior to losing her hearing and receiving bi-lateral cochlear implants, she worked in both the television and film industries as a senior development executive in the TV, movies, and mini-series adaptation genre.

Frank Melchior is head of the audio research team at BBC R&D. He received a Dipl.-Ing. (equiv. to Master of Science) in media technology from the Technical University Ilmenau and a doctoral degree on the topic of spatial sound design and acoustics from the University of Technology, Delft, The Netherlands. Melchior worked as a researcher and project manager at the Fraunhofer Institute for Digital Media Technology. He has spent his professional career developing audio systems including wave field synthesis-based system and leading R&D teams on various topics including authoring, live sound applications, automotive audio and motion picture sound. Before he joined the BBC Melchior was the chief technical officer at IOSONO, Erfurt, Germany, which develops spatial audio solutions. Melchior's research interests include spatial array signal processing, spatial audio reproduction, user interface technology for audio systems and listening experiments. Dr Frank Melchior is very passionate about finding the best way to bring the emotion and creative ideas embedded in sound to the listener.

Anthony Churnside joined BBC R&D in 2008 after completing an MSc in audio acoustics at the University of Salford. He is currently working towards a PhD in designing and creating next-generation audio experiences and broadcasting systems. Churnside also advises television, radio and multiplatform productions on how to make the best creative use of current technology. He is technical director of the relaunched Radiophonic Workshop and is a committee member of the Radio Festival and the International Broadcasting Convention. Churnside was honored with The Royal Television Society's Young Technologist 2010 award and is responsible for the BBC Philharmonic Maestro project which, in 2012, was nominated for Design Week and Webby awards and was given a One Show Interactive Award.

Sascha Spors joined the Deutsche Telekom Laboratories in 2005 as a senior scientist, where he is heading the audio technology group. He obtained a Doctoral degree (Dr.-Ing.) with distinction in January 2006, from the Electrical, Electronic and Communication Engineering Faculty of the University Erlangen-Nuremberg, as a result of his work as a research scientist as the chair of Multimedia Communications and Signal Processing. The topic of his doctoral thesis was the active compensation of the listening room characteristics for sound reproduction systems. His research interests include sound field analysis, sound field synthesis, and massive multichannel adaptation problems. Spors is member of the IEEE, the “Deutsche Gesellschaft für Akustik (DEGA)” and the Audio Engineering Society (AES). In 2011, he recieved the Lothar- Cremer-Preis of the “Deutsche Gesellschaft für Akustik (DEGA).” Spors is a member of the IEEE Audio and Acoustic Signal Processing Technical Committee and chair of the AES Technical Committee on Spatial Audio.

Laurence J. Thorpe joined the Broadcast and Communications Division of Canon U.S.A., Inc., in 2004 as national marketing executive. Thorpe also worked for RCA's Broadcast Division from 1966 to 1982, where he developed a range of color television cameras and telecine products. He holds ten patents from this period. From 1961 to 1966, Thorpe worked in the Designs Dept. of the BBC in London, England, where he participated in the development of a range of color television studio products. — Thorpe graduated from the College of Technology in Dublin, Ireland, in 1961, with a degree in electrical engineering. He received his Chartered Engineer (C. Eng.) and MIEE distinction in 1965 from the Institution of Electrical Engineers in London, England.

Following his formal education, Hitoshi Yoshida joined Canon Inc., where he spent several years in the production department of the optical factory. He started his North American career in July 1990 as a service support specialist for five years and then transferred to Canon Canada, as manager of the BCTV division. Following nine years in Toronto, Yoshida returned to Japan in 2004. After one year, he returned to the U.S. in April 2005. He was assigned as manager, service and support in the BCTV Division until 2011 and later transferred to London where he presently manages the European Service & Technical Support operation.

Thomas Brune joined Technicolor Research & Innovation, Hannover/Germany in 1996. He works in the field of movie and broadcast production infrastructures, image processing and is also a system architect for embedded realtime HW&SW solutions. He led activities for video capture and high-speed interfacing. Brune was responsible for the Technicolor contributions to the EC FP7 funded project “2020 3D media.” He graduated from the University of Hannover in 1996 and has background in microprocessor architectures, video compression, serial interfaces and according protocol stacks and FPGA technology.

Nicola Gutberlet graduated with a degree in computer science from the Technical University of Darmstadt in 2008. The same year, he joined the Image Processing Department of Fraunhofer Institute for Telecommunications HHI in Berlin. He is engaged in several European and German projects. Gutberlet's research focuses on multicamera systems in capturing and post-processing relating to panoramic imaging as well as depth estimation.

Ralf Tanger graduated from the Technical University of Berlin in 1996 with a degree in electrical engineering. From 1993 to 1997 he worked at Daimler-Benz Research in the field of image classification with Neural Networks. In 1997, he joined the Image Processing Department of the Fraunhofer Institute for Telecommunications HHI as researcher. Since 2002 he has been a scientific project manager. Tanger is engaged in several European (COST211ter, NEMESIS, VIRTUE, 2020 3D Media, 3D4YOU, MUSCADE) and German research projects in the fields of segmentation, video conferencing and 3D video. Currently, he is interested in 3D video analysis, depth estimation, and content creation for AS3D. Tanger is a member of IEEE, SMPTE and VDI.

Dirk Gandolph joined Technicolor Research & Innovation in 1993 after receiving an engineering degree from Leibniz University in Hanover. He is working on image analysis for 3D scene acquisition and post-production, and inter alia contributed to the EC FP7 funded project “2020 3D media.”

In 1990, he joined Thomson where he first obtained experience in digital product development for the professional market. Since 1996, he has been involved in the development of signal processing algorithms applied to displays and anti-piracy technologies. He a principal scientist in the research and innovation department of Technicolor, where he is currently in charge of activities dealing with 3DTV rendering and human factors analysis.

Laurent Blondé is principal scientist atTechnicolor Research & Innovation, Cesson Sevigne, France. He received an MSc. degree in optical engineering from the Institut d'Optique, ParisTech, France in 1985. Hired as a research engineer at Thomson Research Labs, he participated in many R&D projects including infrared image synthesis, special effects and virtual studio, display processing, anti-camcorder and color management for dinema applications, color and 3D perception. An image, color, and vision expert and multiproject technical advisor at Technicolor, Laurent likes to be a creative technical leader enriching image processing with physics and perception. He is author and co-author of more than 70 invention disclosures and is associate member of Technicolor's Fellowship Network.

Borel Thierry began his career at Technicolor (formerly Thomson) in 1987 in Germany and has mainly been involved in R&D activities linked to new display technologies including plasma, OLED, and slim rear-projection; first as an engineer and then as display lab manager since 1998. In 2005, he was appointed signal processing research lab manager and led various teams working on color processing for cinema and post-production applications. He has led two European research projects addressing 2D and 3D display technologies. From 2007 to 2008, he was temporarily appointed to Beijing's Technicolor Center to develop the local research lab. Since July 2008, has been the leader of a worldwide 3D research project at Technicolor, aimed at proposing innovative solutions for 3DTV and 3D Cinema workflows with and without glasses.

Sebastian Knorr is managing director and head of the R&D and Knowledge Management Department of imcube labs GmbH. Between 2002 and 2009 he worked as project manager and senior researcher in the field of 3D image processing and computer vision in the Communication Systems Lab at Technische Universität Berlin, Germany. During this time he was involved in several European Networks of Excellence, e.g., VISNET and 3DTV. — In 2007 Knorr invented the process of automatic 2D to 3D image conversion with highly advanced computer vision technology. He received a Dr.-Ing. degree (PhD) with highest honors in 2008. — Knorr is a member of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE), the Association for Computing Machinery (ACM) and the German Society of Television and Cinema Technology (FKTG e.V.). He received the German Multimedia Business Award of the Federal Ministry of Economics and Technology in 2008, and was awarded by the initiative “Germany- Land of Ideas,” which is sponsored by the German government, commerce, and industry in 2009, respectively. In 2012 he received the Scott Helt Memorial Award for the best paper published in the IEEE Transactions on Broadcasting in 2011. Knorr frequently works as reviewer for conferences and journals.

Kai Ide is a researcher at the communication systems group at Technische Universität Berlin since 2008, where he received both his BSc and his MSc degree in electrical engineering in 2007 and 2008, respectively. He is currently pursuing a PhD degree for which he has designed and built a structured light multicamera multiprojector array for realtime 3D scanning. He has been a visiting researcher at the computer vision lab at ETH Zurich and at the quantum photonics integrated circuit design lab at POSTECH. His research interests are focused on 3DTV and applied computer vision with an emphasis on 3D scanning and 3D reconstruction.

Matthias Kunter is the head of the software development and know-how transfer department of imcube labs GmbH. Until 2009 he worked as senior researcher in the field of 3D image processing and computer vision in the Communication Systems Lab at Technische Universität Berlin, Germany. — Kunter spent time in industry at Bosch S.A. de C.V. in Mexico and Siemens AG, Germany. He received a PhD (Dr.-Ing.) with the thesis “Advances in sprite-based video coding towards universal usability” in 2008. — Kunter received the German Multimedia Business Award of the Federal Ministry of Economics and Technology in 2008 and was awarded by the initiative “Germany-Land of Ideas,” which is sponsored by the German government, commerce and industry in 2009, respectively.

Thomas Sikora is professor for communications and director of the Communication Systems Lab at Technische Universität Berlin, Berlin, Germany. — Sikora received Dipl.-Ing. and Dr.-Ing. degrees in electrical engineering from Bremen University, Bremen, Germany, in 1985 and 1989, respectively. In 1990, he joined Siemens Ltd. and Monash University, Melbourne, Australia, as a project leader responsible for video compression research activities in the Australian Universal Broadband Video Codec Consortium. Between 1994 and 2001, he was the director of the Interactive Media Department, Heinrich Hertz Institute, Berlin GmbH, Germany. Sikora is a co-founder of Vis-a-Pix GmbH and imcube labs GmbH, two Berlin-based start-up companies involved in research and development of audio and video signal processing and compression technology. — Sikora has been involved in the International Telecommunications Union and the International Organization for Standardization as well as in several European research activities for more than 15 years. As Chair of the ISO-MPEG video group, he was responsible for the development and standardization of the MPEG-4 and MPEG-7 video algorithms. Sikora has served as editor on a number of publications and has published more than 300 journal and conference papers related to audio and video processing and has co-authored several books.

Brian Vessa is an audio professional with more than 35 years of experience. After attending UCLA Engineering School he became a recording engineer, producing albums and recording orchestras. He was known for hot-rodding studio gear. Vessa transitioned into film post as a music editor and sound editor, became a rerecording mixer at Cannon Films and MGM, then handled audio restoration at NT Audio. He was hired by Sony Pictures in 1998, and is now the company's executive director of digital audio mastering and representative to DCI. Vessa is a member of the Academy Sound Branch, SMPTE and the Audio Engineering Society. He chairs TC-25CSS (Cinema Sound Systems-formerly the SMPTE B-Chain Study Group) as well as D-Cinema and IMF AHG's. He has written many audio specifications, including a white paper on near-field mixing for home theater that has been widely adopted. Vessa enjoys recording jazz, rock, and mixing live sound. He is a drummer and keyboardist in the LA area, an avid backpacker and an award-winning home wine and beer maker.

David J. Weinberg is an engineering consultant and technology journalist on audio, video and film technology. He provides audio and home theater engineering consultation and professional location digital audio recording services to companies, radio stations and individuals. He brings to his work an MSEE, a First Class Radiotelephone license, and five decades of continued study and active involvement in the audio, video and computer industries. He is Chair of the Audio Engineering Society's DC section, and a Manager in the Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers' DC section. Weinberg has authored articles on various aspects of audio for video and film, is Technical Editor of audioXpress (www.audioXpress.com), and serves as Membership Officer for the Boston Audio Society (www.BostonAudioSociety.org) and Editor of its journal, The B A S Speaker.

Nelson Meacham retired after more than 30 years of employment with the Walt Disney Company. The majority of his career was spent designing audio and video systems for theme park attractions in the U.S., Japan, France, and Hong Kong. For five years starting in 1981, Meacham was the assistant sound director for Walt Disney Pictures and in 1994/1995 supervised the installation of a new film and digital screening room for Walt Disney Feature Animation. Meacham graduated from California State Polytechnic University, San Luis Obispo. He is a Life-Fellow of SMPTE, a member of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, and member of the Audio Engineering Society.

Tom Scott has been involved with sound for motion pictures since 1978, employed at American Zoetrope, Dolby Laboratories, Saul Zaentz Film Center and Skywalker Sound. He has been the recipient of two Oscars, Academy Awards for Best Sound on the films The Right Stuff and Amadeus. He is currently employed as the vice president technology at Onstream Media in San Francisco. A Life Fellow of SMPTE, Scott has served the Society as Engineering Director, Motion Pictures, and Editorial Director, Motion Pictures.

Sunil Bharitkar received a PhD degree in electrical engineering from the University of Southern California (USC) in 2004 and is presently the director of technology strategy at Dolby Laboratories. He co-founded the company Audyssey Laboratories at USC with Tomlinson Holman in 2002 and was the vice president of research until 2010. He also taught in the Department of Electrical Engineering at USC. Bharitkar has published more than 50 technical papers and has more than 10 patents in the area of signal processing applied to audio and acoustics, as well as a textbook, Immersive Audio Signal Processing, from Springer Verlag. He is a frequent reviewer for various journals and conferences of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE), the Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, Signal Processing from European Association for Signal and Image Processing (EURASIP), and the Journal of the Audio Engineering Society. Bharitkar is the recipient of of an IEEE Best Paper Award at the Asilomar Conf. on Signals, Systems, and Computers. He is a member of the IEEE, the Acoustical Society of America (ASA), EURASIP, and the Audio Engineering Society (AES).

Grant Davidson received a BS degree in physics from the California Polytechnic State University in 1980, and MS and PhD degrees in electrical engineering from the University of California, Santa Barbara, in 1984 and 1987, respectively. Since 1987, Davidson has been a member of the Sound Technology Research Group at Dolby Laboratories. He is currently a principal staff engineer, with research interests including digital audio and speech processing and an emphasis on perceptual audio coding algorithms. More recently, his research activities also include signal enhancement and spatial audio rendering technologies for mobile devices. Davidson is co-developer of the Dolby Digital (AC-3), MPEG-2 Advanced Audio Coding (AAC), and Dolby E compression standards, and is a recipient of two Emmy Awards for this work. Davidson is a senior member of the IEEE, and has served on the IEEE Audio and Acoustic Signal Processing Technical Committee since 1999.

Louis Fielder received a BS degree in electrical engineering from the Caltech in 1974 and an MS degree in acoustics from the UCLA in 1976. He worked on electronic design at Paul Veneklasen and Associates between 1976–1978. From 1978–1984 he was involved in digital-audio and magnetic recording research at the Ampex Corp. Since 1984, he has worked at Dolby Laboratories on psychoacoustics for audio design and audio coders for music distribution, transmission, and storage applications, i.e., AC-1, AC-2, AC-3, Enhanced AC-3, AAC, and Dolby E. Additionally, he has investigated perceptually derived limits for the performance for digital-audio conversion, low-frequency loudspeaker systems, and loudspeaker-room equalization. Currently, he is working on cinema equalization and acoustics. Fielder is a fellow of the AES, a senior member of the IEEE, a member of SMPTE and the ASA. He was on the AES Board of Governors during 1990–1992, president during 1994–1995, and treasurer 2005–2009.

Poppy Crum is a senior scientist at Dolby Laboratories in San Francisco and a consulting professor at Stanford University, CCRMA. At Dolby, Crum serves as an internal science expert for integrating psychophysical and neuroscience knowledge into algorithm design, human assessment, and basic science discovery. She also represents Dolby's science interests externally, including serving as one of the U.S. representatives to the International Telecommunications Union-Radiocommunication. — Prior to joining Dolby, Crum was research faculty in the Department of Biomedical Engineering at Johns Hopkins Medical School. Her work investigated neural circuits in the auditory cortex involved in hearing in complex acoustic environments. Crum completed her PhD at the University of California, Berkeley, with an emphasis in neuroscience and psychoacoustics and a Masters degree at McGill University with an emphasis in auditory scene analysis. She also holds a degree in violin performance through studies at the University of Iowa and McGill University.

Brian Long has more than 15 years in professional audio and a diverse and extensive knowledge regarding the design and implementation of sound reinforcement and playback systems for all types of scenarios ranging from simple single speaker events to massive show spectaculars and multichannel media presentation environments. Long holds a Master of Fine Arts from the University of Southern California's School of Cinematic Arts, where he specialized in post-production audio and worked on advanced multichannel audio concepts. He is currently a member of the engineering team at Skywalker Sound.

Roger Schwenke, PhD., is a senior scientist and has been contributing his expertise in acoustic measurement and prediction at Meyer Sound Laboratories for over ten years. Schwenke's expertise in acoustics has been applied towards making acoustical measurements and recommendations, including the design and tuning Constellation systems, at world class venues around the world. He has participated in the development of a number of the company's innovative products, including MAPP Online, SIM 3, Constellation Electroacoustic Architecture, the M1D UltraCompact Curvilinear Array Loudspeaker, and LD-3 Compensating Line Driver. Schwenke received a Doctorate in Acoustics from Penn State University in December of 2000; his thesis work in advanced detection and estimation methods was sponsored by the Applied Research Laboratory. He is a member of the Acoustical Society of America.

Peter Soper has been a member of Meyer Sound's Technical staff since 1986. He holds several design and technical patents for loudspeaker technology, and is a member of SMPTE and the Audio Engineering Society.

Glenn Leembruggen is a principal of the consulting engineering firms of Acoustic Directions and ICE Design in Australia and is also an Associate of Sydney University. Playing saxophone in a Chicago style electric blues band, Leembruggen is quite passionate about the left and right brain aspects of sound (physics and the aural experience) and his work designing rooms and sound systems to deliver extremely high quality speech and music. His current work is with courts, parliaments, transport terminals, road tunnels and cathedrals. Among Leembruggen's research interests are the differences that exist between subjective and measured speech intelligibility, cinema sound and the measurement and prediction of acoustic absorption. He is member of the Audio Engineering Society (AES), ASA, IOA, and SMPTE and is part of the Maintenance Team for the STI standard IEC 60268-16.

Charles Robinson received BSEE and MSEE degrees from the University of Illinois, where he specialized in signal processing and began his professional career just as realtime digital audio signal processing was becoming a practical reality. Since joining Dolby Research in 1995, his areas of research have included, acoustics, audio coding, interactive audio, and spatial audio with applications to broadcast, gaming and cinema. Robinson has authored or coauthored over a dozen patents in audio signal processing, contributed to two Emmy-award winning products, and is a member of the Audio Engineering Society and Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers. Most recently, Robinson was the audio research lead for the Dolby Atmos program, where he was responsible for the conception of the audio format and loudspeaker layout embodied by Dolby Atmos.

Sripal Mehta is director of engineering, broadcast technology at Dolby Laboratories where his focus is the development next-generation audio technology for professional broadcast. Mehta has contributed to Dolby's innovations in broadcast and digital cinema including the recent introduction of Dolby Atmos. He has authored two SMPTE digital cinema standards for closed captioning and has chaired the 21DC digital cinema security subcommittee. Mehta holds an MS degree in electrical and computer engineering from Carnegie Mellon University.

Nicolas Tsingos is a senior platform manager at Dolby Laboratories. He designed and prototyped the authoring and rendering tools for the Dolby Atmos cinema technology and now oversees its future evolution. Tsingos received a PhD in computer science from the Joseph Fourier University in Grenoble, France. He has more than15 years of research experience in computer graphics, interactive audio rendering and acoustic simulation. In addition to his current position at Dolby Laboratories, Tsingos holds a tenure research position at INRIA - the French National Institute for Computer Science - and previously was a member of the technical staff at Bell Laboratories.

James M. DeFilippis has worked in radio and television broadcasting for more than 30 years. He recently received the SMPTE David Sarnoff Medal for his work in advancing the art of television engineering. He is a Fellow of the SMPTE.

Masayuki Sugawara received B.S. and M.S. degrees in electric communication engineering, and a Ph.D. degree in electronic engineering from Tohoku University, Sendai, Japan. He joined NHK (Japan Broadcasting Corporation) in 1983. Since 1987, he has been researching solid-state image sensor and HDTV camera at NHK Science & Technology Research Laboratories (STRL). He was an associate professor at the University of Electro-Communications in Tokyo from 2000 until 2004. He has been attending the ITU-R SG6 meeting since 2004 and has also been active in the working parties that deal with program production. Currently, he is an executive research engineer at NHK STRL and is engaged in the research of the ultra-high-definition TV system. — Sugawara is a member of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE), the Society for Information Display (SID), SMPTE, The Institute of Electronics, Information and Communication Engineers (IEICE) and ITE.

Satoru Sawada joined NHK in 1982 and is mainly engaged in program production and live broadcast. He served as the technical director of on-site shooting for the world's first super hi- vision (SHV) live public viewing at the London Olympic Games in 2012. He is a senior engineer in the Outside Broadcast Engineering Division, News Technical Center, in the Broadcast Engineering Department.

Hayato Fujinuma joined NHK in 1993 and has mainly been engaged in post-production as well as HD production from its early stage of development. He has been involved in the SHV project since 2003 and produced numbers of SHV content, mainly working on VE operations. — Fujinuma served as the technical director of the BBC Studio TC0 at the London Olympic Games in 2012. He is a principal engineer at the Technical Operations and Engineering Center in the Broadcasting Engineering Department.

Yoshiaki Shishikui received B.S., M.S., and Ph.D. degrees in electrical engineering from the University of Tokyo in 1981, 1983, and 1997, respectively. He joined NHK in 1983. Since 1986, he has worked in the NHK STRL, where he has been engaged in research on digital signal processing, picture coding, HDTV broadcasting systems, IPTV systems and advanced data broadcasting systems. Currently, he is the head of Advanced Television Systems Research Division of NHK STRL and leads UHDTV and 3DTV research activities. — From 2001 to 2003, Shishikui was with NHK Engineering Services Inc., where he helped to develop video archives and video-on-demand systems. He was a part-time instructor at several universities in Japan. He has been actively involved in standardization activities at SMPTE and ISO-IEC (MPEG).

John Zubrzycki is the Archives Research Section Leader at BBC Research and Development. Zubrzycki joined BBC Research in 1982 and has pioneered the use of fibre-optic networks for studio centers using dense wavelength-division multiplexing. He has also worked on 4th generation mobile technology, producing a 34 Mbit/sec demonstrator in 1998. Zubrzycki led the R&D team that produced the world's first digital wireless camera in 2000, which is in regular use by the BBC and many other broadcasters. He was also responsible for the development and testing of the terrestrial set-top boxes used in the BBC HDTV trials and was in charge of “Beyond HD” projects, including high frame rate TV and SHV, in collaboration with NHK. He led a cross-industry team that carried out an award-winning live London-Amsterdam link of SHV at IBC'08 and led the R&D team involved in the SHV Showcase at the London 2012 Olympic Games.

Rajitha Weerakkody is a research engineer at BBC Research and Development. He joined the BBC in 2008, for research on video coding for audiovisual archiving applications. Weerakkody managed the technical design and construction of the U.K. distribution and public viewing network for the SHV showcase at the London 2012 Olympic games. Currently, he is involved in high-efficiency video coding (HEVC) standardization activities. Weerakkody has a Ph.D. in video compression and industry experience in wireless telecommunications and data networking.

Andy Quested was a much sought-after editor with BBC Resources for many years, working on programs as diverse as “The Human Body” and “Keeping Up Appearances.” About ten years ago, he gave up the life of a hermit editor and moved into the sunshine and bright lights of the BBC Technology Group. — Since 2005, Quested has been leading the BBC's high-definition technology strategy as head of technology for HD and leading the work for the BBC's automated quality control project. He also chairs the EBU Strategic Quality Control Program. — During 2010, the BBC started a series of transmission and production 3D trials. As part of this, Quested has also taken on the role of head of technology for the BBC's 3D output and strategy. — As part of the process of developing 3DTV standards, Quested was asked to become an ITU Special Rapporteur with the task of examining the current world 3D production status and providing a report with recommendation at the September 2011 and April 2012 ITU meetings in Geneva. Quested also chairs the EBU 3D group. In his current role, he is responsible for the BBC's HD and 3D technical strategies and for the quality of the BBC HD television output on all platforms.

Harry Ryan has more than 25 years of experience in the telecommunication field. Ryan has been an independent consultant since 1992 and has had numerous engagements in a broad range of industries including financial institutions, government agencies, as well as media and Telcommunication companies. He holds a BS degree and is currently attending Boston University in pursuit of a Master's degree in Information Technology as it relates to security.

Rajesh Rajah is a solutions manager at Cisco's End-to-End IP Video solution/Videoscape. Before that, he was a solutions architect with diverse experience in end-to-end planning, design and deployment phases of SP carrier ethernet and video/IPTV engagements worldwide. Prior to focusing on IPTV/video, he was involved in designing IP NGN and MPLS-based networks for service providers in different theaters. He has been with Cisco for more than 12 years and has been a speaker at Cisco Live/Networkers, National Association of Broadcasters (NAB), SMPTE, SANOG and other forums. Rajah also holds an issued patent and has several others pending, with the US Patent office, on video, datacenters and carrier ethernet.

Andrew B. Watson is the senior scientist for vision research at NASA Ames Research Center in California. He is the author of more than 100 papers and 6 patents on topics in vision science and imaging technology. In 2001, he founded the Journal of Vision (http://journalofvision.org) where he serves as editor-in-chief. Watson is a Fellow of the Optical Society of America, of the Association for Research in Vision and Ophthalmology, and of the Society for Information Display. He is vice chair for vision science and human factors of the International Committee on Display Measurement. In 2007, he received the Otto Schade Award from the Society for Information Display, and in 2008 the Special Recognition Award from the Association for Research in Vision and Ophthalmology. In 2011, he received the Presidential Rank Award from the President of the United States.

Laurence J. Thorpe joined the Broadcast and Communications Division of Canon U.S.A., Inc., in 2004 as national marketing executive. Thorpe also worked for RCA's Broadcast Division from 1966 to 1982, where he developed a range of color television cameras and telecine products. He holds ten patents from this period. From 1961 to 1966, Thorpe worked in the Designs Dept. of the BBC in London, England, where he participated in the development of a range of color television studio products. Thorpe graduated from the College of Technology in Dublin, Ireland, in 1961, with a degree in electrical engineering. He received his Chartered Engineer (C. Eng.) and MIEE distinction in 1965 from the Institution of Electrical Engineers in London, England.

John Galt is Panavision's chief technology officer. He joined Panavision in 1999 as senior vice president and founder of the Advanced Digital Imaging group. Galt was the project leader of the Panavision/Sony co-development of the Genesis Electronic Cinematography System and is presently engaged in the development of Panavision's next-generation 70mm camera system. Galt has been awarded numerous patents in image processing, high-definition image acquisition, and film digitization.

Branko Petljanski received B.Sc. and M.Sc. degrees in electronic engineering from the University of Novi Sad in 1995. He also received an M.Sc. in electronic engineering and a Ph.D. in computer engineering in 2001 and 2010, both from Florida Atlantic University. His captivation with digital imaging started at NASA Imaging Technology Space Center where he was involved in the development of high-resolution cameras and recording systems. He is working currently in Panavision's Advanced Digital Imaging group as a senior engineer. At Panavision, he has been involved in conceiving and designing equipment for image acquisition, processing and storing. His particular interests are in photography, optoelectronics, and image processing.

Stacey Campbell has been involved with CMOS imager design and utilization in high-performance camera systems since 2003, working first with Conexant then later Micron and Altasens. He currently works as a senior engineer in Panavision's Advanced Digital Imaging group. He received a B.Sc. (Hons) from La Trobe University in 1987.

Brian Caldwell earned a Ph.D. in optics from The University of Rochester in 1988. He has 30 years experience in the fields of lens design and optical engineering, with more than 100 different manufactured products to his credit. In 1988, he founded Optical Data Solutions to develop LensVIEW, an extensive database of more than 30,000 optical designs from the patent literature. After working for a few years at Projectavision and Concord Camera, he founded Caldwell Photographic Inc. in 2001 to do independent consulting and to develop and manufacture optical products. He has worked as an optical design consultant to Panavision since 2001. Commercial products co-developed with Wilfried Bittner include a 60mm UV-VIS-IR apochromat licensed for manufacture by Jenoptik Optical Systems, and a universal photographic focal reducer currently marketed by Metabones as the Speed Booster.

Wilfried Bittner is a mechanical engineer specializing in opto-mechanics, and has more than 35 years experience in the optical and photographic industries, both in Germany and Hong Kong. He has designed a wide range of cameras for big brands like Agfa, Kodak, Polaroid and Nikon. The types of cameras ranged from simple 35mm film cameras to fully automatic digital cameras with folded zoom optics. In 2006, Bittner founded WB Design in Hong Kong to do specialized mechanical design and product development work, such as laser optics and mechanisms for BOSCH laser measuring tools, as well as lens barrels and motorized shutters for specialty lenses. Currently, he is deeply involved in the development of a family of cinema lenses for Panavision.

Winston Ip received a BEng honor's degree in electronics engineering from the University of Liverpool in 1979. He joined Marconi Radar until 1982; then immigrated to Canada to work with different defense projects at MEL defense companies and Litton System Canada. In 1993, he returned to Hong Kong to work with Haking Industrial and Concord Camera where he led a team to design camera logic using different MCUs. During this time he also designed ASICs for Kodak APS, Polaroid single-use and digital cameras. Before he started his own consulting company to work on projects with Caldwell Photographic Inc., he was a vice president of digital media products at IDT and director of electronics at Simatelex.

Daniel Sasaki was educated at Cal State Long Beach. He began his career at Panavision in 1986 when he started as a lens service technician under the supervision of his father Ralph Sasaki. Under the mentorship of the legendary Tak Miyagishima, Sasaki started to pick up his practical optics methodology and began to customize optics for various cinematographers based on this type of philosophy. In 2006, Sasaki left Panavision to further his career in optics technology by joining Dalsa Camera technologies. In 2008, he returned to Panavision and has subsequently been promoted to vice president of optical engineering and is actively working with Brian Caldwell to develop the new 70mm optical system.

Toshihisa Watabe received B.E. and M.E. degrees in electrical engineering from Keio University, Yokohama, Japan, in 1989 and 1991, respectively. Hiroshi Ohtake graduated from the Tokyo Kogakuin College of Technology, Tokyo, Japan, in 1982. In 1982, he joined NHK Science and Technology Research Laboratories. Norifumi Egami received B.E. and M.E. degrees from Kyushu Institute of Technology, Fukuoka, Japan, in 1987 and 1980, respectively, and a Ph.D degree from Tohoku University, Sendai, Japan in 2003. Yuichi Kusakabe received an M.S. degree in applied physics from the University of Tokyo in 1999. From 1999, he has been working at NHK. He is currently a research engineer at the NHK STRL and is engaged in the development of extremely high-resolution imagery systems and their signal processing. He is a member of the Institute of Image Information and Television Engineers of Japan (ITE).

Yukihiro Nishida is senior research engineer, advanced television systems, at NHK Science and Technical Research Laboratories in Tokyo. He has been involved in many areas of broadcasting technologies including HDTV, digital broadcasting, video coding, multiplexing and quality evaluation. One such area is the study of new television systems such as UHDTV. He is also active in the standardization of broadcast technologies in International Telecommunications Union-Radiocommunication (ITU-R), Association of Radio Industries and Businesses (ARIB), and the European Broadcast Union (EBU). Nishida is vice-chairman of ITU-R Study Group 6 on broadcasting services, and is also chair of Working Party 6B covering source coding, interfaces, multimedia and interactivity. He was a visiting research engineer at RAI Research Center in Turin, Italy, in 1992. Nishida graduated from Keio University, Japan, with an M.Sc. in electrical engineering. He is a member of ITE of Japan.

Shoji Kawahito received a Ph.D. degree from Tohoku University, Sendai, Japan, in 1988 and joined Tohoku University as a Research Associate. From 1989 to 1999, he was with Toyohashi University of Technology. From 1996 to 1997, he was a visiting professor at ETH, Zurich. Since 1999, he has been a professor at the Research Institute of Electronics, Shizuoka University. Since 2006, he has been a chief technology officer at Brookman Technology, Inc. — His research interests are in CMOS imaging devices and mixed-signal sensor interface circuits. He has published more than 250 papers in refereed journals and international conference proceedings. — Kawahito has received several awards including the Beatrice Winner Award for Editorial Excellence at the 2005 IEEE-ISSCC, the 2010 IEICE Electronics Society Award and the 24th Takayanagi Memorial Award in 2010. He is a Fellow of the IEEE and ITE and a member of the Institute of Electronics, Information and Communication Engineers (IECE) and the International Society for Optics and Photonics (SPIE).

Tomohiko Kosugi received a B.S. degree from Chubu University, Aichi, Japan, in 2002. He worked at Sanei Hytechs Co., Ltd. from 2002 to 2009, where he was engaged in the design of analog circuit. In 2010, he joined Brookman Technology, Inc., where he has been working on the development and design of CMOS image sensor and analog circuits.

Takashi Watanabe received B.S., M.S. and Ph.D. degrees in physics from Osaka University, Osaka, Japan, in 1974, 1976 and 2000, respectively. He joined Sharp Corporation, Osaka, in 1976. From August 1976, he worked to develop CCD signal processing ICs, linear image sensors and area image sensors. From 1995, he led the development CMOS image sensors and was concerned with first application to mobile phones in 2000. He was also involved in developing log-type imagers and range image sensors. Since December 2007, he has been with Brookman Technology, Inc., Hamamatsu, Japan. Since April 2011, he has been a visiting professor at the Research Institute of Electronics, Shizuoka University. His research interests are CCD and CMOS image sensor device technologies. He holds 145 Japanese patent applications and 48 U.S. patents. Watanabe is a member of the IEEE and ITE of Japan.

Tadaaki Yanagi joined Hitachi Denshi Technosystem Ltd. in 1989 and is currently with Hitachi Kokusai Electric Inc. Tetsuo Yoshida joined Shiba Denki in 1970 and is currently with Hitachi Kokusai Electric, Inc. Hideki Kikuchi joined Link Laboratory Inc. in 2005. Since 2008, he has been engaged in development of prototype ultrahigh-definition TV cameras in the Development division.

Per Böhler has been with the Norwegian Broadcasting Corp. (NRK) since 1963. After graduating from the NRK Engineering School he worked for a few years as an operational engineer. In the remaining years he has worked in the engineering development/technology departments. His professional work has entirely been dedicated to video origination equipment, video processing/recording/compression/display technologies and optical testing of camera lenses for both film and TV cameras. — Böhler has been actively involved in the European Broadcasting Union (EBU) since 1982 until present. He has chaired several EBU project groups and co-chaired/chaired the EBU Production Technology Management Committee (PMC) for 16 years. He is currently Chair of the EBU FTV (Future TeleVision)-LED project and of the EBU Expert Community for Video (EC-V).

John Emmett joined the engineering department of Thames Television in London after gaining a Ph.D. at Durham University, and starting the U.K. audio equipment manufacturers EMO Systems Ltd. While at Thames Television, he worked on subjects as diverse as film archive formats and psychoacoustics, and gained six international patents as sole inventor, and jointly with Lee Lighting, a Technical Oscar for developing the flicker-free Lighting Ballast. — Emmett continued as R&D manager at Pearson Television, and is currently technical director and chief executive of Broadcast Project Research, an independent studio-based research group. Originally representing the U.K. as principal digital audio expert to the IEC, he is well-known for his work on digital audio and video standards. Until recently, he chaired the EBU digital audio advisory group P/AGA, which was responsible for the Broadcast Wave Format.

Alan Roberts joined the BBC's R&D department in 1968 as a research engineer and worked on a wide variety of projects, including standards conversion, teletext, digital video processing, and surface-wave device fabrication, before specializing in color science and production technology. — Roberts was part of the team that worked on the Eureka95 HDTV project and represented the BBC on EBU and Eureka committees as a color scientist. From this HDTV work in the 1980s and 90s he developed the “film-look” favored by drama and wildlife programmakers, devising ways to use the new technology to lower production costs without compromising quality. — Now retired, he continues as a consultant on color science and HDTV matters, advising manufacturers and programmakers on HDTV developments.
