Joel Barsotti is director of software development at SpectraCal, Inc. As a veteran of the software industry, Barsotti spent the first several years working at a graphic design studio managing color critical work stations. He then began writing his own software to calibrate PCs and home theater computers, and was then hired away to SpectraCal. In his current position, he has presided over the development of one of the most sophisticated color management packages available. The research he has done developing this engine makes him uniquely suited to discussing color matching functions and their role in video calibration.

Derek Smith wrote CalMAN video calibration software when he found there was no available software that would properly calibrate his own home theater, and then went on to found SpectraCal when he realized others might be interested. In the previous quarter century he developed an extremely wide variety of software for nearly every kind of device you can connect to a computer, from the most rudimentary UART to peak performing race cars. An extreme skier and Tae Kwon Do instructor, he brings an intense passion for excellence to everything he undertakes, and for several years, his primary focus has been the practical application of color science to ensuring image fidelity in a broad range of industries, from medical imaging to post-production.

L.A. Heberlein is the president of SpectraCal, Inc., leading provider of video calibration software to home theater, commercial A/V, medical imaging, broadcast, video production, and post-production. Presented at the SMPTE 2012 Annual Technical Conference and Exhibition, Hollywood, CA, 23–25 October 2012. Copyright © 2013 by SMPTE. has led teams of software developers for more than 30 years, repeatedly undertaking first forays into new areas of expansion for computer science. These have included implementation of the first commercial operating system on RISC and the first multi-user services for Microsoft operating systems.

Yasuharu Iwaki received an MME degree in electronics and information engineering form Nagaoka University of Technology in 1993. From 1993 he is working for Fujifilm Corp. His work has focused on the development of color management technology for digital photographic printer and digital motion picture devices.

Mitsuhiro Uchida has been working on the research and development of color photographic film at Fujifilm since graduating from Tokyo Institute of Technology. He has expanded his target to film camera, digital photo printer, and digital cameras. He joined the AMPAS IIF committee in 2009 and has been actively contributing to IIF-ACES activity, attending IIF meetings in Hollywood every two months from Japan. Uchida has also contributed a wide spectrum of ACES, especially RRT development. Currently, he is contributing to the logACES standard and marketing Fujifilm's new CCBOXX.

Benjamin Bross is a project manager at the Image Processing department of the Fraunhofer Institute for Telecommunications - Heinrich Hertz Institute, Berlin. He received a Dipl.-Ing. degree in electrical engineering from RWTH University Aachen, Germany, in 2008. During his studies he worked on three-dimensional image registration in medical imaging and on decoder side motion vector derivation in H.264/MPEG-4-AVC. His research interests include motion estimation/prediction, residual coding, and fast encoding techniques. — Since the development of the new High-Efficiency Video Coding (HEVC) standard, H.265/PEG-HEVC, Bross started in 2010, he has been very active in the standardization process as a technical contributor and coordinator of core experiments. In July 2012, he was appointed as co-chair of the editing ad hoc group and became the chief editor of the H.265/MPEG-HEVC video coding standard. At the Heinrich Hertz Institute, he is currently responsible for the development of H.265 / MPEGHEVC conform realtime encoders and decoders.

Heiko Schwarz received a Dipl.-Ing. degree in electrical engineering and a Dr.-Ing. degree, both from the University of Rostock, Rostock, Germany, in 1996 and 2000, respectively. — In 1999, he joined the Image and Video Coding Group, Fraunhofer Institute for Telecommunications–Heinrich Hertz Institute, Berlin, Germany. Since then, he has contributed successfully to the standardization activities of the ITU-T Video Coding Experts Group (ITU-T SG16/Q.6-VCEG) and the ISO/IEC Moving Pictures Experts Group (ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 29/WG 11-MPEG). During the development of the scalable video coding extension of H.264/MPEG-4 AVC, he co-chaired several ad hoc groups of the Joint Video Team of ITU-T VCEG and ISO/IEC MPEG investigating particular aspects of the scalable video coding design. He has been appointed as a co-editor of ITU-T Rec. H.264 and ISO/IEC 14496-10 and as a software coordinator for the SVC reference software.

Detlev Marpe received a Dipl.-Math. degree (with highest honors) from the Berlin University of Technology (TUB), Germany, and a Dr.-Ing. degree in computer science from University of Rostock, Germany. Since 2010, he has been head of the Image & Video Coding Group in the Image Processing Department of Fraunhofer Heinrich Hertz Institute (HHI), Berlin. For more than a decade, he has been an active contributor to the standardization activities of ITU-T VCEG, ISO/IEC JPEG, and ISO/IEC MPEG for still image and video coding. — For his substantial contributions to the field of video coding, Marpe was nominated for the 2012 German Future Prize and received the Karl Heinz Beckurts Award 2011. As a key contributor and co-editor of the H.264|MPEG-4 AVC standard, he was co-recipient of two Emmy Engineering Awards in 2008 and 2009. Marpe is author or co-author of more than 200 publications in the area of video coding and signal processing, and he holds numerous internationally issued patents and patent applications in this field. He is an IEEE senior member and member of the German Information Technology Society.

Sean McCarthy, Ph.D., fellow of the technical staff at Motorolo Mobility, brings a unique convergence of expertise in video compression, signal processing and the neurobiology of human vision to content distribution at Motorola. McCarthy's duties include leading advancements in state-of-the-art of video processing, compression, and practical vision science. He held similar responsibilities previously as chief scientist at both Modulus Video, which is now part of Motorola, as well as at ViaSense, a University of California (UC) Berkeley spin-off that developed commercial applications, based on expert knowledge of the human visual system. The author of several papers on retinal processing, McCarthy holds a number of patents on image and signal processing, and has served on the board and committees of several industry organizations. He earned a B.S. in physics from Rensselaer Polytechnic, and a Ph.D. in bioengineering jointly at UC Berkeley and UC San Francisco.

Jérôme Viéron received a Ph.D. degree in computer science from Rennes 1 University in 1999. He joined Thomson R&D France as research engineer working on advanced video coding. He is an active contributor to standardization efforts led by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and the International Telecommunucations Union-Standardization (ITU-T) groups. He was very active in the H264/MPEG-4 SVC standardization process. In 2007, he joined the Video Processing and Perception Lab of Technicolor R&I as senior scientist exploring new technologies for future video coding applications and standards. He joined ATEME in 2011, as advanced research manager. Viéron is in charge of French and European collaborative R&D projects and works on next generation video coding technologies. He is an active contributor to the standardization process of high efficiency video coding (HEVC) and is implied in the 4EVER (for Enhanced Video ExpeRience) consortium, which aims at researching, developing, and promoting an enhanced Television Experience, using HEVC as well as ultra-HD.

Matthieu Parmentier started his audio career recording classical music CDs. He joined France Télévisions in 1999 as a sound engineer for live programs. From 2003 to 2007, as a news reporter, he was in charge of sound recording, video editing, and outdoor satellite transmissions. Since 2008, he has been working as manager for multichannel audio and HD video development projects, also organizing conferences and professional workshops. Parmentier co-chairs the audio expert community of the European Broadcasting Union. He holds two license degrees in sound recording and video postproduction and a master's degree in audiovisual research (Toulouse University).

Scott Miller is a senior member of the technical staff at Dolby Laboratories where he serves in the Image Technology Research group. He received a B.S. in electrical engineering from Cornell University and has spent nearly 30 years working in the video industry. He started in post-production and systems design before joining Panasonic Research where he turned his attention to hardware and algorithm design for several broadcast and consumer devices. He moved to Dolby in 2005 where he continues to specialize in image display technology and video signal processing. Along the way, he has had the privilege of helping to develop two Emmy award winning products: Panasonic's Universal Video Format Converter and Dolby's Professional Reference Monitor

Mahdi Nezamabadi received a Ph. D. in Imaging Science from the Rochester Institute of Technology in 2008. He was a member of the Spectral Imaging Group of the Munsell Color Science Laboratory and worked on design and implementation of an accurate end-to-end spectral color reproduction system. He also studied the effect of image size on the color appearance of image reproductions. Dr. Nezamabadi joined Dolby Laboratories in 2007. Presently, he is investigating image quality and color management of HDR video. His interests are appearance of softcopy color reproduction, video color processing, image quality, and phenomena such as adaptation and metamerism.

Scott Daly received a B.S. EE degree in 1980 from North Carolina State University, and then worked with early highresolution laser scanning systems at Photo Electronics Corp. in West Palm Beach, FL. Shifting from hardware to wetware, he obtained an M.S. in bioengineering from the University of Utah in 1984, completing a neurophysiology thesis on the temporal processing of cone photoreceptors. Daly then worked in the Imaging Science Division at Eastman Kodak in the fields of image compression, image fidelity models, and image watermarking. Next, he worked at Sharp Laboratories of America in Washington State, where he led a group on display algorithms. — Becoming a research fellow, Daly applied visual models towards digital video and displays, with publications on spatiotemporal and motion imagery, human interaction with wall-sized displays, and stereoscopic displays. These topics led him to join Dolby Laboratories in 2010 to focus on overall fundamental perceptual issues, and efforts to preserve artistic intent throughout the entire video path to reach the viewer. Daly received an Otto Schade Award from SID in 2011 for Applied Perception and a team Emmy Award in ′89-90 for a Video Transceiver as used in a prominent news event. He is currently a member of IEEE, SPIE, and SID.

Karl Paulsen is a SMPTE fellow and the chief technology officer at Diversified Systems. Paulsen is a member of SMPTE's standards development community and a regular industry contributor in his ongoing monthly column on media servers and storage technologies in the TV Technology magazine. He is the author of two books on the subject of video servers and storage systems; the latest is Moving Media Storage Technologies: Applications and Workflows for Video and Media Server Platforms (Focal Press, 2011).

Steve Knee embarked on a degree in music, acoustics and recording at the University of Salford, however, he soon got blinded by the bright lights of TV. Starting as a “multimedia operator” at the MEN Arena for Ice Hockey and Basketball shows, Knee quickly worked his way round the three-camera crew, learning all the main aspects of broadcast production. — After receiving an M.A. degree in creative technology, Knee became a lecturer in music technology at the University of Derby, during which time co-founded the company Cloudbass. While at the University of Derby Knee also founded the degree in multimedia technology and music production, which has since proved its worth with several graduates joining Cloudbass as employees. — Since leaving academia, Knee specializes in editing, EVS/VT and sound in the outside broadcast environment, while guiding Cloudbass to new and heady heights.

Chin Chye Koh holds Ph.D. and M.Sc. degrees in electrical engineering from the University of California, Santa Barbara and a B.Sc. degree in electrical engineering from Washington State University. Koh has held post-graduate positions at Intel Corp. in Arizona and Philips Research in The Netherlands. He is currently a product manager at Nevion USA, where he works on the development of professional broadcast video transport solutions. His current interests include video quality metrics, video compression, and broadcast video transport infrastructure.

John Hudson is director of product definition and broadcast technology in the Gennum Products Group (GPG) of Semtech Corp. His responsibilities include technology strategy, product definition and international standardization for Semtech GPG's video and datacom business. — Hudson has spent 28 years in the broadcast industry beginning his career as a design engineer at Sony Broadcast and Professional Europe. He joined Gennum in 1999 and has been instrumental in developing the company's video and multimedia semiconductor business. — As an active member of SMPTE and a SMPTE Fellow, Hudson serves as Co-chair of TC 10E - Essence, and Chair of the 32NF40 Working Group on SDI Mapping. He is the author of several SMPTE standards and actively contributes to the development of realtime streaming media interfaces for video and D-Cinema production. — Hudson is involved in the formation and development of the HDcctv Alliance. As chair of the technology committee, his responsibilities include the development of all standards and compliance testing programs. He attained a (Higher National Diploma) HND in electronics and communications engineering from the Farnborough College of Technology (U.K.) in 1988. He is the author of ten patents on video processing and signal integrity solutions for multimedia applications and regularly contributes technical papers and presentations to seminars and technology events in both broadcast and CCtv industries.

Alan Smith is product manager for routing at Snell. He has held this position at Snell, and prior to that Pro-Bel, for six years. Before moving into product management, Smith was engineering manager at Pro-Bel, responsible for all routing, control, and modular hardware, and later for control system software development. He has 25 years experience in the broadcast industry in engineering and product management roles.

Kim Francis is product manager for router control systems at Snell. Previous employment includes 20 years with Vistek Electronics Limited (UK), where he was commercial director before the takeover by Pro-Bel (UK) and the subsequent merger with Snell and Wilcox. Francis received a BSC Hons degree in physics. He is a chartered Engineer (C.Eng) and a member of Institute for Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE).

Tom Ohanian is a member of the Digital Media Strategy team at Cisco Systems. He was on the founding team at Avid Technology and is the co-inventor of the Avid Media Composer, film composer, and multicamera systems. He has extensive broadcast engineering, production, and post-production experience and is an Academy Award and two-time Emmy recipient for scientific and technical invention.

David Cardinal is a professional photographer and technologist with a decade of experience as a digital travel and nature photographer and over two decades working in high tech, including many years in software development and management at Sun Microsystems and Amdahl, and the cofounding of FirstFloor Software, later part of Calico Commerce. He cowrote one of the first image management solutions for digital photographers—DigitalPro for Windows. His articles have appeared in dozens of magazines, including many in PC Magazine, Photoshop User, Dr. Dobbs, and Outdoor Photographer.

Paul Gardiner is standards manager at Sony Broadcast & Professional Research Labs, at Sony Europe Ltd., based in Basingstoke, U.K. He studied electronic engineering at the University of Southampton before joining the Independent Broadcasting Authority (IBA) in 1974. His career has included a variety of roles related to the introduction of the UHF color television networks in the U.K. He has been involved in television technical regulation, and in R&D project management with responsibility for several international collaborative research projects. Gardiner has been an active SMPTE member since joining Sony in 2007. He is also a regular participant in the work of ITU R and is chair of the AMWA-EBU FIMS Technical Board.

John Hudson is director of broadcast technology at Semtech Corp. in Burlington Canada. He began his career in the broadcast industry in 1984 when he joined the Design and Development group of Sony Broadcast and Professional Europe as a technician engineer. During his career, he has worked as a design engineer, project leader, system architect, program manager, product-definition engineer, and technology strategist. — Hudson is active in television standards work. He is co-chair of TC10E and chairs the 32NF20 Electrical Interfaces Working Group in SMPTE. He also chairs the Technical Committee of the HDcctv Alliance, which is responsible for the development of standards for the HDcctv Industry.

Dave Schnuelle represents Dolby Laboratories as senior director, image technology, and provides guidance in Dolby's efforts in the television, cinema, and consumer imaging areas. He began his career as an engineer in television outside broadcasts while attending Purdue University. Schnuelle later held positions as chief engineer at various post-production facilities such as Editel and Modern VideoFilm in Los Angeles. Schnuelle worked with Lucasfilm's THX Division, beginning in 1991, where he was responsible for founding the THX Digital Mastering Program for quality-assurance of home video masters and duplicated software. As director of technology for THX, he directed research efforts into new technology for cinemas. During that period, he directly supervised the international digital cinema exhibition of the new Star Wars movies—Episode 1 1999 and Episode 2 2002. — Schnuelle holds four patents on imaging and audio technology and has been deeply involved with film and television standards activities for 30 years. Schnuelle is a SMPTE Fellow and a member of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences.

John Hurst is co-founder and chief technology officer at CineCert, LLC, an internationally recognized developer of digital cinema technology, where he is currently engaged in the development of the D-Cinema Comprehensive Test Plan for Digital Cinema Initiatives (DCI). Hurst has been an active participant in the SMPTE Digital Cinema technology committee and has served as editor of several of the standards published by that committee. He has more than 25 years of experience in sound recording and post-production, including the design and construction of well-known recording studios and post-production sound facilities in the Los Angeles area. He has technical responsibilities for many location recordings and live-to-air broadcasts. Hurst is a member of the Audio Engineering Society and is an active radio amateur and community volunteer.

Ann Marie Rohaly is director of accessibility policy and standards for Microsoft's Corporate Accessibility Group. Before joining Microsoft in 2003, she spent five years at Tektronix, Inc., in several senior positions, including strategic technology manager for the Video Product Line. Rohaly has been an active participant in the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), leading the standardization of Tektronix's Emmy award-winning PQA300 picture-quality measurement technology, and in many other international standards-setting organizations and industry consortia. She played a lead role in the standardization of VC-1 as SMPTE ST 421 and more recently, in the standardization of SMPTE Timed Text (ST 2052). In 2010, she was appointed to the U.S. Federal Communications Commission's Video Programming Accessibility Advisory Committee, which issued a report on closed captioning for Internet-delivered video. Rohaly is a SMPTE Fellow and served on the Board of Governors 2009-2013.

Brian Vessa is a dedicated audio professional with more than 35 years of experience in the industry. After attending UCLA Engineering School he became a recording engineer, producing albums and recording orchestras. His passion was hotrodding studio gear and discovering novel recording techniques. Vessa transitioned into film post as a music editor and sound editor, became a re-recording mixer at Cannon Films and MGM, then handled audio restoration at NT Audio. He was hired by Sony Pictures in 1998, where he is currently executive director of digital audio mastering and representative to Digital Cinema Initiatives (DCI). — Vessa is a member of the Academy Sound Branch, SMPTE and the Audio Engineering Society (AES). He chairs the TC-25CSS committee, as well as D-Cinema and IMF sub-committees. He has written many audio specifications, including a white paper on near-field mixing for home theater that has been widely adopted. Vessa enjoys recording jazz, rock and mixing live sound.

Phil Tudor is a principal engineer at BBC Research & Development, London, U.K. He studied electrical and information sciences at Cambridge University. Tudor's technical background includes software engineering, video compression algorithm development, MPEG standardization, metadata interoperability and the development of AAF and MXF standard file formats for use in tapeless production. Tudor is responsible for R&D projects in the areas of production tools, formats, workflow, media management and wide area production. He is a board member of the Advanced Media Workflow Association. Tudor is a SMPTE fellow, a Chartered Engineer and a member of the IET.

Paul Treleaven obtained a First Class Honours degree in electrical engineering from Imperial College, London in 1972. He started his career in broadcast engineering with BBC Designs Department. His work included design of the interpolation system for the BBC's ‘ACE’ four-field standards converter. In 1979, Treleaven co-founded Avitel, a company designing and manufacturing video, audio and timecode distribution and processing equipment. He continued with Avitel as technical director until 2001. — Treleaven is a member of the International Association of Broadcasting Manufacturers' (IABMs) Technical Task Group, representing the IABM at SMPTE and AES standards meetings and ABU technology committee meetings. He is also a member of the U.K.'s National Standards Body for IEC TC100. Treleaven has served as SMPTE International Region Governor and is a SMPTE Fellow.

Michael A. Dolan is founder and president of Television Broadcast Technology, providing specialized professional encoders, test tools, and technical consulting in the field of digital television. He holds a BSEE degree from Virginia Polytechnic Institute and has worked for and founded various leadingedge computer graphics and realtime systems companies, including early foundational work in W3C technology and analog data broadcasting. Dolan has been involved in digital television engineering for the past eight years, including data broadcast system architecture and digital receiver design and compliance. He also currently chairs the Advanced Television Systems Committee (ATSC) Data Broadcasting Specialist Group (TSG/ S13) and is active in the Consumer Electronics Association (CEA) and the Society of Cable Telecommunications Engineers (SCTE). A SMPTE Fellow, Dolan authors the SMPTE Journal Almanac column and holds several patents in computer Web technology.

Pierre-Anthony Lemieux is a Partner at Sandflow Consulting, where he works with both Hollywood and Silicon Valley clients on worldwide standards, proof-of-concept development, and product architecture. His expertise covers the entertainment technology ecosystem, from content authoring to playback, including audio and video and timed text, file formats, and content protection. His recent engagements include representing clients at industry forums (including SMPTE and W3C,) developing standards for file-based post-production workflows, and implementing audio processing algorithms. Lemieux is a SMPTE Fellow and currently serves as document editor on multiple SMPTE projects, in addition to chairing TC-31FS. He has a Ph.D. in physics from the University of Southern California, Los Angeles, and a B.Sc. degree from McGill University.

Alan Lambshead retired in 2013 from a career with Evertz Microsystems Ltd. in Burlington, Ontario, Canada, which spanned more than 33 years. In his most recent role as vice president, engineering, his responsibilities included the general oversight of R&D and product development, focusing on time code and post-production products. During most of his 33 years at Evertz, Lambshead has served actively on SMPTE technology committees and is the author of several SMPTE recommended practices. He is a SMPTE Fellow and member of the Toronto Section. Lambshead is a widely recognized expert in the field of HDTV time code and sync issues, HDTV production, HDTV metadata and has presented papers at local Sections and national SMPTE conferences. He graduated from McMaster University, Hamilton, Ontario, with a B. Eng in electrical engineering in 1972 and became licensed as a Professional Engineer (P. Eng.) in Ontario in 1988. Lambshead became a SMPTE Fellow in 2009.

John F. Snow represents Xilinx, Inc., where he is a senior staff design engineer in the Digital Video Processing group focused on developing field programmable gate array (FPGA) cores that implement SMPTE interface standards. Prior to joining Xilinx in 2001, he was director of engineering at Evans & Sutherland where he was involved in realtime computer graphics for flight simulation for 20 years. — Snow is active in SMPTE standards work. In addition to chairing the TC-32NF, he co-chairs the 33TS.20 Working Group on Synchronization. He is also a senior member of the IEEE.

John Fletcher is a lead technologist at BBC Research & Development, London, U.K. He studied natural and electrical sciences at Cambridge University before joining the BBC in 1986. He has worked in a variety of fields including acoustics, video coding and subtitling. His main interest in recent years has been the application of information technology to the TV production process, with projects such as the Ingex tapeless recording system. Fletcher is a Chartered Engineer and member of the Institution of Engineering and Technology.

Bob Edge has worked as an engineer, architect, project leader, and program manager on several products and research projects. Some of his early projects include desktop computing products, peripherals, and high-performance graphics devices. He participated in research projects that used data networks to transport realtime audio/video streams. He also worked on Grass Valley products. — Edge has been active in television standards work for more than 15 years, including participation in SMPTE, some European Broadcasters Union projects, Video Services Forum, Advanced Media Workflow Association and other organizations. He has served as SMPTE Engineering Director and as a technology committee chair and is a Life Fellow in the Society. Edge has contributed to the development of more than a dozen SMPTE standards and RDDs. — Edge is the author of many technical papers describing the application of IT and data networking for television production. He has a bachelor's degree in computer science from Oregon State University. — In 2009, Grass Valley received a Technical Emmy for GXF as the first professional audio/video file format. Edge was one of the contributors to the development and standardization of GXF and MXF. In 2012, Edge received the Excellence in Standards award from SMPTE. — In 2011, Edge retired from Grass Valley and he is now consulting on standards projects representing vendors and end-users. This work includes writing standards, managing projects, and providing technical expertise to engineers and managers.

John Footen is an acknowledged industry expert in such areas as business process management, service-oriented architecture, and the Cloud, all of which have a major impact on today's broadcast television and professional media systems. As head of Cognizant's broadcast consulting practice, Footen is responsible for business and technology consulting throughout the broadcast industry. Footen is a sought-after speaker and expert writer on software architecture and workflow issues. He is an active founding member of the Framework for Interoperable Media Services (FIMS) joint taskforce of the Advanced Media Workflow Association (AMWA) and European Broadcasting Union (EBU). He has been responsible for managing many large and complex media solutions projects for many types of media enterprises and has extensive international experience; having lived and worked in North America, Asia, and EMEA. Footen holds degrees in computer science and film and television from New York University. He is also the co-author of “The Service-Oriented Media Enterprise: SOA, BPM, and Web Services in Professional Media Systems,” published by Focal Press.

Chris Simons spent the early part of his career working for U.K. terrestrial and satellite broadcasters then joined Drake Automation Ltd. in 1996. As head of customer support, he established a global support infrastructure delivering major automation projects including BSkyB, DirecTV, Network Ten, SkyPerfecTV, Dish Network, etc. Following the acquisition of Encoda Systems by Harris in 2005 Simons managed the Automation Services organization covering both ADC and D-Series globally. — After a working at Miranda Technologies in 2006, Simons returned to Harris and heads the Automation and Asset Management Product Group, responsible for the ADC, D-Series and Invenio product suite.

Howard Lukk is vice president, production systems at The Walt Disney Studios, where he is responsible for helping to incorporate new technologies into the workflow of the studio. Prior to that, he was director of technology for DCI where he was responsible for researching and documenting Digital Cinema Specifications. Before that he was chief engineer at IVC a post-production facility in Burbank, CA. He has also worked as a freelance engineer on HDTV productions such as Woodstock 25th Anniversary and Major League Baseball. Lukk has been an active member of SMPTE since 1995 and is also an associate member of the ASC.

Thomas Bause Mason is a director for advanced digital media technology in the Advanced Engineering department at NBCUniversal. As part of the NBCUniversal Advanced Technology Team, he helps to research and implement emerging technologies as well as standards for file-based workflows in production, post-production and distribution including traditional broadcast, cable, and the Web. His responsibilities also include UHDTV and Closed Captioning for the Web. He works with many different NBCUniversal operational teams to implement standards and technology on a corporate level. — In the past, Mason worked at Ascent Media where he ran the encoding as well as the DAM system ingest operations and helped business development to implementing new media workflows. Before that he worked in Germany as a programmer for process visualization software and as a developer of database solutions. Additionally, he managed a quality control department for several private broadcast networks at a large broadcast service provider. Mason has a bachelor's degree in media technology and has been a SMPTE member since 2007. He is an associate member of AMWA representing NBCUniversal and a W3C member representing Comcast.

title: Report from the Science and Technology Council of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences
label: SMPTE Motion Imaging Journal ( Volume: 122, Issue: 6, 2013)
keywordsSearch: Report from the Science and Technology Council of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences
SMPTE Motion Imaging Journal ( Volume: 122, Issue: 6, 2013)

Bill Kroyer, Chair, Science and Technology Council, was trained in classic hand-drawn animation at the Walt Disney Studios, but he also was one of the first to explore digital approaches as a computer image choreographer on Tron 1982. In 1988 he received an Academy Award® nomination for his short film Technological Threat, which pioneered the technique of combining hand-drawn and computer animation. Kroyer has since directed the feature Ferngully: The Last Rainforest 1992 and contributed to such films as The Flinstones in Viva Rock Vegas 2000, Cats & Dogs 2001, Scooby-Doo 2002 and Garfield 2004. Kroyer currently serves as a governor of the Academy (Visual Effects branch) and is the director of digital arts at the Dodge College of Film and Media Arts at Chapman University.

George Joblove, Co-Chair, Science and Technology Council, is a digital media technology executive and consultant who throughout his career has played key and pioneering roles in the development and application of digital technology to the entertainment industry. He served for three years as executive vice president of Advanced Technology at Sony Pictures Entertainment, where his focuses included facilitating the application of digital asset management, 4K, and 3D across production, post-production, and distribution. Previously he was at Sony Pictures' visual-effects and animation unit, Imageworks, for ten years, where he served as chief technology officer. Prior affiliations include Industrial Light & Magic (where he co-founded and led the team that pioneered the use of computers to create visual effects for feature films, including such milestones as The Abyss, Terminator 2, and Jurassic Park) and the visual-effects unit of Warner Bros. — Joblove received a Scientific and Engineering Academy Award in 1994 and is a member of SMPTE, the Visual Effects Society, and an associate member of the American Society of Cinematographers. He holds a B.S. in computer science, and an M.S. in computer graphics, both from Cornell University.

Peter Anderson, Chair, Technology History Subcommittee, was the director of photography and visual effects supervisor on U2 3D, the first live-action feature film recorded in digital 3D. After a career in advertising, he joined Douglas Trumbull's Future General visual effects company during the making of Close Encounters of The Third Kind 1977. Anderson went on to create Universal Studios' Hartland visual effects facility, which was used for Buck Rogers in the 25th Century 1979 as well as numerous other Universal productions. In 1981 he joined Disney Studios to film and supervise the visual effects for features such as Tron 1982 and Something Wicked This Way Comes 1983. It was for Disney's Epcot that Anderson developed the modern 3D systems and technologies for filming Magic Journeys 1982, Captain EO 1986 and Muppet*Vision 1991. Since leaving Disney, Anderson has continued to film and supervise many three-dimensional productions including the 3D IMAX releases of Cirque Du Soleil: Journey of Man 1999, Ultimate G's: Zac's Flying Dream 2000 and Wild Oceans 2008. Anderson also serves on the Academy's Visual Effects Branch Executive Committee and the Scientific and Technical Awards Committee.

Lisa Zeno Churgin, Chair, Public Programs and Education Subcommittee, graduated from Oberlin College with a B.A. in english before moving to New York to pursue a career in film editing. She has since served as editor on dozens of films including Reality Bites 1994, Dead Man Walking 1995, Unstrung Heroes 1995, Gattaca 1997, The Wedding Planner 2001, Moonlight Mile 2002, House of Sand and Fog 2003, In Her Shoes 2005, The Last Kiss 2006, The Ugly Truth 2009, Priest 2011 and Pitch Perfect 2012. Churgin received an Oscar nomination for The Cider House Rules 1999, and along with her many feature credits, she has edited such television productions as Tim Robbins' “Embedded” and episodes of Tom Hanks' HBO miniseries “From the Earth to the Moon.”

Ray Feeney has worked to provide leading-edge scientific and engineering solutions to the film industry since the mid 1970s. The new technologies offered by Feeney and RFX, Inc., the company he founded in 1978, have served as the catalysts to produce ground-breaking visual effects for both feature films and television. — In conjunction with leading filmmakers and software engineers, Feeney also founded Silicon Grail, a company that develops digital compositing software to more efficiently create visual effects for feature films. — No stranger to Academy recognition, Feeney has won four Scientific and Engineering Awards from the Academy during his illustrious career: in 1988, for developing one of the first motion control camera systems; in 1991, for his work on the Solitaire Film Recorder; and in 1994, honoring his development of film input scanners and the Cinefusion bluescreen extraction technology. In 2001, Feeney was awarded the John A. Bonner Medal of Commendation 2001 for his pioneering efforts to improve visual effects in the motion picture industry, and the Gordon E. Sawyer Oscar in 2007. Feeney also served as chair for the Science and Technology Council from its inception in 2003 until 2011.

Andy Maltz, Director, Science and Technology Council. The Academy reconstituted its Science and Technology Council in 2003, and as its first director, Maltz is responsible for developing and implementing its operational plan, administering the Council's day-to-day operations and individual contributions to selected Council initiatives. Previous to the Academy, Maltz was CEO of Avica Technology Corp., where he led the first worldwide commercial deployment of digital cinema servers, drove the development of key technologies for digital cinema, and was heavily involved with the digital releases of many major motion pictures in the U.S., Europe, and Asia. Previous to Avica, Maltz served as a consultant to companies such as Sharp Electronics and Microsoft, where he spearheaded the development of the Advanced Authoring Format. Prior to these assignments, he was executive vice president of operations and engineering for nonlinear editing pioneer Ediflex Digital Systems. — Maltz serves on the U.S. National Archives Public Advisory Committee for Electronic Records Archives, is an associate member of the American Society of Cinematographers, and is a fellow of SMPTE where he serves on several engineering committees and the SMPTE Journal Board of Editors. Maltz received a BSEE from the State University of New York at Buffalo.

title: Report from the American Society of Cinematographers Technology Committee
label: SMPTE Motion Imaging Journal ( Volume: 122, Issue: 6, 2013)
keywordsSearch: Report from the American Society of Cinematographers Technology Committee
SMPTE Motion Imaging Journal ( Volume: 122, Issue: 6, 2013)

Curtis Clark, ASC, studied theater at the Art Institute of Chicago's Goodman School of Drama and cinematography at the London Film School. He began his career by shooting numerous documentary films in Britain before transitioning to shooting feature films. — Following on the success of his short film, The Arrival, Clark recently completed his highly praised short film Eldorado. — A member of the ASC Board of Governors, Clark is chairman of the ASC Technology Committee. Since its inception in 2003, the Committee under Clark's leadership has achieved a series of notable successes including its collaborative work with Digital Cinema Initiatives, LLC (DCI) to produce standardized evaluation material for assessing the performance of digital projectors and other elements of DCI standards-based digital cinema systems. — The ASC Technology Committee, at Clark's instigation, embarked on the development of a groundbreaking project to create cross platform data exchange for primary RGB digital color correction referred to as the ASC CDL (Color Decision List). The ASC CDL was recognized by the Academy of Television Arts and Sciences with a prestigious 2012 Prime Time Emmy Engineering Award.

David Reisner uses his industry-leading expertise in motion picture image quality, color, workflow, Digital Intermediate (DI), and digital imaging in production, post-production, and exhibition to defend creative flexibility and create best practices. — He was a principal in creating the ASC Color Decision List (ASC CDL), now used in the production of about 80% of feature motion pictures. Reisner was also a principal in creation/design of the ASC-PGA Camera Assessment Series, the ASC-DCI StEM (Standard Evaluation Material) test movie, and the ISDCF 3D luminance demonstration. He was vice-chair of the SMPTE working groups that drafted the key digital cinema image standards, and a member of the AMPAS ACES working groups. — Reisner is founding secretary of the ASC Technology Committee, an ASC associate member, and an active Member of the Visual Effects Society. — Reisner designed one of the first digital music synthesizers, the first VLIW CPU, the first popular portable video player, an early Internet music and movie distribution service, and co-designed the first lightweight portable computer. He has trained killer whales and shot magazine covers and book jackets.

David Stump, ASC, has worked on numerous motion pictures and television productions as director of photography, as visual effects director of photography, as visual effects supervisor, and as stereographer, (including both live action work and 2D to 3D conversion work), earning an Emmy Award, an Academy Award for Scientific and Technical Achievement and an International Cinematographers Guild Award. His credits include such high profile projects as The Last Stand, Immortals, Flight Plan, Fantastic Four, X-Men 1 & 2, Into the Blue, Red Riding Hood, Garfield, Batman Forever, Hollow Man, Men of Honor, Deep Blue Sea, Stuart Little, Contact, Batman & Robin, Mars Attacks, Executive Decision, Stargate, and Free Willy, among many others. — Stump currently serves on the AMPAS' Science and Technology Council. He also serves as co-chair of a SMPTE study group on High Frame Rate for Digital Cinema.

Ron Garcia, ASC, is a Life member of SMPTE and is the inventor of a Film Calibration system used to control color management in film-to-tape transfers and film recorders. Garcia is a member of the Academy of Television Arts and Science, the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, and a committee member of the Academy Sci-Tech Awards in 2008. He has been a member of the American Society of Cinematographers since 1994.

Lou Levinson received an MFA from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago in 1979, having worked his way through school as a tape operator and colorist. After graduating, he worked at Columbia Pictures Videocassette services, where he helped to maintain the first flying spot scanner installed in the midwest. In September 1980, he was hired as a colorist at Modern VideoFilm (MVF), becoming the 13th employee there. Thirteen years later, he left to join colorist the MCA/MEI Telecine Research Center as a colorist, working in what was the third HD telecine room in the world. From 1998 to 2008, Levinson worked as a senior colorist at Post Logic Studios. From 2008 to 2012, he was a supervising colorist at Kodak-Laser Pacific/HIG/Technicolor. He is currently a consultant and free-lance colorist. A longtime ASC Associate Member, he has been on the ASC Technology Committee since its inception and is currently chair of the Digital Intermediate/Finishing subcommittee.

Al Barton has spent 29 years as a technologist in production, post-production, and manufacturing for television and feature films. Most recently he worked in production/post-production and distribution of feature films for Sony Pictures. Barton has participated in the International Organization for Standardization (ISO), the International Telcommunications Union(ITU), and Inter-Society Digital Cinema Forum (ISDCF) committees. He chairs the Workflow subcommittee of the ASC Technology Committee. Barton also participates in the AMPAS committees. He was a key member of DCI and helped create the digital cinema specification.

Ron Burdett is an experienced business and technology management executive in the entertainment industry. He received a BS degree in mechanical engineering from Bradley University. Burdett is founder and president of Sunset Digital and has worked as general manager at Technicolor and Eastman Kodak Co. He is currently a member of the ASC Technology Committee, as well as co-chair of the ASC Motion Imaging Workflow subcommittee.

William Feightner graduated from California State University Fresno with B.A. degree and proceeded onto law school. After one year as a law student he was offered a summer job at Compact Video in Burbank. That part-time job led to his career in the entertainment industry. He received a technical achievement award from the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences for the creation of a Digital Color Separation process for archival of motion pictures. Feightner has received an Emmy Award for special effects work on the television series “Moonlighting,” a Technical Achievement Award from the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences and a Monitor Award for the opening segment of “The Magical World of Disney.

Gary Demos has been a pioneer in the development of computer-generated images for use in motion pictures, and in digital film scanning and recording. He founded Digital Productions (1982- 1986), and was awarded an AMPAS Scientific and Engineering Award in 1984 along with John Whitney Jr. “For the Practical Simulation of Motion Picture Photograph By Means of Computer-Generated Images.” Demos also founded Whitney-Demos Productions (1986-1988), DemoGraFX (1988-2003), and Image Essence LLC (in 2005). — Demos is the recipient of the AMPAS 2005 Gordon E. Sawyer Oscar for lifetime technical achievement. Since 1990, he has been exploring layered compression coding and is active in preparing for future imaging and image processing technology. Demos is involved in the ASC Technology Committee and the AMPAS ACES project. He has presented numerous papers at SMPTE, and is a SMPTE Fellow.

Don Eklund currently works at Verance Corp. in San Diego as vice president of business development. Prior to that he held an executive position with Sony Pictures where he helped execute the launch of DVD, UMD, and Blu-ray.

Eric Rodli has been involved in the management and development of entertainment technology since the late 1980s when he became president of Iwerks Entertainment; a pioneer in large-format film, motion simulation theaters, and other immersive technologies. He subsequently has had senior roles in a variety of entertainment and media organizations, including being a partner in the entertainment consulting practice of PwC as well as president of Kodak's Motion Picture Division. He currently is a consultant for Laser Light Engines, a leader in providing laser illumination systems for cinema and related applications. He is an Associate Member of the ASC. Rodli received a B.A. in economics from University of California, San Diego, and an M.B.A. from the University of Chicago.

Garrett J. Smith is currently chief technology officer at Ha Productions, based in Santa Barbara, CA. He previously served as vice president, production technology and digital mastering operations at Paramount Pictures. During his 24-year tenure at Paramount, Smith participated in the development of DVD, HDTV, and Digital Cinema Initiatives (DCI). Prior to Paramount Pictures, he worked in various post-production positions including post-production supervisor for “Ripley's Believe It or Not;” director, post-production for Columbia Pictures Television; and manager, film services at CBS Network Television. Smith is a member of AMPAS and serves on the Science and Technology Council. He is also an Associate Member of the ASC and an adjunct associate professor at the University of Southern California School of Cinematic Arts.

John Scheele is a visual effects supervisor and producer, working in CG and animation for films and television. His work includes Blade Runner (2007 Final Cut), World Trade Center, Batman Forever, The Adventures of Buckaroo Banzai Across the 8th Dimension, and TRON 1982. Scheele is co-chair of the Joint Technology subcommittee on Virtual Production.

David Morin participated in the early development of motion capture and 3D software at Softimage, as director of special projects when Softimage was part of Microsoft, and vice-president of special projects and content group when Softimage became part of Avid Technology. Morin later joined Manex Entertainment as president of the MVFX division, a visual effects house. Today Morin assists the Media & Entertainment division of Autodesk from his base in Los Angeles. He currently chairs the Autodesk Film CTO Advisory Council, a product focus group of large studio facilities. He is also cochair of the Virtual Production Committee.

Pete Ludé is a prominent engineering leader in broadcast and digital media. He has been involved in designing and implementing hundreds of broadcast and media systems, including the launch of digital video for DirecTV, pioneering HDTV systems for network broadcast and recent 4K workflow systems for motion picture production. Most recently, Ludé was senior vice president of Sony's Silicon Valley R&D labs, where his work included workflow software for movie production, stereoscopic imaging, and the next-generation of 4K laser projectors for digital cinema. — is Past President of SMPTE, and a SMPTE Fellow. He is also co-founder and chairman of the Laser Illuminated Projector Association, and is a frequent speaker on the future of broadcast, Ultra HD television, stereoscopic 3D, and laser displays. His blog can be found at http://digidrivel.blogspot.com/.

Philip Laven is chairman of the DVB Project, acting on behalf of the European Broadcasting Union (EBU) where he was director of the Technical Department from May 1997 until August 2007. Before joining the EBU, he worked for the British Broadcasting Corp. (BBC) where most of his work was associated with research and development (R&D), including being chief engineer R&D with responsibility for all of the BBC's R&D activities. As controller of engineering policy from 1993 to 1997, he played a leading role in the development of the BBC's policy on many technical developments, such as the introduction of digital audio broadcasting and digital television. Between 1994 and 2009, he was chairman of the ETSI/EBU/CENELEC Joint Technical Committee (which is responsible for setting European standards for broadcasting systems). In April 2013, he was appointed Chairman of the FOBTV initiative.

Jerry C. Whitaker, vice president of standards development at ATSC, supports the work of the various ATSC technology committees and assists in the development of ATSC standards and related documents. He serves as secretary of the Technology and Standards Group and secretary of the Technology Group on ATSC 3.0 and is closely involved in work relating to educational programs. — Whitaker is a fellow of SMPTE. He has served as a board member and vice president of the Society of Broadcast Engineers. Whitaker is the author and editor of more than 30 books on technical topics, including The “Standard Handbook of Video and Television Engineering,” 4th edition; “NAB Engineering Handbook,” 9th edition; “DTV Handbook,” 3rd edition; and “The Electronics Handbook,” 2nd edition. Prior to joining ATSC, Whitaker headed the publishing company Technical Press based in Morgan Hill, CA. Whitaker was previously editor, editorial director, and associate publisher of Broadcast Engineering magazine and Video Systems magazine.

Tadaaki Yokoo has been the executive director of the Association of Radio Industries and Businesses (ARIB) since 2007. Before joining ARIB, he worked for NHK (Japan Broadcasting Corporation) for 33 years, where he was involved in various engineering strategy and development work, including HDTV and digital TV. He was stationed in London, U.K., from 1993 to 1996 as the executive vice president of NHK Enterprises Europe Limited.

Lynn Claudy is senior vice president of technology for the National Association of Broadcasters. He joined NAB in 1988, assuming his present position in 1995. He previously held technical positions in the communications systems integration and consumer electronics manufacturing businesses. He has a B.A. degree from Oberlin College, a BSEE from Washington University in St. Louis and an MSEE degree from the Illinois Institute of Technology. He is a member of IEEE, SMPTE, SBE and AES.

Thomas C. Russell is SCTE's senior director of standards. A technology professional for more than 30 years, Russell has wide-ranging experience in leading the development of telecommunications standards, consumer communications devices, and advanced broadband access equipment in both engineering and product management roles. He holds a B.S. degree in computer science from Syracuse University and an M.S.E.E from Capitol College. At SCTE, Russell oversees the standards development process, represents SCTE to the ITU's SG9, and chairs SG9's Focus Group on Smart Cable Television. In his more than nine years at SCTE, he has managed the development of more than 100 new and revised technical standards for the cable industry.

Brian Markwalter is senior vice president of research and standards for the Consumer Electronics Association (CEA). Markwalter is responsible for overseeing CEA's ANSI-accredited standards development operation and extensive market research capability. Under Markwalter's direction, CEA hosts more than 70 committees, subcommittees, and working groups that produce standards used in millions of consumer devices. CEA's market research has a rich 75-year history, producing objective research, tracking sales data and forecasting trends. These programs have resulted in three Technology Emmy awards for CEA standards and give CEA members free access to nearly $1 million in annual market research. Markwalter received a bachelor's degree and master's degree in electrical engineering from the Georgia Institute of Technology and is a licensed professional engineer.

Amal Ghosh is senior vice president of R&D at eMagin Corporation, NY. His professional career of more than 25 years includes his tenure at IBM T. J. Watson Research Laboratories and IBM Microelectronics Division and Eastman Kodak Company. He has been working in the flat panel display area for more than 20 years. In 2003 he received SID's Special Recognition Award for his work on OLEDs and FEDs. In 2009, he received the SID Fellow award for his work on OLED microdisplays and also the SID Mid-Atlantic Chapter award for leadership, dedication, and service to the chapter. Currently, he is the President-Elect of SID International. He obtained a Ph.D. in physics from Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

Pete Putman is the president of ROAM Consulting L.L.C. and provides training, marketing, and product testing/development services to manufacturers, dealers, and end-users of displays, display interfaces, and related connectivity products. — Putman is a contributing editor for Sound and Communications magazine, the leading trade publication for commercial AV systems integrators. He also edits and publishes HDTVexpert.com, a Web blog focused on HDTV, digital media, wireless, and display technologies. — Putman holds a Bachelor of Arts degree in communications from Seton Hall University, and a Master of Science degree in Television and Film from Syracuse University. He is an InfoComm Senior Academy Instructor for the International Communications Industries Association (ICIA), and was named ICIA's Educator of the Year for 2008. He is a member of both SMPTE and Society for Information Display (SID).

Al Kovalick has worked in the field of hybrid AV/IT systems for the past 20 years. Previously, he was a digital systems designer and technical strategist for Hewlett Packard. Following HP, from 1999 to 2004, he was the chief technical officer at Pinnacle Systems. For the next six years, he was a Corporate Fellow at Avid. In 2011, Kovalick founded Media Systems Consulting. — Kovalick is an active speaker, educator, author, and participant with industry bodies including SMPTE and the Advanced Media Workflow Association. He has presented more than 50 papers at industry conferences worldwide and holds 18 U.S. and foreign patents. He is the author of the book Video Systems in an IT Environment, 2nd edition. In 2009, Kovalick was awarded the David Sarnoff Medal from SMPTE. He has a BSEE degree from San Jose State University and MSEE degree from the University of California at Berkeley. He is a SMPTE fellow. Kovalick also writes the Cloudspotter's Journal for TV Technology magazine.

Brad Gilmer is president of Gilmer & Associates, Inc. He is also the executive director of the Advanced Media Workflow Association and the Executive Director of the Video Services Forum. Gilmer been a member and active participant in SMPTE since 1984. He was the first recipient of the SMPTE Workflow Systems Medal. — Gilmer was previously employed at Turner Broadcasting System in Atlanta where he and his staff were responsible for engineering and operations for the Entertainment Division. He is author of the monthly “Computer and Networks” column in Broadcast Engineering magazine, editor-in-chief of the “File Interchange Handbook” (Focal Press), and a contributor to the NAB Engineering Handbook.

Felix Poulin “has grown up” in studios and control rooms as his parents worked in TV production. His inherited interest in media production led him to a diploma in electrical engineering at the École Polytechnique de Montréal completed by a research project at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. After graduating, he began work as a wireless and digital audio expert on international productions, including Cirque du Soleil. Prior to the EBU, he has worked for national broadcaster CBC/Radio-Canada as engineer in production technology. Poulin is managing multidisciplinary work groups related to media networks and storage at the EBU Technology and Innovation in Switzerland.

Giorgio Dimino is head of the research unit on digital archives and television production at RAI Radiotelevisione Italiana, Research Centre of Turin. His interests include the application of information technology in the broadcast production chain, the design of modern media archives, and the evaluation of technical quality in video and audio signals. Dimino is co-chair of the Joint EBU-AMWA FIMS Task Force.

Neil Dunstan is the marketing and membership manager for the Advanced Media Workflow Association and has 30 years experience with both media companies and their major suppliers, including the BBC and Sony. With a background in strategic sales and marketing, he leads the industry communication, enthusiastically seeks new members and brings a customer perspective to AMWA activities.

Wes Simpson is president of Telecom Product Consulting, which he founded in 2000 to provide high-quality research, marketing, business development, training and product management services to companies wishing to capitalize on the expanding market for high performance video telecommunication products and services. Simpson is a frequent television industry speaker at events such as VidTrans, SMPTE, NAB, and IBC, and he is a regular columnist for TV Technology. Recently, Simpson has developed and delivered well-received training seminars for the VSF, the IEEE BTS, and SMPTE's Regional Seminars. He has written two books, which have both been released as second editions by Focal Press: “IPTV and Internet Video” in 2009 and “Video Over IP” in 2008. Simpson has more than 30 years of experience in the design, development, and marketing of products for video and telecommunication applications. He holds a BSEE from Clarkson University and an MBA from the University of Rochester.

Wes Simpson is president of Telecom Product Consulting, which he founded in 2000 to provide highquality research, marketing, business development, training and product management services to companies wishing to capitalize on the expanding market for high performance video telecommunication products and services. Simpson is a frequent television industry speaker at events such as VidTrans, SMPTE, NAB, and IBC, and he is a regular columnist for TV Technology. Recently, Simpson has developed and delivered well-received training seminars for the VSF, the IEEE BTS, and SMPTE's Regional Seminars. He has written two books, which have both been released as second editions by Focal Press: “IPTV and Internet Video” in 2009 and “Video Over IP” in 2008. Simpson has more than 30 years of experience in the design, development, and marketing of products for video and telecommunication applications. He holds a BSEE from Clarkson University and an MBA from the University of Rochester.

Steve Storozum has more than 30 years of experience in telecom and video products and services. He earned an A.B. in physics from Washington University, St. Louis; an M.S.E.E. from Carnegie Mellon University; and pursued a Ph. D. in electrical engineering at Virginia Tech. He is currently with Level 3 Communications where he supports the network engineering needs of clients in Media and Entertainment markets. Before Level 3, Storozum held senior marketing, business development, and engineering positions at telecom, datacom, and video equipment suppliers. He is a senior member of the IEEE and is former president and current board member of the Video Services Forum. Throughout his career, he has also contributed to development of television, networking, and digital cinema standards through SMPTE and IEEE. Storozum has presented numerous talks at industry conferences and has contributed articles on datacom, video, and optical communications to various publications and websites.

Spyridon V. Gogouvitis was born in Athens, Greece, in 1982. He received a Dipl. -Ing. from the School of Electrical and Computer Engineering of the National Technical University of Athens (NTUA) in 2006 and a Ph.D. from the Electrical and Computer Engineering Department of the National Technical University of Athens in 2013. He currently works as a Researcher in the Telecommunication Laboratory of the Institute of Communication and Computer Systems (ICCS). In the past, Gogouvitis was actively involved in several European Union (EU) and National funded projects such as the Interactive Realtime Multimedia Applications on Service Oriented Infrastructures (IRMOS) project. He has also worked as a developer for the Hellenic Army Information Systems Support Centre and as a consultant for the General Secretariat for Information Systems of the Hellenic Ministry of Economy and Finance. Currently, he is NTUA's team leader in the VISION Cloud EU Project. His research interests include grid and cloud computing, workflow management, as well as mobile and ubiquitous computing.

Michael C. Jaeger works at Siemens Corporate Technology as a research scientist, project manager, trainer, and consultant for distributed systems, storage technology and server applications with an emphasis on open source software. He is a certified software architect. He regularly provides training on design patterns for building software architectures. Jaeger has more than ten years experience in professional research and development. He also contributed to five EU-funded research efforts before the VISION Cloud project. Jaeger earned a university diploma degree in computer engineering and a Dr.-Ing. degree in computer science, both from TU Berlin in Germany.

Hillel Kolodner is a senior technical staff member in the Systems Technologies department at the IBM Haifa Research Lab. In the past he has worked on the implementation of Java for multiprocessor servers, especially on automatic memory management (garbage collection). More recently, he has worked on virtualization and management technologies for cloud computing. Currently, he is working on cloud object stores and is the principal investigator (PI) for VISION Cloud, an European Commission FP7 Integrated Project developing advanced technologies for cloud object stores. Kolodner holds a Ph.D. and M.S. degree in computer science from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, as well as a B.A. in Mathematics and a B.S.E. in computer science from the University of Pennsylvania.

Dimosthenis Kyriazis received a diploma from the school of Electrical and Computer Engineering of the NTUA in 2001 and a MSc degree in “Techno-economics” in 2004. In 2007, he received a Ph.D. in the area of service oriented architectures with a focus on quality aspects and workflow management from the school of Electrical and Computer Engineering Department of NTUA. His expertise lies in service-based, distributed, and heterogeneous systems, software and service engineering. As a senior research engineer of the Institute of Communication and Computer Systems (ICCS) of NTUA, he has participated in several EU and nationally funded projects leading research for addressing issues related to quality of service provisioning, fault tolerance, workflow management, performance modeling in service oriented environments, and application domains such as multimedia, post-production, virtual reality, finance, and e-health.

Francesco Longo received a Ph.D. in advanced technologies for information engineering at the University of Messina (Italy) in 2011. He is now a post doctoral researcher within the VISION Cloud European project. His main research interests include performance and reliability evaluation of distributed systems with focus on the use of non-Markovian stochastic Petri nets.

Mirko Lorenz is a journalist, information architect and trainer. For the past seven years he has been a member of the innovation team at Deutsche Welle. His key role is being a messenger between newsrooms and technology providers, contributing through research, conceptual work, and project management for development. Since 2010, Lorenz has been focused on “data-driven journalism,” as a conference organizer, book contributor, and trainer for journalists. One recent successful project in this area was his project management for Datawrapper, a widely used, open source tool to create basic, correct charts in four steps. Lorenz is a contributor to the “Data Journalism Handbook,” published in 2012 by O'Reilly.

Alberto Messina began his collaboration as a research engineer with RAI in 1996, when he completed his M.S. thesis about objective quality evaluation of MPEG-2 video coding. Messina's current interests range from file formats and metadata standards to content analysis and information extraction algorithms. His current area of expertise is Automated Information Extraction & Management/Information and Knowledge Engineering, an area in which he is author of more than 70 technical and scientific publications. Messina has been an active member of several EBU Technical projects and now leads the Strategic Programme on Media Information Management. He worked in several EC projects and currently he is active in TOSCA-MP and VISION Cloud. He has served on the Programme Committee of several international conferences and was general co-chair of the International Workshop on Automated Information Extraction in Media Production (AIEMPro) workshop from 2008 and 2011. Messina actively participates EBU and MPEG, where he contributed to MPEG-7 Audiovisual Description Profile.

Maurizio Montagnuolo received a Laurea degree in telecommunications engineering from the Polytechnic of Turin in 2004, after developing his thesis at the RAI Research Centre. In 2008, he received a Ph.D. in business and management from the University of Turin, in collaboration with RAI. His initial contributions to computer science were in the area of artificial intelligence, specifically in the semantic classification of audiovisual content. He participated in several national and EU funded projects in automatic content analysis, indexing, and search. His current research interests are mostly in the area of web data mining and multimedia data mining. Montagnuolo is also co-author of several scientific works published in journals or presented at international conferences in these subject areas.

Eliot Salant has held a number of managerial and technical leadership positions over the past 20 years at the IBM Haifa Labs. Additionally, he has served as project coordinator for several large EU-sponsored cloud-computing projects, including RESERVOIR and VISION Cloud. Salant holds a B.Eng. degree in mechanical engineering from McGill University, an M.S. degree in biomedical engineering from the Technion—Israel Institute of Technology, and an M.S. degree in computer science from Union College.

Francesco Tusa received a Master's degree in open source and computer security, and started Ph.D. studies in advanced technologies for information engineering at the University of Messina. In April 2011, he defended his Ph.D. thesis “Security in distributed computing systems: from Grid to Cloud.” He has been actively working as IT security and distributed systems analyst in cloud computing, virtualization, and storage for the European Union Projects “RESERVOIR” and “VISION Cloud.” Tusa is also involved in the design and implementation of the CLEVER cloud middleware. His scientific activity has been focused on studying distributed systems, grid and cloud computing. His research interests are in the area of security, virtualization, migration, and federation of distributed computing systems. Tusa is a member of the MDSLab Computer Engineering group at the University of Messina.

Al Kovalick has worked in the field of hybrid AV/IT systems for the past 20 years. Previously, he was a digital systems designer and technical strategist for Hewlett-Packard. Following HP, from 1999 to 2004, he was the CTO of Pinnacle Systems. For the next six years he was a Corporate Fellow at Avid. In 2011 Kovalick founded Media Systems Consulting in Santa Clara, California. Kovalick is an active speaker, educator, author, and participant with industry bodies including SMPTE and AMWA. He has presented more than 50 papers at industry conferences worldwide and holds 18 U.S. and foreign patents. He is the author of the book Video Systems in an IT Environment (2nd ed.). In 2009, Kovalick was awarded the David Sarnoff Medal from SMPTE. He has a BSEE degree from San Jose State University and MSEE degree from the University of California at Berkeley. Kovalick is an SMPTE Fellow. He writes “The Cloudspotter's Journal” for TV Technology Magazine. He can be contacted at www.theAVITbook.com.

Ron Quartararo is currently director, business development in the Communications, Media and Entertainment group at Hitachi Data Systems. Prior to Hitachi, Quartararo has spent more than 20 years in the media and entertainment (M&E) industry in senior level management roles in strategic planning, operations, sales, marketing, and business development. His career includes engagements at Verizon, Ascent Media, StorageTek/Sun Microsystems, Arbitron, and RKO. In those roles, he has helped grow revenue within the companies' M&E verticals, develop new strategic solutions, create and manage new partnerships, and drive grow-to-market strategy. Quartararo has been published in the NY Times, Broadcasting & Cable, Broadcast Engineering, among other publications, and holds an MBA in finance from St. John's University.

Jay Yogeshwar is a leading technology expert and business executive with more than 20 years experience as a research scientist, entrepreneur, and as a Fortune 500 global business leader in the field of media and entertainment. He has created advanced media solutions that leverage best of technology, software, systems, and services packaged for the communications and media markets. Yogeshwar has led innovation in startups and within large corporations by creating a technology vision to create large viable and sustainable businesses. He is a world-renowned expert in media technologies and IT systems covering the areas of post-production, media asset management, media distribution, media archives, and video surveillance. Yogeshwar's awards and credits include a technical Emmy for DVD technology, ten U.S. patents in media technologies, presentations and membership in professional organizations such as IEEE, SMPTE, IBC and the International Emmy's. He currently serves as the director for Media and Entertainment Vertical Practice at Hitachi Data Systems.

Mark Brown has been serving the media and entertainment industry for more than 20 years and has a proven track record engaging many of the media and broadcast industries' most influential corporations. Brown has provided strategic implementation and operational consultation in coordination with business objectives to more than 40 of the media industry's leading companies, including AT&T, Fox, Sprint, DirecTV, Hulu, Yahoo!, Microsoft Studios, Sony Pictures, Disney Studios, as well as numerous major network broadcast and cable clients. — Brown's diverse background has incorporated direct engineering, project, and corporate level management, as well as high profile business and product development roles with Verizon, Ascent Media, SignaSys Inc., Sony Electronics, Tektronix/ Grass Valley Group, Science Applications International Corporation (SAIC), Lockheed Martin, and Hughes Electronics. He has been published in various trade publications and has book acknowledgments covering centralized broadcasting and digital content management, and content centric multiplatform environments. He is currently chief operating officer at MPS Broadband America.

Brian Campanotti is the chief technical officer at Front Porch Digital, leading industry advancement in cloud-based and on-premises global content storage management (CSM), media asset management (MAM) and content publishing, migration and preservation solutions. He is responsible for innovations in the area of cloud-based solutions for “big data” as well as media-centric content handling, delivery and storage. He was one of the primary inventors of the Archive eXchange Format (AXF) and is active in standards-body activities helping to promote innovation and openness in the industry. — Campanotti and his team have won Emmy Awards for their work in content collection preservation technologies and for innovation in serial digital video technology. Campanotti began his career at the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC) and has founded several start up companies. He holds a degree in electrical engineering from the University of Toronto.

He is known as the father of the widely-used Broadcast eXchange Format standard, and has led this effort since its inception in 2004. Lennon also serves as Director of Standards for SMPTE. He has been active in a wide array of other industry organizations, including the Society of Cable Telecommunication Engineers (SCTE), the Advanced Television Systems Committee (ATSC), and Advanced Media Workflow Association (AMWA).

Harold S. Geller is chief growth officer of Advertising Digital Identification LLC (Ad-ID), a U.S.-based advertising-metadata system, which is a joint venture of American Association of Advertising Agencies (4A's) and the Association of National Advertisers (ANA). Geller speaks and writes extensively regarding interoperability, digital workflow, and metadata in advertising, and is the co-author of four white papers on the subject. His advertising career spans nearly 30 years in the U.S. and Canada. He has worked in media buying/planning, account management, financial, and technology roles at MindShare, Ogilvy & Mather, McCann Erickson, and Ted Bates and Foster Advertising. Geller is a graduate of Seneca College (Toronto, Ontario, Canada) where he studied radio and television broadcasting.

Ian Hamilton has been an innovator and entrepreneur in Internetworking infrastructure and applications for more than 20 years. A founding member of Signiant, he has led the development of innovative software solutions to address the challenges of fast, secure, content distribution over the public Internet and private intranets for many of the media and entertainment industries' largest companies. Before Signiant, Hamilton was chair and vice president of product development at ISOTRO Network Management. He was responsible for launching ISOTRO's software business unit and created the NetID product suite before the company was successfully acquired by Bay Networks. Previously, he was a member of the scientific staff at Bell Northern Research, performing applied research and development in the areas of Internetworking and security. Hamilton is a member of the FIMS technical board and an advocate for applying service oriented architecture to file-based media workflows to improve operational efficiency and business agility.

Tony Vasile has been involved in software design and architecture for more than 20 years. He currently works at Signiant as a development manager and cloud solutions architect. Vasile has been involved from the beginning of Signiant's entry into the media and entertainment space and has worked with many of Signiant's customers to define and develop products to meet today's industry needs. He is currently focusing on Signiant's Cloud-based solutions, SaaS product offerings, and Signiant's SDK and API offerings. Vasile is currently a member of the FIMS Technical board and actively involved in working groups defining further FIMS standards.
