Ralf Einhorn has a professional background in research and development with a strong focus on distributed network services and infrastructures. He has worked on service-oriented architectures, web technologies, storage systems, and network supported A/V technologies. — As senior R&D engineer in the production workflow lab at Thomson/Technicolor Corporate Research Einhorn was responsible for the IT-based distributed movie production testbed and worked on various international projects. He took a major role in designing architectures for system integration of interactive multimedia applications in virtualized environments. — Einhorn studied electrical engineering and computer science at the TU Braunschweig and the University of Hannover. He earned a Ph.D. (Dr.-Ing.) at the Institute for Computer Networks and Distributed systems at the Computing Centre Lower Saxony and at the L3S Research Centre. Einhorn is co-founder and CEO of TIXEL, a company focused on high-performance data transfer in wide area IP networks.

Andreas Aust is currently chief technical officer at TIXEL and has more than 17 years of experience in developing, designing, and architecting software systems for a variety of media related projects covering signal processing for audio codecs, mobile entertainment platforms, scalable software frameworks, and optimized network protocol stacks. — Since 2005, Aust has focused on high-performance network applications and service-oriented architectures. He has managed many research projects and holds several media and IT-related patents. — Aust studied electrical engineering at the RWTH Aachen, where he earned an engineering degree (Dipl.-Ing.) in 1996. From 1996 to 2009, he held various positions at Thomson/Technicolor. He was part of the incubator team from 2001 to 2004, starting a new U.S. Research Lab in Princeton. Aust co-founded TIXEL in 2009.

Lars Fürst studied at The Technical University of Dortmund, Germany, where he earned a degree (Dipl.-Ing.) in Information Technology Engineering from the Institute of Robotics and Information Technology. During his study, he focused on digital A/V signal processing, communication engineering, and software development. — After graduation, Fürst started his professional career as a R&D engineer in the production workflow lab at Thomson/Technicolor Corporate Research. His research was focused on service-oriented architectures for realtime media production workflows, distributed storage architectures and file systems. After five successful years with Thomson/Technicolor, Fürst joined a team of engineers at TIXEL. He has been responsible for software product development of high-performance data transfer solutions, standardization, as well as pre-sales and is currently in charge of TIXEL's business development.

Michael Wittmann studied electrical engineering with an emphasis on psychoacoustics and cybernetics at the Technical University Munich (TUM). He is co-founder and chief technology officer of David Systems and has profound knowledge in signal processing, audio electronics and software development. Founded in 1991, DAVID Systems is a pioneer in offering end-to-end software-based solutions to enable tapeless workflows in radio, television, and rich media broadcast applications. David Systems has a history of experience in CMS/MAM-based media exchange and delivers integrated solutions, which scale from a single mobile device (media upload for journalist) to multi organization media exchange (ARD-File exchange for news, music and video).

He has published in leading journals such as the Proceedings of the IEEE and IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence. He has also presented at SMPTE and National Association of Broadcasters (NAB) conferences. Bhat currently holds five patents in the area of digital television.

Helt served as technical manager of the European project “Limelight,” aimed at the design of a complete digital film restoration system from 1994 to 1997. He is also founder and chief executive officer of DUST, a company specializing in digital restoration and processing of film from 1997 to 2002. — Helt designed the color conversion and calibration software for digital cinema from 2004 to 2006 as well as projection measurement systems. He is chief scientific officer of Highlands Technologies Solutions and its current interest include visual perception models and measurement theory.

Valérie La Torre taught mathematics and physics in various high schools for six years, before joining Doremi Technologies in 2010. Jürgen Burghardt is currently a consultant for broadcast and AV/IT business development, project management, and training. He received a M.Sc. degree in electrical engineering from Ruhr Universität Bochum. — Burghardt previously worked at Sony Deutschland GmbH – Professional Solutions Europe, where he was head of broadcast marketing, broadcast strategy, and market development. He was also a lecturer for students of media-economics at the University of Applied Science in Wiesbaden. Joerg Houpert studied electrical engineering at the University of Bremen, with a focus on digital signal processing and psychoacoustics. Houpert is a member of SMPTE.

Timo Meyer graduated from the University of Bremen in 2009 with a diploma in electrical engineering/information technology. Yves Raimond holds a Ph.D. from Queen Mary, University of London. His thesis was entitled “A Distributed Music Information System,” and defined a framework for applying a range of semantic Web technologies for managing and distributing music-related information. As part of his thesis, Raimond contributed extensively to what would become the “Linking Open Data” community project. Since 2008, he has been working for the BBC, first on the bbc.co.uk/programs service, publishing structured data about all BBC programs, and then in BBC R&D on unlocking archives by automatically interlinking them with related datasets. As part of this project he has worked on a prototype combining automated interlinking with Linked Data sources and crowdsourcing to open up the BBC World Service archive.

Chris Lowis is a software engineer at FutureLearn, a UK-based massive open online course (MOOC) platform. He has an academic background in acoustics and signal processing, holding a doctorate in acoustics and having worked for the German Aerospace Centre, University of Southampton and BBC R&D before joining FutureLearn.

Roderick Hodgson received a B.Sc. in artificial intelligence and computer science from the University of Edinburgh in 2009. Following graduation, he joined BBC Research & Development where he worked on projects involving standardization of new approaches to accessibility, applying machine learning technology to subtitle data as well as speech-to-text data, research in camera calibration technologies, and research into high frame-rate video. Hodgson is currently working as an engineer for SQR Systems, a cyber-security company, where he is researching new technology for secure data distribution over untrusted networks.

Dominic Tinley trained as a radio journalist at the University of Westminster before moving into digital media. In 1998, he joined the BBC as one of its first Web developers. He is now an independent advisor, and since 2008 has supported BBC R&D in planning and managing collaborative research projects.

S. Merrill Weiss is a consultant in electronic media technology and electronic media technology management. His career spans 47 years in electronic media and related fields, with 38 years in management and consulting. He received B.S. and M.S. degrees in electric engineering from the Keio University, Yokohama, Japan, and a Ph.D. degree in engineering from the University of Electro-Communications, Tokyo, Japan.

Takuji Soeno is a research engineer for the Advanced Television Systems Research Division of NHK STRL. He received B.E. and M.E. degrees in applied physics and physico-informatics from Keio University, Yokohama, Japan. In 2004, he joined NHK and established his career as a video engineer engaging in TV program production. Since 2010, he has been in charge of the research and development of UHDTV systems, particularly cameras, image sensors, and digital signal processing. He is a member of ITE.

Takayuki Yamashita is a senior research engineer for the Advanced Television Systems Research Division of NHK STRL. He is currently working on the research of UHDTV systems and his research fields include the development of camera systems, image sensors, and high-bandwidth digital signal processing. Yamashita also has an interest in the research of capturing system for next-generation 3DTV. He joined NHK in 1995 after receiving B.E. and M.E. degrees in electronic engineering and information science from Kyoto Institute of Technology, Kyoto, Japan, in 1993 and 1995, respectively. He has also been involved in the research of HDTV camera systems since 1999. He is a member of SMPTE and ITE and is also active in the standardization of broadcast technologies in ARIB.

Masayuki Sugawara received B.S. and M.S. degrees in electric communication engineering and a Ph.D. degree in electronic engineering from Tohoku University, Sendai, Japan. He joined NHK in 1983. Since 1987, he has been researching solid-state image sensor, HDTV camera, and ultra-high definition television system at NHK STRL. He was an associate professor at the University of Electro-Communications, Tokyo, Japan, from 2000 to 2004. He has been attending ITU-R SG6 meeting since 2004 and been active in the working parties that address program production. Currently, he is deputy director of NHK STRL. Sugawara is a member of IEEE, SMPTE, the Institute of Electronics, Information and Communication Engineers (IEICE), and ITE.

Arihiro Saita received an M.S. degree in physics from Shizuoka University, Shizuoka, Japan, in 1995. In 1995, he joined Fuji Photo Optical (integrated with Fujifilm in 2010). Since 1995, he has been working on the development of color separation systems. He was involved in the development of HDTV broadcast cameras, Subaru telescope, and the Japanese lunar explorer Kaguya in cooperation with NHK. He is currently working on color separation systems for UHDTV cameras at the Optical Device & Electronic Imaging Products Development Center of Fujifilm.

(imaging division, now Aptina LLC) and with Xerox Corp. He has more than 20 publications and holds 25 patents. He has more than 30 years of experience in signal and image processing, high-performance computing, and hardware development. Since the early 1980s, he has focused on computer graphics, video, and display technology. Before joining Dolby Laboratories Gish was principal engineer at Evans & Sutherland, executive scientist at Terabit, and chief technology officer at Interactive Machines, Inc. — Gish received screen credit for his work on The Last Starfighter, the first full-length motion picture to use extensive CGI. He received special recognition from ISO/IEC for his contributions to the development of the high profiles for H.264/AVC, which were awarded an Emmy in 2008. His current interests include compression algorithms, high-dynamic range, and wide color gamut imaging technology, and forensic watermarking.

Foessel was the 2014 recipient of the Josef-von-Fraunhofer award for the development of easyDCP, a tool for creating and playback of Digital Cinema Packages. In 2014, he was elected to the president of the FKTG (Fernseh- und Kinotechische Gesellschaft e.V.), the German equivalent to SMPTE.

He has since worked continuously in the broadcast industry, at BBC Research Department, Thomson in France, and for the past 20 years at Snell. He has carried out original research in compression coding, transcoding and analysis, motion estimation, motion compensated frame rate conversion and other temporal processing of image sequences. More recently, he has been working on image segmentation for application in mobile video, novel methods for resizing and re-purposing video material, stereoscopic 3D analysis, and flexible, scalable motion processing of video.

Fumiaki Usui studied applied physics at Waseda University in Tokyo and joined Canon in 1988 as an optical design engineer. At Canon, he has been developing advanced optical technologies primarily for broadcast lenses and cinema lenses. From 1990, on the cinema lens front, he was deeply involved in developing the well-known Super16mm series cinema zoom lenses. In 2000, he started developing the 2/3 in. Digital Cinema Lens lines, including zooms and primes. Usui is currently involved in UHD (Ultra High Definition) optical technology development and was deeply involved in the development of Canon's latest 4K cinema lens lines, including the latest CN20×50 (50-1000mm) super telephoto 4K cinema lens.

Ryuhei Kamata joined Canon in 2002 as a sales staff for the broadcast and cinema lenses. In 2011, when Canon launched the new line of Cinema EOS products, including the cinema lens lines, he joined the U.S. division, where he has been involved in developing the cinema lens business in the U.S.

Laurence Thorpe joined Canon USA Inc. in 2004 and is currently involved with developing its professional cinematography business. Before Canon, he worked at Sony Broadcast Company from 1983 to 2004. Thorpe also worked for RCA's Broadcast Division from 1966 to 1982, where he developed a range of color television cameras and telecine products. From 1961 to 1966, he worked in the Designs department of the BBC in London, England, where he participated in the development of a range of color television studio products. Thorpe is an IEE Graduate (1961) of the College of Technology in Dublin, Ireland, and received a Chartered Engineer (C. Eng.) and MIEE distinction in 1965 from the Institute of Electrical Engineers in London, England.

Debargha Mukherjee received M.S. and Ph.D. degrees in electrical and computer engineering from the University of California at Santa Barbara in 1995 and 1999, respectively. Between 1999 and 2010, he worked at Hewlett Packard Laboratories, conducting research on video and image coding and processing. Since 2010, he has been with Google Inc., where he is currently involved with open-source video codec development. Before that he worked in YouTube on video quality control and 2D to 3D conversion. Mukherjee has authored more than 75 papers on various signal processing topics and holds more than 20 US patents. He was a student paper award winner at IEEE ICIP in 1998; a keynote speaker at the SPIE Stereoscopic Displays and Applications conference, and the CVPR 3D Cinematography workshop, both in 2012. Mukherjee currently serves as associate editor of the IEEE Transactions on Image Processing, and the SPIE Journal of Electronic Imaging.

Jingning Han received a B.S. degree in electrical engineering from Tsinghua University, Beijing, China, in 2007, and M.S. and Ph.D. degrees in electrical and computer engineering from the University of California at Santa Barbara in 2008 and 2012, respectively. He is currently with the WebM Codec Team at Google Inc., in Mountain View, CA, where he is involved in video compression, processing, and related technologies. His research interests include video coding and computer architecture. Han was a recipient of the Outstanding Teaching Assistant Awards from the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the University of California at Santa Barbara, in 2010 and 2011, a Dissertation Fellowship in 2012, and the Best Student Paper Award at the IEEE International Conference on Multimedia and Expo in 2012.

Jim Bankoski is an engineering director working on Google's WebM project. He is the former CTO of On2 Technologies, and a technical contributor to all of On2's and later Google's codecs from Tm2x through VP9, including video codecs widely used in Flash and Skype and now WebM.

Ronald S. Bultje received a Ph.D. from Cornell University in 2011. He then joined Google's video codec design team, where he contributed to the design and release of VP9. Since 2013, he has worked for Two Sigma Investments in New York. Bultje has also contributed to open source video technology projects, most notably FFmpeg (since 2002), and still does so today.

Adrian Grange joined Google in its acquisition of On2 Technologies where he had worked since 2000. He has contributed to the development of each version of the VPx codec from VP3 to VP9. Previously, he worked on several digital TV and set-top box projects, wrote an MHEG5 engine for a UK Freeview terrestrial TV project, and developed computer vision algorithms for a high-speed industrial inspection system for the ceramic tile market.

John Koleszar joined On2 Technologies in 2005, where he worked as an engineer on codec development and optimization for numerous embedded systems. After joining Google in 2010, he focused on deployment of the VP8 codec, and research and design of VP9 for the WebM Project. Koleszar is currently working to deliver Internet video from new heights as a member of the Project Loon avionics software team. He holds a B.S. degree in computer systems engineering from Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute.

Paul Wilkins graduated from Cambridge University in 1986 and has been working in the field of video compression since the early 1990s. Before joining On2 Technologies Inc. in 1999, he developed a video codec that was later released as VP3 (the basis of the open source codec Theora). He served as On2's director of research and development and later as co-chief technology officer (with Jim Bankoski), and was instrumental in the development of all the company's subsequent video codecs. In 2010, On2 was acquired by Google and Wilkins took on a new role as technical lead for codec development within the WebM team.

Yaowu Xu is currently a technical lead manager at Google, working on video codec development. Before joining Google, he was the vice president of codec development at On2 Technologies, where he was involved in the development of On2's VPx series of video codecs, including VP3.2, VP4, VP5, VP6, VP7 and VP8. These video codecs were broadly adopted by the industry and have fueled the phenomenal growth of Internet video. Xu's education background includes a B.S. degree in physics, an M.S. and Ph.D. degree in nuclear engineering from Tsinghua University, Beijing, China. He also holds M.S. and Ph.D. degrees in electrical and computer engineering from the University of Rochester in NY. Xu has published many technical papers on image processing and holds many patents in the area of digital video compression.

He worked at General Instrument on the Eurocypher project for British Satellite Broadcasting (BSB). After several years developing scientific instruments at Scripps Institution of Oceanography, he was a director of systems engineering at Tiernan Communications, developing realtime MPEG-2 video encoders for DSNG and HDTV network distribution. He switched to consumer products as a principal engineer in Plantronics' Advanced Technology Group, where he developed several advanced technology prototype headsets incorporating DSP, Bluetooth and Wi-Fi. Since then, he has consulted for several clients, including GoPro, Intel, Clair Global and TiVo. — Reuss is active in the SMPTE Standards Community, where he serves as co-chair of the Technical Committee for Coding of Essence (TC-10E). Yannic Alff has been working as systems engineer at Kabel Deutschland Vertrieb und Service GmbH (Vodafone group) since 2014. Thomas Göllner has been working as systems engineer at Kabel Deutschland Vertrieb und Service GmbH (Vodafone group) since 2014. In 2012, he joined Dynamic Digital Depth (DDD) in Los Angeles, CA, as a senior research engineer in image technology. His interests lie in image and video compression and enhancement, 3D video processing, and subjective and objective video quality evaluation.

Kevin Stec has more than 30 years of experience in professional and consumer video development. He is currently the vice president of image technology research at Dynamic Digital Depth where he is responsible for investigating 3D ecosystems. He previously held the position of senior director of image technology at Dolby Laboratories, overseeing development of image-processing technology for digital cinema, broadcast, and consumer entertainment applications. He spent the majority of his career at Panasonic, working in a variety of R&D and product development groups; his last position for the company was as general manager of Panasonic AVC American Laboratories. Stec joined DemoGraFX in 2001 as the vice president of engineering; in 2003, DemoGraFX was acquired by Dolby Laboratories. — Stec has worked on the development of HDTV since 1981 and was awarded a Technology and Engineering Emmy Award in 2000 for advancements in video format conversion. He holds a number of patents in the area of digital video signal processing. Stec has participated on numerous SMPTE technical committees relating to video recording and digital video technology. He has been a session chair at the Advanced Motion Imaging Conference, a Hollywood Section Manager and is on the SMPTE Board of Editors. He is a SMPTE Fellow and also a Gold Member of the Hollywood Post Alliance. He holds an electrical engineering degree from University of California, Santa Barbara.

Toshiaki Kojima has worked in both the audio video (AV) and information technology (IT) worlds over the past 32 years. He joined Sony in 1982 after graduating from Waseda University, Japan. For the first 20 years of his career he was involved mainly in the design of professional videotape recorders, from 1 in. to the e-VTR. In 2004, he received a Sports Emmy statuette in recognition of the role of the e-VTR when NBC was awarded a Sports Emmy for coverage of the Athens Olympics. Following the e-VTR project, he moved into research and development (R&D) with the aim of replacing dedicated professional AV interfaces with those of general IP. This effort is ongoing. — Kojima is an active participant in various network-related industry and standardization bodies, including FIMS, the Video Services Forum (VSF), SMPTE and the Joint Task Force on Professional Networked Streamed Media (JT-NM). He holds 20 Japanese and international patents, and is a Massachusetts Institute of Technology Fellow.

John Stone has been general manager of Sony Broadcast & Professional Research Labs (BPRL) in the U.K. since 2002. The mission of BPRL is to provide innovation and new technology for the Sony B2B business in the areas of professional media and broadcast as well as other markets such as healthcare and security. Stone leads a strong team of engineers with expertise in activities ranging from feasibility study, algorithm development, system prototyping through to product and solution development. The current focus of the BPRL team is in the areas of 4K content creation, sport production, video codec, as well as IP networking for broadcast production.

Jian-Rong Chen is a principal engineer at Sony Broadcast & Professional Research Labs in the U.K. His technical background includes telecommunication and data network modeling and simulation, network management software, video over IP and software development. Chen was a member of a team within Sony BPRL that developed an SDI over IP routing system prototype, which demonstrated the technical feasibility of using IP network for live production in 2002. Before joining the broadcast industry, he worked in the telecommunication industry on ATM switches, and also on European Union sponsored research project ICM (Integrated Communication Management of Broadband Networks). He is a member of IEEE.

Paul Gardiner is standards manager at Sony Broadcast & Professional Research Labs within Sony Europe Ltd, based in Basingstoke, UK. He studied electronic engineering at the University of Southampton before joining the Independent Broadcasting Authority (IBA) in 1974. She has also designed and conducted a number of user studies (e.g., pairwise protocol, eye tracking) to validate computational models and image processing algorithms. Previously, she worked at INRIA Rennes (France) and Philips Research (the Netherlands), where she was involved in compression algorithms. She holds two master's degrees defended in 2003 from the University of Nantes and the Ecole Centrale de Nantes, France.

Catherine Serré has been a researcher in the imaging science lab at Technicolor Research & Innovation in Rennes, France, since 2004. She graduated from INSA Rennes in electronics and computer engineering. She has been a project leader of several collaborative projects: PELOPS (ITEA), Futurim@ges (FUI3), and NEVEx (FUI11). Before 2004, she worked in the research and development department of live video production equipment at Thomson-Grass Valley.

Tania Pouli is a researcher at Technicolor Research & Innovation in Rennes, France. Her work focuses on HDR and color imaging, with the aim of treating these two aspects as a single entity. After completing a Ph.D. degree in 2011 at the University of Bristol, focusing on image statistics and color transfer, she moved to the Max Planck Institute for Informatics as a postdoctoral candidate. She has organized and copresented a number of successful courses and tutorials at Special Interest Group on Graphics and Interactive Techniques (SIGGRAPH), SIGGRAPH Asia, and Eurographics, including a course on color transfer at SIGGRAPH 2012 and a Eurographics State of the Art Report on image statistics. She is the lead author of the book “Image Statistics in Visual Computing,” published by CRC Press.

Sripal Mehta is principal architect, broadcast at Dolby Laboratories. His focus is the innovation, development and deployment of next-generation audio. Mehta has spent 15 years at Dolby working in the areas of professional audio, digital cinema security, and playback, and most recently, object-based immersive and personalized audio for the cinema and home. As a member of SMPTE, he has authored two digital cinema standards and has chaired the digital cinema security subcommittee. Mehta holds bachelor’s and master’s degrees in electrical and computer engineering from Carnegie Mellon University.

Thomas Ziegler received a Ph.D. in electrical engineering for his research on the optimization of digital signal processor architectures with respect to audio coding. After his academic career, he worked at the Fraunhofer Gesellschaft, FhG, in the field of hardware close development of high-efficiency audio codecs. In 2000, he joined Coding Technologies—the inventors of HE-AAC—where he led the implementation of HE-AAC playback for satellite-based and terrestrial digital radio as well as for mobile applications. Since the acquisition of Coding Technologies by Dolby in late 2007, Ziegler coordinated Dolby’s embedded strategy as director embedded engineering. Today, he is driving the playback side of Dolby’s Personalized Audio offerings in the broadcast space. Ziegler has contributed to many publications as principal or co-author, and for many years, he gave lectures at the University of Fulda on source coding for multimedia.

William Redmann is currently a Fellow and Sr. System Architect at Technicolor, where he assembled Technicolor’s Digital Cinema Interoperability Testing Center (ITC) and worldwide hard drive distribution platform. He began his career mixing technology and entertainment by obtaining a master’s degree in engineering at UCLA while building practical electronic props for Battlestar Galactica and Buck Rogers. He was twice director of technology at Walt Disney Imagineering, developing and fielding ride systems including Indiana Jones at Disneyland Park, and 20 interactive attractions seen at DisneyQuest, Orlando. Redmann has 33 US patents issued and more than 40 pending in fields including digital cinema, virtual reality audio, online media production, distributed network streaming media and interactive systems, 3D displays, online communities, content distribution to mobile devices, healthy play for children, travel planning, and electric vehicle infrastructure. His favorites are a roller coaster you design then ride, and a keyboard for dolphins to communicate with people.

Roger Dressler was deeply involved with the development of the consumer surround sound market and the many related technologies during his 25 years at Dolby Laboratories. He is currently consulting and participating in SMPTE’s immersive audio standards activities.

Brian Vessa is a dedicated audio professional with more than 35 years of experience in the industry. After attending the University of California Engineering School, he became a recording engineer, producing albums and recording orchestras. His passion was hot-rodding studio gear and discovering novel recording techniques. Vessa transitioned into film post as a music editor and sound editor, became a re-recording mixer at Cannon Films and MGM, then handled audio restoration at NT Audio. Vessa is a member of the Academy Sound Branch, SMPTE, and AES. He chairs the SMPTE Technical Committee on Cinema Sound Systems, TC-25CSS, as well as D-Cinema and IMF sub-committees, and is a recent chair of the DCI Technical Committee. Glenn Leembruggen is a principal of the consulting engineering firms Acoustic Directions and ICE Design in Australia and an Associate of Sydney University. Having studied electrical engineering and acoustics, his skills encompass loudspeaker and sound system design, room acoustics and noise control. Much of Leembruggen’s work includes designing sound systems that deliver extremely high quality sound and intelligibility for courtrooms, parliaments, transport terminals, road tunnels, cathedrals and performance spaces. Since 1992, Leembruggen’s team has received many awards for its sound system designs. In 2014, he undertook the editorial duties and the data processing for the substantial B Chain Theatre Testing Report. Underpinning Leembruggen’s work is his passion for sound and music; marrying the physics and engineering with the aural experience and playing saxophone in a Chicago style electric rhythm and blues band. His research interests include Speech Transmission Index (STI) and the differences between subjective and measured speech intelligibility, beam-steered loudspeakers, and acoustic absorption systems. Leembruggen has authored a number of AES and SMPTE Journal papers on sound system design, STI and cinema-screen behavior and is a frequent presenter at IOA and AES conferences on aspects of intelligibility, electro-acoustic design and acoustics. Leembruggen is a Fellow of the Institute of Acoustics, and member of the the Audio Engineering Society, the Acoustical Society of America, the Australian Acoustical Society, and SMPTE and is a member of the Maintenance Team for the STI standard IEC 60268-16.

George Joblove has played key and pioneering roles in the development and application of digital technology to the entertainment industry throughout his career, and currently advises technology- and media-oriented clients as an independent consultant. He served as executive vice president of advanced technology at Sony Pictures Entertainment, where his focuses included facilitating improved workflows and image quality across production, postproduction, and distribution. Previously, Joblove was chief technology officer at Sony Pictures’ visual-effects and animation unit, Imageworks, and he co-founded and led the digital-effects department of Industrial Light & Magic. Joblove received a Scientific and Engineering Academy Award in 1994. He has two patents in 3D photography and cinematography. He is a member of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, a past co-chair of its Science and Technology Council, and an associate member of the American Society of Cinematographers. He holds a B.S. in computer science, and an M.S. in computer graphics, both from Cornell University.

Suzanne Farrell is a research engineer for Dolby Laboratories. Her research includes psychophysical studies on viewer preferences, and preserving high dynamic range content on lower dynamic range displays through tone and gamut mapping. She graduated from Rochester Institute of Technology with a degree in Motion Picture Science.

Timo Kunkel is a senior researcher for Dolby Laboratories. His main areas of research are high dynamic range and wide color gamut imaging, advanced display systems, virtual reality technologies and psychophysics. He has published on topics such as color and dynamic range perception of the human visual system and on creating novel color appearance models. Over the last 15 years he also worked as an architecture and landscape photographer focusing on computational photography approaches as well as head of pre-press imaging and co-founder of a German children’s book publisher. He received a Ph.D. in computer science from the University of Bristol, U.K. and M.Sc. in physical geography, remote sensing and environment modeling from the University of Freiburg in Germany.

Scott Daly is a senior researcher for Dolby Laboratories working on fundamental perceptual issues and efforts to preserve artistic intent throughout the entire video path to reach the viewer. His background includes a B.S.E.E degree from North Carolina State University, and an M.S. in bioengineering from the University of Utah in the 1980s. Applying visual models towards digital video and displays, he has publications on spatiotemporal and motion imagery, human interaction, with wall-sized displays, high dynamic range, cinema display, and stereoscopic displays. Awards include the Otto Schade Award from SID in 2011 for Applied Perception and a team Emmy Award in 1989–1990 for a video transceiver used in a prominent international news event. He is currently a member of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers IEEE, the International Society for Optics and Photonics, and the Society for Information Display.

Jeffrey Riedmiller is senior director of the Sound Group in the Office of the CTO at Dolby Laboratories in San Francisco, CA, where he leads a team of creative researchers and technology visionaries responsible for driving the evolution of Dolby’s long-term technology vision and master roadmap for sound and related media ecosystems. Riedmiller’s professional career in audio, broadcast and electronics engineering spans 26 years. Joining Dolby in 1998, he worked extensively on the design, development and launch of multichannel audio for over 80 digital cable and satellite television services throughout North America. He is also the visionary creator of several revolutionary technology and product innovations that have become the foundation of how television loudness is estimated and controlled worldwide today. Riedmiller is an active member of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE), Society of Cable Telecommunications Engineers (SCTE) and its Standards Committees. He holds several patents and has authored and presented several technical papers for the Audio Engineering Society (AES), National Association of Broadcasters (NAB), Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE), National Cable Telecommunications Association (NCTA), and SMPTE.

Sripal Mehta is principal architect, broadcast at Dolby Laboratories. His focus is the innovation, development and deployment of next generation audio. Mehta has spent 15 years at Dolby working in the areas of professional audio, digital cinema security and playback, and most recently, object-based immersive and personalized audio for the cinema and home. As a member of SMPTE, he has authored two digital cinema standards and has chaired the digital cinema security subcommittee. Mehta holds bachelor’s and master’s degrees in electrical and computer engineering from Carnegie Mellon University.

Nicolas Tsingos designed and prototyped the authoring and rendering tools for the Dolby Atmos cinema technology and the spatial coding tools for Dolby Atmos content delivery to the home. Tsingos received a Ph.D. in computer science from the Joseph Fourier University in Grenoble, France. He has more than 15 years of research experience in computer graphics, interactive audio rendering and acoustic simulation. In addition to his current position at Dolby Laboratories, Nicolas holds a tenure research position at INRIA - the French National Institute for Computer Science—and previously was a member of the technical staff at Bell Laboratories.

Robert Bleidt is division general manager of Fraunhofer USA Digital Media Technologies. He is the inventor of the award-winning Sonnox/Fraunhofer codec plug-in, widely used in music mastering, led the extension of Fraunhofer’s codec business to a open-source model by inclusion in Android, and developed Fraunhofer’s Symphoria automotive audio business. Before joining Fraunhofer, he was president of Streamcrest Associates, a product and business strategy consulting firm in new media technologies. Previously, he was director of product management and business strategy for the MPEG-4 business of Philips Digital Networks and managed the development of Philips’ Emmy-winning asset management system for television broadcasting. Prior to joining Philips, Bleidt served as director of marketing and new business development for Sarnoff Real Time Corporation, a video-on-demand venture of Sarnoff Labs. Previously, he was director of mass storage technology and inventor of SRTC’s Carousel algorithm. Before joining Sarnoff, Bleidt was President of Image Circuits, a consulting engineering firm and manufacturer of HDTV research equipment.

Arne Borsum studied media technologies at the Ilmenau Technical University, Germany, before starting as a research engineer at Fraunhofer in 2004. After a short engagement at the Fraunhofer IDMT in Ilmenau, he joined the Audio and Multimedia division of the Fraunhofer IIS in Erlangen, Germany. Borsum worked on various projects in the field of digital audio processing, audio coding, software development and DSP implementation. His speciality became downmixing technologies, loudness, dynamic range control and related metadata solutions. As a technical expert in the field of audio for broadcasting, his focus of work evolved into application engineering for TV and the workflow in broadcast infrastructures in order to establish Fraunhofer audio technologies in these services. Further, he represented the Audio and Multimedia division of Fraunhofer IIS in standardization bodies and committee groups such as EBU, IEC, HDMI Forum and AES. In 2013, Borsum was appointed senior engineer. From April 2014, he worked as independent contractor for Fraunhofer IIS, acting as business development manager for audio production. In this role, he continued his work in application engineering and committee work with focus on the integration of MPEG-H Audio into broadcast infrastructures. Since February 2015, Borsum works for Innovationszentrum für Telekommunikationstechnik (IZT) in Erlangen, Germany, as product manager for Digital Audio Broadcasting.

Harald Fuchs received his diploma in electrical engineering from the University of Erlangen, Germany in 1997 and joined Fraunhofer IIS in the same year. From 1997 to 2002 he was a software developer for video codecs and multimedia streaming systems. From 2002 onwards he concentrated on multimedia systems aspects and standardization. He actively contributed to several standardization organizations (including MPEG, DVB and HbbTV), and was author or co-author of several standards documents and IEEE papers. Since 2009 he focused on audio technologies for broadcasting and broadband streaming applications. Since 2011 he has been senior business development manager, audio for TV Broadcast.

S. Merrill Weiss is a consultant in electronic media technology and technology management with over 48 years of experience in broadcast operations and in designing facilities for radio and television stations, television networks, major studios, and similar organizations. He has spent more than 38 years in developing technology for digital audio and video and in helping to write standards for its implementation, having produced the SMPTE/EBU tests that led to the first digital television standard, upon which practically all subsequent digital video standards are based. He is a SMPTE Fellow, received the SMPTE David Sarnoff Gold Medal Award and the SMPTE Progress Medal, received the NAB Television Engineering Achievement Award and the ATSC Bernard J. Lechner Outstanding Contributor Award, received the IEEE Broadcast Technology Society Matti S. Siukola Award twice, and is recognized by the Society of Broadcast Engineers as a Certified Professional Broadcast Engineer. Weiss holds six patents for broadcast transmission technology and is a graduate of the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania.

Paul Gardiner is standards manager at Sony Broadcast & Professional Research Labs within Sony Europe Ltd., based in Basingstoke, U.K. He studied electronic engineering at the University of Southampton before joining the Independent Broadcasting Authority (IBA) in 1974. His career has included television technical regulation and R&D project management with responsibility for various international collaborative research projects. He has also regularly been involved in the work of the International Telcommunications Union Radiocommunication Sector (ITU-R). Since joining Sony in 2007, Gardiner has been an active participant in the SMPTE standards community. He is a SMPTE Fellow.

Edward Reuss specializes in video, audio, and Wi-Fi networks, particularly for very low-latency applications. Earning an MSEE at Colorado State University, Reuss started in test and measurement, for Hewlett Packard (Agilent), Tektronix, and Wavetek. After several years developing scientific instruments at Scripps Institution of Oceanography, he worked as a director of systems engineering at Tiernan Communications, developing realtime MPEG-2 video encoders for digital satellite news gathering (DSNG) and high-definition television (HDTV) network distribution. He switched to consumer products as a principal engineer in the Plantronics' Advanced Technology Group, where he developed several advanced technology prototype headsets incorporating DSP, Bluetooth, and Wi-Fi. Since then, he has consulted for several clients, including GoPro, Intel, Clair Global, and TiVo. In addition to his involvement in the SMPTE standards community, Reuss is also a senior member of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) and is a voting member of the IEEE 802.11 Wireless Local Area Networks Working Group.

Dave Schnuelle represents Dolby Laboratories as senior director, image technology, and provides guidance in Dolby's efforts in the television, cinema, and consumer imaging areas. He began his career as an engineer on television outside broadcasts while attending Purdue University. Schnuelle later held positions as chief engineer at various post-production facilities such as Editel and Modern VideoFilm in Los Angeles. Schnuelle worked with Lucasfilm's THX Division, beginning in 1991, where he was responsible for founding the THX Digital Mastering Program for quality-assurance of home video masters and duplicated software. As director of technology for THX, he directed research efforts into new technology for cinemas. During that period, he directly supervised the international digital cinema exhibition of the new Star Wars movies—Episode 1 (1999) and Episode 2 (2002). Schnuelle holds four patents on imaging and audio technology and has been deeply involved with film and television standards activities for 30 years. He is a SMPTE Fellow and a member of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences.

Dean Bullock has been working in the cinema industry since joining Dolby Laboratories in 1996 as an embedded systems engineer working on the Dolby D-Cinema processor product line. As an engineering director, Bullock led Dolby's Digital Cinema engineering team and then the cinema engineering quality assurance group. Currently, he is director of technology strategy for Dolby's Cinema group. He has worked to implement SMPTE and other standards since starting at Dolby and since 2009 he has been actively participating in SMPTE committees. Bullock holds a B.S. in computer and electrical engineering from Purdue University.

Mike Radford is vice president of engineering for 20th Century Fox. His responsibilities include both standards work within SMPTE as well as the design and development of critical production software systems in the area of D-Cinema key management, mastering, and workflow. He is also chair of the DCI Technical Committee. Before that, Radford worked for Fox Television in its Advanced Engineering Group, where he specialized in radio frequency propagation modeling and developed software systems to predict digital television (DTV) coverage and interference. Using the tools he authored, he participated in the design of more than 50 new Fox DTV broadcast facilities across the country.

Michael A. Dolan is founder and president of Television Broadcast Technology. He has been involved in digital television engineering for the past eight years. He currently chairs the ATSC Data Broadcasting Specialist Group (TSG/S13) and is active in the Consumer Electronics Association and the Society of Cable Telecommunication Engineers.

He chairs the SMPTE Technical Committee on Cinema Sound Systems, TC-25CSS, as well as D-Cinema and IMF sub-committees, and is a recent chair of the DCI Technical Committee. He has written many audio specifications, including a white paper on near-field mixing for home theater that has been widely adopted.

Kurt Graffy spent more than 15 years in concert/theater sound and lighting design/production in the California/San Francisco Bay Area, both as lead designer of the SF Arts Commission Technical Resources Group and as a freelance mixer/designer. Leaving the arts scene, he was with Data General Corporation as computer systems field engineer prior to joining Paoletti-Lewitz Associates as staff acoustical consultant in 1985. He joined Arup Acoustics, an international acoustical consulting firm based in the U.K., in 1998 when he established their San Francisco office for acoustics. At Arup, he is a principal consultant in Acoustics, responsible for room acoustics and audio system design, measurement, and specification, including computer model testing and analysis. Graffy is a member of the Acoustical Society of America, the Audio Engineering Society (where he Co-Chairman for the Technical Committee on Acoustics and Sound Reinforcement) and SMPTE, where he also served as a chief writer for the B-Chain Cinema Testing Report.

John Hurst is co-founder and chief technology officer at CineCert, LLC, an internationally recognized developer of digital cinema technology. Hurst has more than 30 years experience in entertainment technology, at first in the practical application of recording and post-production, then later following his interests in product development. He has been involved in developing technologies for D-Cinema since 2000. Under his direction, CineCert has produced several benchmark D-Cinema projects, among them the Waimea KDM authoring system, the DCI Compliance Test Plan, and the open source AS-DCP file access library. Hurst has developed many SMPTE standards for D-Cinema. He is a SMPTE Fellow.

Pierre-Anthony Lemieux is a partner at Sandflow Consulting, where he works with both Hollywood and Silicon Valley clients on worldwide standards, proof-of-concept development, and product architecture. His expertise covers the entertainment technology ecosystem, from content authoring to playback, including audio and video and timed text, file formats, and content protection. His recent engagements include representing clients at industry forums (including SMPTE and W3C,) developing standards for file-based post-production workflows, and implementing audio processing algorithms. Lemieux is a SMPTE Fellow and currently serves as document editor in multiple SMPTE projects, in addition to chairing TC 31FS. He has a Ph.D. in physics from the University of California, at Los Angeles (UCLA) and a B.Sc. from McGill University.

Thomas Bause Mason is director, advanced digital media technology, NBCUniversal. As part of the NBCUniversal Advanced Technology Team, Bause researches and implements emerging technologies as well as standards for file-based workflows for production, post-production and distribution, including traditional broadcast, cable, and the Web. In addition, Bause works with many different NBCUniversal operational teams, implementing standards and technology at the corporate level. Formerly, he worked at a major Hollywood post-production company where he built and ran encoding operations and supported business development with implementing new media workflows. Previously, Bause worked in Germany as a programmer developing process visualization software and database solutions. He also managed a quality control department for several private broadcast networks at a large broadcast service provider. Bause has a bachelor's degree in media technology. He has been a SMPTE member since 2007. Bause served a two-year term as the co-chair 35PM TC and chaired the now completed SMPTE Studio Group on UHDTV Ecosystems.

Friedrich Gierlinger has worked at IRT, the Research and Development Institute of public broadcasting corporations of Germany (ARD, ZDF, DRadio), Austria (ORF) and Switzerland (SRG/SSR), since 1979. As an employ of the IRT he was involved in the development of different measurement techniques for analog and digital standard television for the public broadcasters and their standardization. He chairs the German system and measurement expert group and is member of a working group of measurement and service department leaders of the Public Broadcasters in Germany. In the European Broadcasting Union, Gierlinger is co-chair of the Quality-Control working group as well as a member of the Beyond-HD working group. In addition to the TC-32NF, he is member of several other SMPTE groups.

John F. Snow represents Xilinx, Inc., where he is a video connectivity architect responsible for implementation of video interfaces in Xilinx field programmable gate arrays, including SDI and HDMI. Prior to joining Xilinx in 2001, he was director of engineering at Evans & Sutherland, where he was involved in realtime computer graphics for flight simulation. He has a B.S. degree in electrical engineering from Brigham Young University and is a senior member of the IEEE.

Chris Lennon is president and CEO of MediAnswers, specialists in media technology workflow. He has more than 30 years of experience in the media business, and has led large projects on every continent except for Antarctica (where he'd love to go some day). He is known as the father of the widely-used Broadcast eXchange Format (BXF) standard, and has led a wide array of industry-wide efforts over the years. With MediAnswers, Lennon works with major media organizations around the world on leading-edge media technology projects. He also served as Standards Director for SMPTE, where he is a Fellow and past award winner. In addition to co-chairing the 34CS Technology Committee, Lennon serves on several SMPTE Drafting Groups.

John Footen began his work in television 30 years ago. He attended New York University where he received degrees in film and TV production, as well as computer science. He quickly combined the disciplines and played leadership roles in multiple manufacturing companies in developing products that used computers in media applications such as nonlinear video editing, video servers, and more. During this period, the teams he led received patents and two technical Emmys for their work. Over the past ten years, Footen has moved into systems integration and consulting where he has an opportunity to address many of the real-world workflow issues seen across many types of media companies. He has pioneered the use of SOA (Service Oriented Architectures) in media, giving numerous educational talks and articles on the subject and originally co-chairing the FIMS (Framework for Interoperable Media Services) effort by the Advanced Media Workflow Association (AMWA) and the European Broadcasting Union (EBU). Footen has authored a book on SOA in Media and is a SMPTE member as well as a Senior Member of IEEE.

Annie Chang is the vice president of post-production technology for The Walt Disney Studios. Chang oversees the research and implementation of new technology into Disney's feature post-production and mastering pipelines through new file-based workflows and standards efforts. She chairs the Interoperable Master Format Working Group at SMPTE and represents Disney in the UHD Alliance as a board director. Prior to Disney, she spent six years at THX Ltd. as the senior engineer for the Digital Mastering Program and three years in DVD authoring and compression. Chang holds a B.S. in engineering technology from Texas A&M University.

title: Laser Projectors and the Future of Digital Cinema

Mark Clowes is a strategic product manager for digital cinema projection systems at Sony Professional Solutions Europe. He began his career in Sony's broadcast division where he held a number of engineering roles. For several years he was a product marketing manager and successfully established new tape formats in the factual programming and news production communities. He later went on to head a team to launch high-definition production equipment into the U.K. film and television sectors. Following a period with BBC Technology, Clowes rejoined Sony in the newly-established digital cinema business where he has been at the forefront of introducing their 4K projection systems. He holds an honours degree in communication engineering and an MBA from Aston Business School. Sony has a long history in laser development. Beginning with laser diode manufacturing in 1986, they became a leading supplier to the compact disc, digital videodisc, Blu-ray, and games console markets. They began high power laser diode development in 2003. In 2005 they demonstrated a 60,000 lm laser projection exhibit at the Aichi Expo onto a 50 m wide screen, and in 2012, they showed the viability of high frame rate 3D projection with a laser light source using advanced de-speckling techniques for high-quality images on a silver screen. While they have not yet released a laser-illuminated projector for cinema onto the market they have been actively investigating all of the options for large-screen laser projection with particular emphasis on solving the conundrum of combining the benefits of laser-illuminated projection within the economic constraints of cinema exhibition.

He holds a B.A. in physics and mathematics from Northwestern University and a Ph.D. in mathematics from the University of California.

Sheng Qu is a senior staff engineer at Dolby Laboratories, Inc., and manages Dolby Vision Pro Encoder and Dolby Vision consumer decoder deliverables. He has more than 13 years of engineering experience in the consumer video development, including more than seven years as tech lead in the Advanced Imaging Technology Department at Dolby Laboratories, Inc. Qu holds BSEE and an MSEE from Tsinghua University, and an M.S. in computer science from Iowa State University. Such systems have been implemented and deployed by companies such as QuickFire Networks (http://www.quickfirenetworks.com) and Kontron (http://www.kontron.com).

Chris Lennon is president and chief operating officer of MediAnswers, specialists in advertising and media workflow. He has more than 30 years of experience in the media business, leading large projects on every continent except for Antarctica. He is a past Standards Director for SMPTE, and is a SMPTE Fellow and award winner. In his spare time, he is an accomplished race car driver, and heads up a high performance driving program.

Harold S. Geller is chief growth officer at Advertising Digital Identification LLC (Ad-ID) a U.S.-based advertising-metadata system, the UPC code for Ads across all platforms, which is a joint venture of American Association of Advertising Agencies (4A's) and the Association of National Advertisers (ANA). Geller speaks and writes extensively regarding interoperability, digital workflow and metadata in advertising and is the co-author of six white papers on the subject. His advertising career spans more than 30 years, in the U.S. and Canada. He has worked in media buying/planning, account management, financial, and technology roles at MindShare, Ogilvy & Mather, and McCann Erickson, and the defunct Ted Bates and Foster Advertising. Geller is a graduate of radio and television broadcasting from Seneca College (Toronto, Ontario, Canada).

Clyde D. Smith is the senior vice president of new technologies for Fox Network Engineering and Operations. In this role, he supports broadcast and cable networks, production, and post production operating groups in addressing their challenges with new technologies focusing on standards, regulations and lab proof of concept testing and evaluation. Prior to joining Fox, he was senior vice president (SVP) of global broadcast technology and standards at Turner Broadcasting System, Inc. where he provided technical guidance for the company's domestic and international teams. He previously held positions as SVP of broadcast engineering research and development at Turner, SVP & chief technology officer at Speer Communications, and supervisor of communications design and development engineering for Lockheed Space Operations at the Kennedy Space Center. Smith also supported initiatives for Turner Broadcasting that were recognized by the Computer World Honors program with the 2005, 21st Century Achievement Award for Media Arts and Entertainment and a Technology and Engineering Emmy Award for Pioneering Efforts in the Development of Automated, Server-Based Closed Captioning Systems. In 2007 he received the SMPTE Progress Medal and 2008 he received the Storage Visions Conference Storage Industry Service Award.

Bruce Devlin has been working in the media industry for 30 years and oversees media technology in Dalet Digital Media Systems. Formerly the chief technology officer of AmberFin, the vice president of technology for Snell, and principal engineer at both Thomson in France and the BBC, Devlin has designed the gamut, from from ASICs to software algorithms. Best known for being @MrMXF, Devlin wrote the book and chaired the SMPTE working groups on the format.

Ken Rudman leads product marketing for NexGuard. He has previously headed product management for Technicolor Digital Content Delivery, and been active in product and program management for leading Internet startups Citysearch, Overture/Yahoo!, and Idealabs for the past 15 years.
Until Spring of 2015, Mathieu Bonenfant served as vice president, products and solutions for NexGuard, where he provided product management leadership for the NexGuard Forensic Watermarking products.

Mehmet Celik is senior research scientist and teamleader research at Civolution. He received a Ph.D. degree in the area of image watermarking from the University of Rochester, NY in 2004. He subsequently joined the Information and Systems Security Department, Philips Research, The Netherlands and in early 2008 moved to business unit content identification, which spun off as Civolution later in 2008. At Philips and later at Civolution, Mehmet has focused on theoretical and practical aspects of audio and video watermarking and fingerprinting (near duplicate search) algorithms. His research resulted in various patents, patent applications, scientific publications, and is utilized in commercial products. His wider research interests include multimedia security, content indexing, and retrieval, image and video processing, and cryptography.

Joe Daniel is responsible for defining customer-specific solutions for the delivery of high-value video content through Internet and cable/satellite, as well as PreRelease workflows at Civolution. Daniel interfaces with service providers and equipment manufacturers to help integrate Civolution watermarking technology into their systems. Prior to joining Civolution, Daniel was an engineering manager at DivX Inc.

Jaap Haitsma started his career in 1997 as a research scientist at Philips Research. For seven years, he developed algorithms for watermarking and fingerprinting of audio and video. Based on the output of this research, a business unit was formed at Philips to commercialize these algorithms, and in 2004 Haitsma joined this unit as chief technology officer (CTO) to setup its own R&D department. This business unit within Philips was spun out as Civolution in 2008. Currently, he serves as CTO of the NexGuard group at Civolution and leads R&D.

Jean-Paul Panis is senior software engineer and manages the PayTV and DCI development team at Civolution NexGuard Labs, based in France. He has worked on defining and implementing watermarking solutions for more than ten years. With Dutch roots, he has studied at the University of Twente, The Netherlands, and holds a master's degree in computer science.

Frederik Zilly is head of the Computational Imaging and Algorithms group in the Moving Picture Department of Fraunhofer IIS in Erlangen, Germany. He received a diploma degree in physics from Free University of Berlin, and a Ph.D. degree in computer science from Technical University, Berlin. Before joining Fraunhofer IIS, he was scientific project manager in the Immersive Media and 3D Video group in the Image Processing Department at Fraunhofer HHI in Berlin where he was involved in several German and European research projects related to 3DTV. In this function, Zilly was mainly responsible for the development of the stereoscopic analyzer (STAN) and coordinated the activities of the Fraunhofer HHI concerning the European research project MUSCADE. Zilly has been honored for his work on the assistance system STAN (Stereoscopic Analyzer) with the Award for Outstanding Merit in Young Scientists, the Rudolf Urtel Prize 2011. He serves as reviewer for different international conferences and journals. His research focus lies in multicamera image processing algorithms.

Matthias Ziegler received a diploma in electrical engineering from Friedrich-Alexander University Erlangen, Germany, 2012. He has been with Fraunhofer IIS since that time and is working on algorithms for computational imaging. His research focus is on light-field production workflows and algorithms, including disparity estimation, plenoptic cameras, and high-dynamic range.

Joachim Keinert, chief scientist at Fraunhofer IIS, has diplomas from both the University of Stuttgart, Germany, and Télécom ParisTech (formerly ENST) in Paris, France. In 2009, he received a Ph.D. with honors in the domain of electronic system level design for image processing applications. His research interests focus on high-dynamic range video capture and processing as well as light-field imaging and depth acquisition. Keinert actively participates in the JPEG compression standardization where he co-chairs the Systems group. He is experienced in development of hard- and software for image processing in both embedded and general-purpose systems. Currently, he leads several image processing projects in the context of light-field imaging and 3D capturing.

Michael Schöberl received a diploma in electrical engineering with honors in 2006 from the University of Erlangen-Nuremberg. He then joined the Fraunhofer IIS and started to work on high-quality imaging systems in the Electronic Imaging department. In 2007, he joined the Chair of Multimedia Communications and Signal Processing at the University of Erlangen-Nuremberg to continue the research on theory and algorithms for high-end camera systems in a close cooperation with Fraunhofer IIS. In 2013, he received a Ph.D. with honors in electrical engineering for his work on digital cameras. He is currently working as a chief scientist in the Electronic Imaging department at Fraunhofer IIS, with a focus on research and innovation management.

Siegfried Foessel is head of the Moving Picture Technologies department at the Fraunhofer IIS in Erlangen and spokesman of the Fraunhofer digital cinema alliance. He was responsible for projects such as the camera development ARRI D20/D21, the DCI (Digital Cinema Initiatives) certification test plan, and the JPEG 2000 standardization for digital cinema. Foessel is a member of various standardization bodies and organizations such as SMPTE, Fernseh-und Kinotechische Gesellschaft e.V. (FKTG), the International Organization for Standardization (ISO), and the German Institute for Standardization (Deutsches Institut für Normung e.V [DIN]). He became a SMPTE Fellow in 2014. Foessel was the 2014 recipient of the Josef-von-Fraunhofer award for the development of easyDCP, a tool for creating and playback of Digital Cinema Packages. In 2014, he was elected president of the FKTG, the German equivalent to SMPTE.

James Stellpflug has more than 20 years of industry experience in facility design and integration, mobile satellite communication, and mobile TV production, and has designed and operated new digital mobile uplinks for multi-affiliate networks with both CBS and ABC. Stellpflug has been with EVS Broadcast Equipment since 2000. During his tenure with EVS, he has been involved with teams that have earned awards including a Technical Emmy for EVS Super Slow Motion systems, as well as a Sports Emmy for Olympics coverage. Stellpflug holds a Bachelor of Science degree in broadcast technology management, emphasis in engineering from the University of Wisconsin, Platteville, and is a member of SMPTE, SBE and PMI.

Stephane Houet leads product management for EVS in the category of multimedia solutions, with a focus on the C-Cast cloud enabled platform of tools. He has a degree from Haute Ecole Mosane d'Enseignement supérieur in Liege, Belgium, and certifications for Amazon Web Services architecture and accreditation.

Yoshiaki Shibata is a chair of SMPTE TC-30MR Study Group (SG) UMID Applications. In 2001 Shibata met the UMID for the first time at Sony Corp. Since then, he was heavily involved and played a crucial role in the development and implementation of the UMID applications, initially for the traditional professional VTRs (HDCAM™) and then for the modern file-based media products (XDCAM™), during which he was fascinated by the potential key roles of UMID in the future file-based media production environment. At the end of 2010, Shibata left Sony, and later, founded metaFrontier.jp, LLC, Japan's first independent consulting firm specifically for the media and metadata technology. With his well-received presentation at the SMPTE 2011 Annual Technical Conference, regarding the challenges and solutions to realize an ever-envisioned UMID application in practice as a trigger, Shibata joined the SMPTE Standard Community and established the SG under TC-30MR in 2012. So far, the SG has already standardized the UMID Application Principles as the latest RP 205 for which Shibata is awarded by the ITE (The Institute of Image Information and Television Engineers, Japan), has successfully developed the UMID Resolution Protocol, which is now under SMPTE standardization, and has intensively explored the promising UMID applications specifically for the MXF technology whose deliverable is now made available online. Shibata is a member of SMPTE, ITE, and MPTE (Motion Picture and Television Engineering Society of Japan).

Heiko Sparenberg received a Diploma degree in computer science in 2004 and a Master's degree in 2006. He joined Fraunhofer IIS in Erlangen as a software engineer in 2006. Sparenberg is currently head of the Digital Cinema group at Fraunhofer, responsible for several software developments, including the easyDCP software suite for digital cinema. In 2015, he received a Ph.D. degree for his work, with focus on improved data workflows in a professional movie post-production using scalable media codecs including JPEG 2000 and H264.

Al Kovalick has worked in the field of media infrastructure and file-based workflows for the past 25 years. Previously, he was a digital systems designer and technical strategist for Hewlett-Packard (HP). While at HP, he was the principal architect of HP's first video-on-demand server. Following HP, from 1999 to 2004, he was the chief technology officer of Pinnacle Systems. More recently, he served at Avid Technology as a strategist and Avid Fellow. In 2012, Kovalick founded Media Systems Consulting in Silicon Valley specializing in media infrastructure and related technologies. Kovalick is an active speaker, educator, and author. He has presented more than 50 papers at industry conferences worldwide. He holds 13 US patents. He is the author of the book Video Systems in an IT Environment (2009, 2nd ed). Kovalick has a BSEE degree from San Jose State University and an MSEE degree from the University of California at Berkeley. He is a SMPTE Fellow, Director of Education, recipient of the SMPTE David Sarnoff Medal and member of the Tau Beta Pi engineering honor society.

Thomas Edwards is vice president, engineering & development at Fox Networks Engineering & Operations, where he has worked on advanced technology projects such as mobile DTV, 3D, and the Fox network satellite distribution system. Before joining Fox in 2007, he was senior manager, Interconnection Engineering for the PBS Interconnection Replacement Office, where he was responsible for the engineering planning of the PBS Next Generation Interconnection System (NGIS). He also has had significant experience with streaming media production and delivery at the Internet service provider DIGEX and the IP-over-satellite company Cidera. Edwards has contributed to the Report of the SMPTE Task Force on 3D to the Home, the NAB Engineering Handbook, and the SMPTE/EBU/VSF Joint Task Force on Networked Media. He holds a master's degree in electrical engineering from the University of Maryland, and is a member of Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineering (IEEE) and a SMPTE Fellow.

Michael Bany is the president of DVBLink, Inc., and has been a consulting network engineer for Fox Sports the past 15 years. While at Fox he has been involved with the engineering and support of their extensive private line video and data network. He has been the chairperson or contributed to various Video Services Forum Activity Groups, including Studio Video over IP, Test and Measurement, SMPTE 2022 over SONET/SDH, Hitless SMPTE 2022, COP3VBR, HBRAV-IP, QoE, etc. Before joining Fox, Bany was a telecommunications engineer with LDDS Worldcom and did Enterprise network consulting for various firms. Bany holds a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering with a minor in computer science from Iowa State University, and is a member of SMPTE and VSF.

Nikolaus Kerö received a master's degree in communication engineering with distinction from the Vienna University of Technology, after which he led the ASIC design division at the university's Institute of Industrial Electronics, successfully managing numerous research projects and industry collaborations. His research activities centered on distributed systems design, especially highly accurate and fault-tolerant clock synchronization. In 2001, he co-founded Oregano Systems Design & Consulting Ltd. as a university spin-off. As well as offering embedded systems design services to customers, Oregano transferred research results into a complete product suite for highly accurate clock synchronization under the brand name syn1588, for which Kerö manages both development and marketing. He is an active member of the IEEE 1588 standardization committee and the SMPTE 32NF standards group and holds frequent seminars on clock synchronization both for industry and academia.

Thomas Kernen is a technical leader in Cisco's Service Provider Video Software and Solutions (SPVSS) architecture team. His main area of focus is defining architectures for transforming the broadcast industry to an all IP video infrastructure. Kernen is a member of the IEEE Communications and Broadcast Societies, SMPTE, and the Royal Television Society (RTS). He is active within a number of trade and industry organizations including the Digital Video Broadcasting (DVB) Project, the SMPTE Standards Committees and the European Broadcasting Union (EBU) working groups.

Tobias S. Müller received a bachelor's' degree in electronic engineering and a master's degree in embedded systems from the University of Applied Science in Vienna. In 2013, he obtained a master's degree for his thesis “Optimization of the Control Algorithm for an IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol Engine,” which focuses on his main field of expertise: clock synchronization in distributed, asynchronous computer systems. He is currently employed by Oregano Systems as software and system engineer and works on complex projects in the field of high precision clock synchronization. In 2014, Müller started his second master's degree program in software engineering. He is working on his master's thesis on automatic error detection and correction in large clock synchronization networks.

Martin Schimandl studied information technology at the University of Applied Sciences in Wiener Neustadt; his master thesis focused on optimizing hardware based Ethernet packet scanning engines for efficient PTP implementations. In 2009, Schimandl joined Oregano Systems where is he a currently working as a senior embedded software design engineer with special focus on clock synchronization. His main areas of interest are efficient software design for resource limited embedded systems and fully automated multi-node software test systems. Schimandl is responsible for the complete IT infrastructure of the company as well. In his spare time, he enjoys reading novels of Jasper Fforde and contributes to various open source projects.

Jörg Huschke is a master researcher in the radio protocol research group at Ericsson GmbH, Germany. He is with Ericsson Research at the Ericsson Eurolab since 1997. He has been task leader in European research projects DRiVE and WINNER, where he led the work on estimating the spectrum requirements for the ITU IMT-2000 and IMT.advanced family of systems towards WRC-07. Since 2008, he has been working towards 3GPP standardization of MBMS for LTE and on its performance evaluation. Furthermore, he is active in the EBU Strategic Program Cooperating Terrestrial Networks (mobile subgroup). Since 2016 he is also leading the radio interface team in the German research project KoI on evolved LTE and 5G based wireless communication in factory automation. He received the diploma degree in electrical engineering from the Georg-Simon-Ohm University of Applied Sciences in Nuremberg, Germany in 1993.
